NOTICE TO CI Tull EDITOR of "The Examiner" invites corre spondence on all subjects of public interest.
LET-r- sus should be brief and pointed. Their object must be to impart or seek information, not abuse.
IRRESPONDENTS. LETTERS must in all cases be accompanied by the name and address of the writer. Commuyicsrioxs received early in the week— except urgent matters—can always be given the best attention.

div.head: FOOD ADULTERATION.
div.p: FOOD ADULTERATION.

Sir,—Food adulteration is one of the most heinous and guilty practices to be found in Eng- land to-day. It is really an act of national treachery. The soldier who betrays his country is hardly more guilty than the man who sup- plies poor people with cumulative poisons under the mask of food. There is no palliation for a crime of such enormity. This odious feature of present-day commerce may be traced to its root in falsely-directed capital. "Riches are a power like that of electricity, acting only through in- equalities or negations of itself." When the electric current leaves its appointed course, fatality and ruin ensue. So with capital. Thera is nothing more fatal to the serenity, morality, , and nobility of a nation than misapplied capital. J.C.

div.head: MR. HAROLD SMITH ON HONOURS.
div.p: MR. HAROLD SMITH ON HONOURS.

Sir,—Being one of the many Liberals present, who helped to swell the small number at Mr. Harold Smith's meeting at Parr Hall last Friday, I noticed he faithfully reproduced (as usual) his famous brother's brilliant sarcasm (delivered in Liverpool about a fortnight ago), concerning the 1,600 or 1,700 honours and titles this Government have bestowed since 1906. Of course, his argument means that they have all fallen to the Liberal side; he makes no mention of the scores and hundreds of knighthoods and decorations given to men of science, civil ser- vants, actors, &c., which are included in his total, and last, but not least, the "Tories" (of all people) accepting peerages and Privy Coun- cillorships, including Mr. F. E. Smith. It is a very good point for a debating society, but one would expect somettang else from the Member for Warrington for the time being, and one who claims something of the mantle of Beaconsfield. Your readers will remember Mr. Bonar Law 'accused Mr. Asquith of corruption, .and asked for a list of the appointments made in the lifetime of this Government. This was given him, together with a list of Tory appoint- ments for a corresponding time previous (at the request of a Liberal Member). But we have not heard of any vote of censure; nothing of the kind, although Mr. Asquith offered the Tory leader time for discussion. It is one thing for Mr. Smith to come down to tell the faithful supporters these horrible things, but it is quite another when he is confronted and his leader asked to formulate a charge across the floor of the House of Commons. R. A. H.

• CANADIAN CONDITIONS AND PROSPECTS. Sir,—As you are aware the situation in Canada at toe present tune is occupying some atientiou in the public mind, and as i nave been twice on extended tours to that country within the past six months my impressions of the immediate prospect there may be of some interest to your readers. On account amy work for the organisation with which I have the honour to be associated for the past ten years, it has been necessary that I should study Canadian conditions and affairs minutely, and, notwithstanding some gloomy reports in circu- lation regarding the Dominion, from the ob- servations I was able to make and the opinion I obtained from reliable sources during my last visit, I am confirmed in ray optimism as to the Canadian future. The general depression in monetary circles has no doubt been reflected with some severity in Canada, and to an extent retarded industrial enterprise, causing a cer- tain amount of slackness in the urban centres, emphasised greatly by the advent of winter; but against this there has to be placed the fact that the past season's wheat harvest was a most bountiful one, and that the call for increased agricultural activity has never been more pro- nounced. This is to be accounted for by the domestic demand for a greater food supply, at- tendant on the rapid growth of the population, and the removal of fiscal barriers on the U.S.A. frontier in conjunction with the gradual exten- sion of transport facilities permitting of easier access to the world's markets. The necessity and demand for the products of mixed farming are becoming more and more insistent, and the opportunities for agriculturists with ideas are maturing meanwhile. The Salvation Army has always discouraged the rush to the towns and cities of Canada and endeavoured to secure as many settlers as possible for the land. It might also claim to be doing its share in diverting to more productive fields the stream of our own rural population the congestion that causes so many and grievous social complications. Already we have a large application from Cana- dian sources for agricultural help. In regard to the general demand for labour in the Dominion I might summarise my estimate as follows :- 1. *orkers for the land skilled and unskilled will be wanted in greater numbers than ever this spring. 2. The man of adaptibility and pioneering in- stincts, with only his thews and sinews for capital, will always find abundant opportunity. 3. Small capitalists prepared to cultivate the land near one of the large cities or to settle in or around one of the smaller growing townships out West, will have plenty of scope for build- ing up his own fortunes and giving his family a chance. He will also have an opportunity of participating in the work of community ing, and perpetuating the best traditions of the British Empire in his new cosmopolitan stir- roundings. 4. Opportunities are not restricted to the West. In the Eastern Provinces—New Bruns- wick and Nova Scotia—a movement of indus- trial development and expansion is in progress, which should prove attractive to new settlers. 5. For artisans and mechanics, owing to reasons already stated, there may be a limited demand in the coming year, but at the present moment it is impossible to form a reliable fore- cast. With the advent of spring I am inclined to think the position may change. It may, however, be worse before it is better, or it may slowly and quietly revive. Adopting the motto of the late General Booth —"The British Empire for the British"—the Emigration Department of the Salvation Army guides the surplus population of the British Isles to the wing's Dominions overseas. it gives disinterested advice to all contemplating going abroad, guarantees employment to every man willing and able to work on the land, and in most cases insures against unemployment. The resources of its organisation are especially adapted to the needs of women, for whom there is a continuous demand in the Dominion as domestic servants, and during the spring_and summer months weekly conducted parties are arranged for their convenience, while in all the . important centres of Canada Army hostels have been established, where they receive a warm welcome, and are initiated into the life of their adopted country under sympathetic guidance. DAVID C. LAMB, Commissioner. The Salvation Army Emigration Offices, 122, Queen Victoria-street, London, E.C., January 12th, lal4.

div.head: FREEDOM FELLOWSHIP DISCUSSIONS.
div.p: FREEDOM FELLOWSHIP DISCUSSIONS.

Sir,—Will you kindly permit me space to pro- test against the action of the " Freedom Fellow- ship" in deleting discussion at a meeting held under their auspices last Monday night? Syndicalists generally wax eloquent in their denunciation of political opponents, who omit discussion because of the proverbial train to catch, &c. When we consider its name, coupled with its revolutionary aims, and its vague and indeterminate policy, a discussion of the pros and cons becomes not only desirable, but neces- sary. I hope the "Freedom Fellowship" will justify their name by allowing their advertised discussion, that exponents and opponents may naturally benefit thereby. GILBERT MANION. 49, Folly-lane.

ALCOHOLIC DRINK : " A DIVERSITY OF OPINION" AT SANKEY BRIDGES. Sir,—l was greatly surprised on reading in your last week's issue the discussion which fol- lowed Mr. T. Lowe's lecturette at the Sankey ingedsomagee- oßnrei whoges Ardeualltl yS cbheol ioelv. e sI ifinn tdhtihs aetntl geri tee that in some industries nothing but ale will 'keep a man fit for his work, and that such com- modities as tea, coffee, cocoa, after having been tried, are found to be of no use. I should like to be informed what those Tndustries are, for I have a fairly wide practical experience of all kinds of laborious and fatigu- ing work. After having tried to keep up with beer, I proved it failed, and I will guarantee that there are thousands who are not total ab- stainers who will prove that continually drink- ing beer will not keep a man fit for work. I give this challenge to the person making the ridiculous statement. He can choose his own trade and put two men to work at it. One.shall have beer when he feels thirsty, and the other shall be a teetotaler and drink either tea, coffee or cocoa. Let each man work for the same length of time, so many hours—l would suggest 12 hours. Then let both men be examined by a doctor as to their physical condition, and I think the member that made the statement will very soon lose the delusion he has in his head that in some Industries the work makes ,heavy drinking unavoidable.
J. W. BRADLEY. 12, (landy's-terrace, Lythgoes-lane.

div.head: INCREASING RENTS.
div.p: INCREASING RENTS.

Sir,—The cause of Mr. Rathbone's " tired and languid feeling" cannot,. I am -sure, be laid at my door. I admit that my own feelings have been anything but pleasurable, but, then, in these days a property owner has, no right to expect otherwise. lam content to allow the eulogy of his own abilities to pass unchallenged, for 1 know that some measure of success, real or apparent, is necessary to encourage a corre- spondent. Most readers who have followed Mr. Rathbone closely must now realise that the "People's Budget" has missed fire; has, in fact, become an additional asset to the "bloated landlord," while the golden shower which was to reward the confidences of the poor is about to fall to the feet of the idle rich! All the dust-throwing in the world will not blind the eyes of the worker to the fact that the "rare and refreshing fruit" has rotted on the tree, or been gathered earlier in the day by those "artful dodgers," the dukes and the aristocracy. Yet the cry was "Tax all these, but spare us !" How many more attempts are to be made, and how many failures are to be recorded by the representatives of the democracy? • The Free Trader says all taxes have to be borne by the consumer. This is the case against Tariff Reform, yet, when it domes to taxing land, the duke, the earl, and the aristocracy, are said to pay. House rents are going up; building has stopped. Is this another instance of the con- sumer paying the tax, or is it due to increased rates, cost of materials, and dear money? Mr. Rathbone can answer as he likes. He says I have evaded the point, and he repeats the ques- tion: "Is the landlord entitled to charge 6s. 4d. a week for a house that was previously rented at 55.?" On the assumptioa that no increase in the assessment takes place before March 19th, 1915, ss. 9d. ought to satisfy present needs. Therefore the 6s. 4d., as I said before, will come in force on the date the new valuation takes place. The question resolves itself into what is a reasonable and fair profit. The meaning of "reasonable" and " fair " has been so mis- interpreted of late that legislation has stepped in to safeguard the people's interests. Consider the dividends paid by most companies. Do the directors consider whether it is a fair and reasonable profit they charge their customers? Consider Brunner, Mond's, who pay 27 per cent.? Maypole, deferred 160 per cent.; Lever Bros., 15 per cent. If this is reasonable, why is there so much crying out against the paltry 51 per cent. of the property owner? It requires no skill to see that new property pays less than six per cent. Can the landlord afford to reduce his rents, or.should the manufacturer lower his per- centage of profit, either by reducing the price of his goods or paying more wages? The number of property owners in Warrington is less than seven hundred. In Oldham there is said to be ten thousand. There can only be two reasons, apart from population,. to account for the vast difference. Either 'the People are more thrifty in Oldham, or the return for the money invested is greater than it is in Warrington. The rents here are very low, but when they are raised to the level of those "sit and do nothing shares" tenants will commence to buy their own houses, and participate in the wonderful harvest being reaped by the landlord. Mr. Rathbone writes: "Then I have another item of interest for Mr. Smith. I understand there is a kind of rent 'auction' being tried in Warrington, and it would be interesting to have Mr. Smith's views." I have not heard of this method of letting houses before, but I fail to ' see any reason why the owner of property should ed not be allow to adopt this method of disposing of his houses. under""auction" c ti o the system. Most otsthapte°tphleey go oamto Personhlly, I see nothing in the impres I make g d bargains. At any rate, they have a hand •in making the bargain. goingaueti ont to Referring to the manufacturers. Mr. Rathbone thaarse r h se use d i s ptrhoevi Vw? works says "Mr. Smith has not produced a shred of evidence to prove his statements." How much ask i night taad d inn: Do y minanourfdaecr h - that it may take eight g ours to do what took four hours before niht g turns were introduced? Ought the manufacturers to pay more rates for the privilege? Then there is the "Tenants' Defence L • eague. My attention is specially directed towards this organisation. Mr. Rathbone throws out thh statement like he used the Chancellor's name, but my answer to tl •ns is: When rents in War- rington are raised to the same level as rents in Leeds, the existence of the "League" may be as necessary to safeguard the interests of the tenants as the trade union is necessary to safe- guard the interests of the workmen from the said-to-be-grasping manufacturers. Mr. Philip Snowden said: " Competition.is the wrangling of savages round a table at which they
J.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAYS FEBRUARY 7, 1914

might sit in peace." The property owner has recognised this, and is emulating the principle that has brought so much success to the Socialist. The United States Steel Trust made a profit in 1906 of £31,500,000, and the total wage bill for that year was less than £30,000,000; Messrs. J. P. Coates, Ltd., made a profit of £3,500,000 in one year. If Mr. Rathbone is out for reform, here is a wide field for his abilities. Here, at his door, lie vast resources for future taxation. Wealth that Aladdin never dreamed of, wealth that makes the tale of the "Arabian Nights" sink into insignificance. GEO. SMITH. The Limes, Orford.

AUSTRALIA AND THE DRINK QUESTION. Sir,—The following comments relative to the trend of events in Australia may interest some of your readers. With regard to New Zealand, one of the things that matter at the next Igeneral election will be the temperance ques- tion. A strenuous effort is being made by the supporters of no-licence and prohibition to carry the day. There is no denying the keen struggle for victory. In New Zealand education re- ceives annually £900,000 of the people's money. The public bar obtains over £3,000,000. Less than £1,000,000 is spent in making industrial efficiency, and more than £3,000,000 in unmaking it. Australia spends in round figures £15,000,000 per year on alcohol. There are plenty of people who recognise the traffic has no claim upon an enlightened populace. New Zealand is tackling the problem with zest. Several of the Austra- lian States are getting a move on, and the mag- nitude,of the problem must not be allowed to induce hesitation. For several general elec- tions the people of New Zealand have had rising majorities in favour of prohibition. The pres- ent law on the Statute Book provides for a three- fifths majority, before the day is gained. The history of the three-fifths majority is briefly this: In 1893 Sir H. Stout introduced a direct Veto Bill on behalf of the N.Z. Alliance, which provided that the issue of licences or no licences should be determined by a majority of those who vote. A majority in the Hoilse voted for the Bill, upon which it was superseded by an unsatisfactory Government measure, requiring three-fifths to carry its very limited form of no Licence, which reached the Statute Book. At a Wellington public meeting in connection with the succeeding Alliance annual meeting, Dr. Newman, moved that no Licensing Act would recognise the right of the people if it did not give them the power by a majority of votes cast to determine for themselves whether the traffic shall or shall not exist in their respec- tive localities. This resolution was unanimously carried. In 1895 the Government introduced another Bill, which became law, extending the popular vote to all kinds of liquor licences, but still embody- ing the three-fifths principle. A strong, but un- successful attempt was again made in committee of the House, vigorously supported by the tem- perance party outside, to substitute the simple majority rule. Perhaps the powers that be think a three-fifths majority will ensure sta- bility and prevent the pendulum of public opinion swinging backwards and forwards. In any case it is a! handicap. Should success even- tuate, however, the other side will be faced with a three-fifths Majority in order to recover their position. To attempt to check drunkenness prohibition ' orders are taken out against certain individuals. It is a punishable offence for a person prohibited to obtain intoxicating drink from any person whatsoever; or to enter licensed premises, and for any person whatsoever to eupply, the pro- hibited person with any intoxicating drink. The order may be obtained privately, on application to a magistrate by any person wishing to be pro- hibited; may be made by a magistrate against , any person who has been three times convicted for "drunkenness in six Months; may be granted by a magistrate presiding at any open court when evidence is conclusive that any person by excessive drinking of liquor mis-spends, wasted, or lessens his or her estate or greatly injures his or her health, &c. An order has a currency of twelve months and is renewable. I met people in New Zealand who were high and dry Tories in England, and out there had developed quite Radical tendencies. Perhaps the environment had something to do with it. or the ocean breezes had cleared the brain of cob-webs en route. The fact remains, numbers of people do change. Neither the Common- wealth of Australia nor New Zealand permits the past to be their gaoler. In the march of time people outgrow laws that in former days were expedient and defensible. Our institutions are but "the tents of a night, to be stricken whenever truth puts the bugle to her lips" and sounds a march to higher level of living. There are numbers of social and political questions demanding earnest consideration both here and oversea. Reciprocity, of ideas for mutual wel- fare must be right. A word re emigration in conclusion. There appears to be room for hundreds of thousands in Australia and tens of thousands ill New Zea- land. The recent Dominions Commission. with Lord Emmott:' as chairman, endorse that. Clash- ing of interests may occur here and there:tut a common-sense policy and right judgment will ensure minimum of friction. The dream of a white Australia will be realised if the white man's ear is not deaf to the call of empty spaces. Otherwise the yellow man may come, and rightly so. However, by degrees the fron- tiers of settlement are being pushed onward. pioneers blaze the track that the broadway of commerce may follow later- and new territory thus won for harvest. THOS. H. FORD.

div.head: Some Conflicting Traits in Individuality and in Personality.
div.p: Some Conflicting Traits in Individuality and in Personality.
AN ADULT SCHOOL TOPIC.

Conflicting traits which exist in the same person proved the basis of an interesting lectur- ette delivered to the Sankey Bridges Men's Adult School on Sunday. The lecturer was Mr. John Monks, and he-entitled the theme "Individu- ality and personality."

Mr. Monks said that, judging by the way in which the words were often used, it seemed that they were interchangeable terms. Yet, whilst admitting that the line dividing the two was very fine, there was a distinction. This could be illustrated by taking some well-known char- acter. It would be found in some cases that there was "a subtle, illusive something" about a person which was eminently attractive even when we were aware of flaws in the individual character which attracted. In other cases the reverse would be the order. This personality seemed to be beyond the control of the person possessing it. With regard to individuality, there was a difference, in so far as its expression was controlled by the individual. Yet it was not quite clear whether this individuality was influenced by such factors as heredity and environment, or whether it was complete in itself. If the former, then the question arose whether man was altogether responsible for his character. If the latter, then man was a self- contained unit. This would lead us to the con- clusion that man was truly selfish, and that there was no such thing as unselfishness. In the subsequent discussion there was much difference of opinion as to whether individuality and personality were not one and the same thing, and in the flow of thought many good things were said, showing much philosophical acumen.

In the Bible lesson on "The Foremost Group," Mr. Barnard, who introduced, pointed out the prominent characteristics of the chief disciples, expressing the view that Christ favoured them not because they possessed knowledge or bril- liancy, but because they were loyal. The President,--in summing up, said the "Foremost Group" would be best understood if we realised that we were dealing with ordin- ary men. These men Went through a process of development, a preparation for their work in the world.

div.head: LONGFORD.
div.p: LONGFORD.

Mr. F. Leigh opened what proved to be a very interesting discussion on the "Foremost Group of Disciples" on Sunday. The speaker said that the three disciples were ordinary working fishermen, and in their training in the School of Christ they were under the same conditions as the others. The speaker strongly urged that although the object and principles of our schools were that we should recognise that we were all placed uponn, a basis of equality as- men, yet we should be open-rainded and eager to learn from our fellows.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH MEN'S.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH MEN'S.

There was an attendance of twenty men to hear an interesting paper by Mr. W. Hewitt on the life of Thomas Edward, the Scots' naturalist. The lecturette was entitled "A Successful Life," and the lecturer showed how, despite constant poverty and circumstances that would have crushed most men, Thomas Edward made a name for himself as a profound student of Natural History. The fact was recalled, for example, that no less than three collections were sold by the naturalist to enable him to pay his way. As a boy he was engaged in factory work before he had entered his teens, and his great joy was to be working on night shifts, when lie used the daylight for studying birds, beasts and insects. Only in later years could he read and write, so that he was entirely self-taught, so far as Nature was concerned. It was shown that Edward received public recognition even from scientific men, who ought to have acknowledged his genius. This is not the first time that the school has studied the lives of poor men, who gave a wealth of genius and Industry to the world. In the discussion the thought was brought out that probably much was lost to the community through the lack of opportunity to men of original minds. The Bible /esson was on the inner circle of the disciples-.--Deter, James and John. The members joined freely in the discussion On the qualities needed in disciples as shown in these three Apostles. The committee of the school was able to report a healthy condition of affairs. The roord has been lately made far more comfortable through the labours of members themselves, and the financial position is quite satisfactory. During ensuing Sundays lecturettes' topics n elrindg i e Ibsen, Woolman, Dickens, Lowell, Art and Reli- gion, Wonders of Nature, Co-operation, and Trade Unionism.

div.head: ACADEMY-STREET MEN'S.
div.p: ACADEMY-STREET MEN'S.

- On Sunday morning Mr. David P. Boyd con- tinued his lecture on "India," to an augmented school, including members of the Women's School, to whom his portrayals of woman's easy life, the native woman's love of striking yet wonderful blend of colours in their dresses, and the engagement of reliable native night-watch were particularly interesting. The vivid and lucid description, however, of how the Parsees, llindoos and Mohammedans dispose of their dead by burning—or partly burning—or expos- ing in the "Hanging Gardens" for carrion, or throwing into the rivers for crocodiles and alligators, or the burial without coffins, sup- plied a striking contrast.

- India, however, is a land of learning and skilled craftsmanship. The children are brought up from infancy in the trades of their fathers, and they are wonderfully dexterous at an early age in modelling even while at play in the streets. Superstition is still rife. The Indians are a race of philosophers; they never hurry, but their work is permanent, not shoddy or jerry-built; and as an example of Eastern work the speaker alluded to Joseph's granary, which is still extant in Egypt. The Indians are far in advance of us in the study of psychology, and their jugglery and legerdemain—in which cer- tain families specialise—are marvellous in the extreme.

div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
MONDAY. Before the Mayor and a full Bench of magistrates. . _

A SHERLOCK HOLMES.—A particularty clever capture of two alleged deserters was effected by, Detective-Sergeant Reddington in a /odging- house in Stanley-street. He noticed that they were wearing army boots, and when he spoke to them they said they had bought the boots at a second-hand shop. Then he pulled away the white scarfs around their necks, and disclosed the fact that they 'wore 'army shirts. They then stated that they had deserted from the 2nd Battalion King's Own Scottish Borderers, sta- tioned at Dublin. The men, John Henry Holt (19), a native of Oldham, and Norman Gordon (20), a native of Scotland, were remanded pend- ing the arrival of an escort from the battalion at Dublin,

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.

THE TREATMENT OF ANIMAL DISEASES. In his recent speeches in the country Mr. Runciman suggested a new line of attack upon animal diseases, says " The Times." He indi- cated his intention of striking at the root of the scourges by instituting an efficient veterinary service of investigation instead of persevering with what appears sometimes to be the hope- less task of extirpating them by compulsory notification and slaughter. The latter proce- dure has proved effective in dealing with very serious plagues of a certain class, such as pleuro- pneumonia and foot-and-mouth disease, but it has failed to rid the country of certain .others, and is out of the question with the esser but vexatious diseases. Sheep scab, parasitic mange, and glanders all show a steady and continuous decrease. In the case of swine fever, however, things have gone on from year to year in the same monotonous -course, entire piggeries being destroyed and the movement of pigs restricted over wide areas without material influence upon the annual number of outbreaks. It will be welcome news to pig owners that the Board of Agriculture are dissatisfied with the ineffective struggle, and that they think it possible that the plague cannot be exterminated by existing methods. The new policy of the President of the Board includes as its central feature the provision of an efficient veterinary service, a service thor- oughly equipped for research, educational and administrative work. The idea will have the approval of stockowners of all classes. 1

THE KING AND THE LABOURER. A Royal Example to Farmers. The King has set an admirable example in endeavouring to improve the conditions of the labourers on his Norfolk estate, and 'men of all parties will applaud. On the Royal farm itself the terms of employment have always been generous; but what has now been done is to fix certain relatively generous minima, and to ar- range that these shall be observed not only on the King's farm, but on all those of which he is the landlord. His tenants, it appears, have readily co-operated in this reform, and its es- tablishment is now settled. It secures for every labourer on the estate a Saturday half-holiday, continuity of employment, rain or shine, and a minimum wage of 16s.—a minimum about 2s. above what is a common wage in the neighbour- hood, though from 4s. to 6s. below what is paid in nearly all cases on the King's own farm. ja this matter, says "The Daily Chronicle," the King continues the policy of his father, who was never tired of trying to make Sandringham in all respects a model estate. He is not the only important country landlord to take a lead this winter in improving the conditions of the labourers on his land; but he has gone as far as any, and the prominence of his Royal example should give a healthy impetus to a movement which has every Pnosible justification, and none too many active followers.

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.

In the Royal Horticultural Society's tests last year (1 btrawberries, the following are recom- mended : British Queen, fruit large, 'excellent flavour, crop heavy, ripe July 5; Connoisseur, best flavoured of all, ripe June 26; Cropper, large fruit, white flesh, excellent crop, ripe June 23; Progress, fine late variety; Rival, small fruit, heavy crop. Overcrowded growths of winter jasmine may be removed during the next few weeks. A, top dressing of manure may be given, and will greatly help the plant for next flowering season. Vacant lands in the vegetable garden will be greatly improved by being thrown up in ridges. It is the best way of getting rid of insect pests, as the frost can penetrate through the roughly thrown-up soil.

A BEAUTIFUL EARLY CROCUS. In some sheltered spots the flowers of the charming crocus Sieberi are already shelving, and, given a few sunny days, will soon be fully open; and so reveal the beauty of the orange- coloured stigmata. This colour makes • a fine contrast to the soft lilac hue of the petals, which, it must be admitted, are rather easily damaged by bad weather. However, it is a crocus that we would not like to be without, coming as it does in the wake of the snowdrops and winter aconites.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 7, 1914.

div.head: COMMANDER.
div.p: THE COMMANDER.

Commander Evans, CB., RN., will be greeted by a huge audience when he begins his lecture on Captain Scott's Expedition in Warrington next Saturday. This will be no novel experi- ence for the gallant officer, because he has already spoken in most of the large cities of the United Kingdom, and in nearly every instance hundreds of people have been turned away, owing to lack of space. It is the intensely human interest of what Commander Evans has to say that enables him to get so firm a grip upon the attention of his hearers. Just a plain sailor's story, without the least attempt at eloquence or fine language; and for this reason, as well as others, it appeals so strongly to an audience.

We are apt to get a little despondent now and then about the present-day character of our race. Those who have the good fortune to hear Commander Evans will know that Great Britain can still produce men cast in the heroic mould of those who have made her fame through the centuries.

Commander Evans is young, slim, and clean shaven, the "pink of perfection "—to use an old phrase—of a British naval officer. He went out as seccind in command to Captain Scott, but owing to illness did not go with the party on that last Southern journey of Surgeon Atkinson and others, those who discovered the missing col- leagues dead, gathered their records and effects,
THE SOUTH POLE, apd the regions traversed by the various expeditions.

read the burial service over their bodies, and erected a cairn and cross to their memory over the inner tent in which they buried them. l' Evans took command later, and had the grim task of breaking the awful news of the fate of Captain Scott and his gallant comrades to the world. The King afterwards received Com- mander Evans in audience and conferred upon him the Companionship of the Bath (Civil), in recognition of his services with the Expedition, 1910-12. His Majesty also condoled with Com- mander Evans on the death of his wife, whose death occurred after an operation on board ship, when the commander and some of his party were on their way back to England after their return to New Zealand from the Antarctic. The visit of the explorer to Warrington has been arranged under the auspices of Mr. R. H. Pearson, of Warrington, and Mr. J. P. Johnson, Kendal. Commander Evans leaves on March 4th for America, where he will deliver thirty lectures. The prices for admission to, the Warrington lecture are exceptionally popular compared with those which have prevailed in many other towns, namely, 55., 2s. Gd., 2s. and Is. 6d. A number of is. 6d. and Is. tickets are being kept back for sale at the doors only for the conveni- ence of those persons travelling by the district trains.

div.head: MYSTERIES, ARE THEY COINCIDENCES?
div.p: MYSTERIES, ARE THEY COINCIDENCES?

"There are more things in Heaven and earth, Horatio, Than are dreamt of in your philosophy." As time advances the truth of these words becomes more and more evident to us. It is quite probable that many phenomena now unexplained could be fully understood were we already acquainted with the many hidden powers, forces and agencies of our little planet.

div.head: STRANGE COINCIDENCE.
div.p: A STRANGE COINCIDENCE.

Whilst staying in the country with friends some years ago my hostess's brother vfas ex- pected from India. It was a beautiful moon- lit night when my host and his wife walked to the station about half a mile distant to receirb their relative. Passing the Church- yard on their way they noticed that a new grave had been digged near their family burial place. Soon after they had left the Hall a telegram arrived for my friend and I took it myself to the station. It conveyed the sad intelligence that the expected guest had died on the passage home and had been buried at sea. On the way back to the Hall we found there was no new grave in the vil- lage cemetery. A strange coincidence! Here are two other incidents, vouched for; I give the words of the gentleman who re- lated them to me.

"A. widowed sister of mine is the mother of a grown-up family. One of the sons, a young fellow of nineteen, in 1894 left home for Africa and settled in Bulawayo. During the Jameson raid he joined the famous party on their disastrous ride to Johannesburg and was killed before the Hrugersdorp figh i t n an affair of pickets at 4 a.m. At the same time my sister, the mother of the youngster was awakened suddenly, and looking up, saw her son standing at the bedside. He was hat- less; the bosom of his shirt was torn open showing a bullet wound in his breast, to which he silently pointed. "A second case, in which my sister again was the subject of warning- was that she was awakened one night by a weird cry which seemed to come from her bedside. She got up, lit the gas and searched, but could find nothing. The clock pointed at 2.25 a.m. Later information showed that a great and most intimate friend of hers had died that morning at 2.25 and had uttered a great cry when life left her." _
In this coincidence, one might imagine that the supernatural did enter in some way and degree into our lives.
AFT.Eat TWENTY YEARS.

One of the most remarkable coincidences is the following. We have as far as it is hu- manly possible ascertained that it is an abso- lutely true story, for obvious reasons we al- tered the names. Ranleigh Castle is situated three miles from the village which takes its name from it or vice versa. Sir John Ranleigh had just brought home a young bride, and the festivi- ties prepared for the occasion were too many for delicate Lady Ranleigh and she was taken suddenly seriously ill. 'Doctor Wing- field, the village practitioner was summoned by a mounted messenger and arrived within an hour at the Castle. The illness was of the gravest character, due to complication in the heart. Youth and the grekat exertions and per- petual watching and nursing of the doctor saved the bride's life. When convalescence came to the patient the physician showed signs of great fatigue, and his pale and hag- gard face told only too clearly that his dwn he:alth was in a precarious state. He admit- ted the necessity of spending some time in rest and therefore thgaged a youlng assis- tant, tsnyhow for the night service. How- ever, he arranged with Sir John that if he were needed, really needed, his night bell should be pulled three times in quick succes- sion as a sign that the call was to the Castle His services were fortunately not required. Twenty years had passed. Sir John and his wife were surrounded with a family of boys and girls of whom the eldest had just left her home as the bride of Captain Max_ well. Dr. Wingfield was still the village physician. He and his wife occupied still their old house which was greatly improved and modernised. They were on intimate terms with the Baronet and his lady, and the Doctor especially was almost a daily guest at their board. _ - - -

There had been no repetition of Lady Ran- illniss and the professional services were needed only to help over the usual children's complaints. The last of the guests of Sir John and Lady Ranleigh, who had formed the house party for the marriage fetes had departed, and all was quiet again around Ranleigh Castle. The Baronet had asked Dr. and Mrs. Wingfield to an informal dinner, and walk- ed with them part of the way to their home, the hostess, feeling tired after the excitement of the last few days, retired earl', as did the younger members of the family. The doctor had been asleep some time when he uins suddenly awakened by three rapid pulls at his night bell. He started up—such a thing had never occurred before—but sud- denly he remembered the incident which had escaped his memory. It was no doubt a call to the Castle; he was wanted at once, Sir John had not forgotten the arrangement of twenty years ago. Dr. Wingfield slipped into his clolhes and opened the door. No one was to be seen. The groom evidently had returned after hav- ing pulled the bell. He hastened to the Castle. Great consternatiou reigned there. Lady Ranleigh had a few moments before been dis- covered dead in her bedroom. A groom was then saddling a horse to summon the Decor and his arrival caused the greatest astonish- ment. She had died of heart failure. Again a Coincidence ?

A CURIOUS DREAM. Some years ago a young man, the son of a Devonshire farmer, had a curious dream that if he went to London and would remain at mid-night on London Bridge he would find a fortune. As the dream repeated itself three times he resolved to tell his father the strange occurrence. But his father only laughed at the tale and refused to provide his son with the means of going to London. However, the vouth could not get the dream out of his lead and made up his mind to work his way up to the great city as best he could. After many days travelling he at last ar- :ivcd weary and tired in the metropolis. The first night of his arrival saw him walking up and down London Bridge. No- thing happened save that he noticed that he was being watched by a constable on his beat. Again he came to the spot at mid-night, again nothing occurred. He now began to think that his father was right. What chance was there of finding a fortune on the bridge ? Still he decided to try once more. He was not there more than a few minutes when he was arrested by the solitary policeman. "Now come on, this won't do, I know your little game," said the custodian of the peace. The youth protested his innocence but the 'constable was deaf to the protestation of his prisoner, he had seen the likes of him before, suicide was his game and he should take him to the police-station as a suspected person. Upon this the boy told his story at which the man in blue had a good laugh. "Why, bless me," he said, "if I took any notice of them things, I should be wandering about now somewhere in Devonshire a-look- ing for my fortune. Why, do you know, I dreamed three times I was down there on a farm a-digging up heaps ot goal from under an old apple tree in the orchard," and the constable described minutely a peculiar old tree that actnally grew in the orcimrd of the very farm the youth came from. The Devonshire lad kept his own counsel and made the best of his way back to his home where he received a good jacketing from his father. He said nothing, but after all had gone to bed he visited the spot des- cribed by the constable, armed with a pick- axe and shovel. He had not dye down very deep wnen lie, Caine across a heap or goid coins that bad been buried there some hun- dreds of years before and which amounted to a large sum. But the most remarkable coin- cidence in this case came out at the enquiry over the _treasure-trove. Many years ago the farm had keen occupied by an ances- tor of the policeman who had the dream and there is little doubt that the money was buried by ennui of his forefathers,
We are experts in this Branch of optical science, and have confidence in recommending our methods, which are the result of 25 years' practical experience.
(F.m.s.e, by Exam),

div.head: SERVANT GIRL'S DEATH.
div.p: SERVANT GIRL'S DEATH.
Sequel to a Drowning Case in the
River Mersey at Howley.
SWEETHEART & LANDLADY CENSURED.

The cause which led a prepossessing servant girl to take her life in the River Mersey at Row- ley was not made very clear at the inquest conducted by Deputy Coroner Jones at the .War- rington Coroner's Court on Monday. The victim-of the tragedy was Beatrice Jones, 20 years, daughter of Mr. Francis Jones, 32, St. Peter's-place, and she, until two dilys before her demise, had been in service in a refreshment house in VVinwick-road. The father said Beatrice had been a servant in different places for about four years. He saw her last on Tuesday, 27th January, when she said she was going on all right, except that she had ' had some trouble with a young man on the pre- vious Sunday night. She also stated that she was to get married in April, but did not know what she was going to do until then.

div.head: STAYED OUT ALL NIGHT.
div.p: STAYED OUT ALL NIGHT.

May Deakin, refreshment-house keeper, 28, Winwick-road, said the girl had been in her ser- vice for about four months. About three weeks ago on a Sunday night she did not return to her place, and when she came on the Monday she said that she had been to a birthday party. She promised not to stay out all night again, and witness kept her in the situation. Deceased left on Tuesday night, 27th January, and witness heard nothing more about her until Detective-Sergeant Holland called and inforavA her that the girl's body had been found in the River Mersey. Beatrice had never complained of being in any kind of trouble. Elijah Ball, 22, Manchester-road, told bow he spoke to the girl on the bank, as she was acting strangely. She went on and some little time later he saw her take a running jump into the water. He ran to the spot, but could not see her, so be got assistance and he budy was re- covered within ten minutes.

div.head: SWEETHEART'S STORY.
div.p: THE SWEETHEART'S STORY.

He was with her on Sunday night, 25th January, but they parted on quite friendly terms. On Tuesday, 27th January, she came to his lodgings, and slept

div.head: Woman's Most Dangerous Age.
div.p: Woman's Most Dangerous Age.

div.p: TWO WITNESSES CENSURED.
The foreman of the jury: Mr. Walsh, said : The jury think that the witnesses, Morris and Hardman, have not given their evidence in a satisfactory way, and we think they should be censured.

The Deputy Coroner called the two forward, and, addressing them, said: The jury are not satisfied with the way you have given your evi- dence, and I am not satisfied that you have told the truth. You are evidently keeping something back, and for that you might have got your- selves into trouble, and have found yourselves in another court.

div.head: RUNCORN'S VITAL STATISTICS.
div.p: RUNCORN'S VITAL STATISTICS.

At Runcorn Urban District Council.on Tues- day the Medical Officer reported that 26 births and 48 deaths had been registered during the 'past month, compared with 24 births and 40 deaths for the corresponding period of last year.
At a cost of a little less than £40,000 per annum the Liverpool Corporation propose a coin- plete scheme for the prevention and treatment of tuberculosis in the city.. ,

div.head: TRAGEDIES OF THE WEEK EtiD. Two Sudden Deaths Investigated by the Deputy Coroner.
div.p: TRAGEDIES OF THE WEEK EtiD. Two Sudden Deaths Investigated by the Deputy Coroner.

Two tragedies marked. last week-end in War- rington, and these were investigated by Del fifty- Coroner Jones on Monday. The first case was that of James Chad wick (33), a general labourer, of 50, Chorley4 zreet, who died suddenly while at work in the to., mery of Messrs! Waring and Co.. Ltd, Winwick-f treet, on Sunday morning.. Philip Newton, general labourer, 14, Nc rman- street, said that he was assisting Chad v ick to roll a barrel, when he (witness) started to cough. Chadwick said lie had been coughing a 1 ot dur- ing the night, and immediately after he seemed, to go strange and fall down. He we s dead before witness could assist him. Dr. R. Smith, the police surgeon, slid he had made a post-mortem examination of tk te body and found the heart much enlarged.. It i xeighed 16oz. instead of the normal weight of 8 or 10oz. The liver weighed 51b. instead of 31b., the normal weight. There were signs of fatty deger .eration of the heart.
The jury, on the doctor's evidence, ret urned a verdict of "Death from natural causes."

Eliza Edwards (69), wife of Edward Edwards, groom, 50, Allen-street, after showing a new lodger to his bedroom on Saturday vdternoon, became giddy and fell down a flight of stairs. She died almost immediately. The husband said that the deceased had suLered for some time from attacks of giddiness.
Samuel Leavey, an old man of 79 ye ars, said he was a lecturer on the metric sytitem of weights. and measures.

The Coroner: I hope you make a lot o f money out of the metric system P—Very little, sir, but I'm an old-age pensioner. (La-tighter) Witness told how he heard the deceased fall down the stairs. She was bleeding at ± he nose when he picked her up, and died almost imme- diately.
The jury returned a verdict of " Acci idental death."

"For the very many benefits you have obtained for us we would like to tender our warmest thanks, especially for the substantial increases of pay, the provision of a recreation club, one day's rest in seven, and the establish- ment of .a reserve class for the time-expired men "We fully realise that to be .effective, dis- cipline of a Force such as ours 'mist necessarily be strict. That this should be m aintainerl, and that you still retain our affeets,on and regard speaks volumes for the way in which your onerous duties are performed. " You have always given us die mnst atient hearing in any trouble or difficulty, anti for the assistance and the innumera'ole acts of kindness you have extended to every individual member we thank you. You have been a friend and n guide to all.

The talk then drifted on to other mercen- ary marriages, and Theresa pondered over the man she had come here to meet—with a view to loving, if possible. " Perhaps my existence has driven him to be mercenary, poor fellow," she thought. "Perhaps it is his only course. And yet—" her thoughts flew back to her guardian, and she questioned herself, "Would he have mended his fortunes by marrying a woman if he did not love her ? " And in her heart she felt that Sir Edward would rather have broken stones on the road than do such a thing. In the days which followed, driving, danc- ing, motoring, bridge-playing, gave Theresa ample opportunities for studying her cousin; and day by day her heart sank as she thought of her father's wish. Day after day Theresa's pretty eyes and piquant pale face seemed to attract Harold Sturge's careless at- tentions, and he would plunge into an at- tempted flirtation which was almost insult- ing in the abruptness of its beginning and ending; for the cautious gentleman was care- ful that nothing of the nature of a flirta- tion with any other girl should take place when Miss Tuggs was present. " Haven't you a Christian name, Miss Gar- net ? " he asked in his caressing, indolent voice, as he lolled idly near Theresa alone in the drawing-room on the mornin; of the day on which she with subdued excitement was expecting Sir Edward to come to fetch her home. " Yes," she replied coolly. " Won't you tell me what it is ?" he whis- pered. "No. I keep it for my older friends," she retorted. .
" hen shall Ibe old enough ?" " I fancy you will never be old enough," she said sadly. 4, you're afraid I shan't like it," he de- clared.

Perhaps you won't," she agreed. "I like your gown, at any rate," he said boldly. "It's wonderful how some girls get: 3 good effect with no money, and others with heaps of money look dowda." "Then, I suppose, you know that I ,aln poor, and your words are a compliment. "Oh, you don't look poor, von mow; but I believe someone told me jou are." leaned familiarly over her. " I like a girl to look rich, and then—well, I only wish for both our sakes she could be as rich as she looks."

Why ?" she asked bluntly. " Then I'd marry her." " How noble of you," ironically. "Would you really marry a girl you didn't care for ?" "I should care for—you," he said boldly. "I was speaking of you.'- "Do you think you could make me hap- py she asked, realising now to the full the selfishness of the man she had hoped to for, for her father's sake. " I know you could make me happy," he Whispered, taking her hand. "Don't take my hand, Mr. Sturge. You don't want the hand of a poor girl, do you ?" The danger of the situation made him cau- tious again. Miss Garnet attracted him strongly, but he could not afford the Plea- sure. care
• " Why has cruel fate made you poor ?" he exclaimed.
" lam as rich as I wish to be," she laughed. "And I don't think you are the nn!n to die for love." _
"Do o—u -lino.; the man who would F" She paused. " Yes," she said slowly. " I do.•'

"Shall you marry him ?" "Marry him!" The question startled her. She had never thought of marrying him. Her cousin's next words broke in upon a sudden wave of cha- otic thought. " I would die for you," he declared softly. She really was very pretty; and there was of course no question of dying. It seemed the gallant thing to say. " But you had better not say rash things, Mr. Sturge," she said, rising to put an end to a conversation which was already onnoxi- ous to her. "When I see you ready to die— or live—for me, I will—" " What ?" he asked, nervously, fearing that he might already have gone too far for his comfort. '—Believe you," she concluded with a: laugh. "For father's sake I will try to think gently of him," she thought, " but it is hard.' The chance of proNing his words came with startling swiftness to Harold Sturge. By mid-day Sir Edward was at Wildwych, and Theresa's heart was light as a bird's. Her cheerfulness seemed infectious too, and, that the sunny spring day might not be wasted, a picnic was arranged to see Castle corbet, a few miles away. Some of the party, walked, some motored, some drove. Harold Sturge and Sir Edward Ellington escorted Miss Tuggs and Theresa on horseback, and, under the influence of the dazzling afternoon they lingered by the way. When at length they reached the ruined castle and dismounted, the rest of the party had begun its explorations, and no one was to be seen. So leaving Harold Sturge loung- ing on the grassy slope by the river, with the two girls in iiis charge, Sir Edward rode off in search of a grown. It was then that some brilliant yellow flowers growing by the water attracted Ther- esa's eyes, and with a cry of delight she ran to ,pick them. Oh, get some for me," cried Miss Tuggs; and in another moment they were all three clambering down the slippery bank. But before any of the lovely flowers were gathered, while Theresa held the first stem yet in her hand, the crumbling earth fat the edge of the deep water broke beneath her an instant, feet, and in with a startled cry, she was plunged into the dark swift waters. In the space of but a few moments the next scene had begun and ended. But the recollec- tion of it never died from Theresa's mind. Rising to the surface she cried aloud to the two figures on the bank for help. Her breath was failing her, her heavy habit dragged her down. But the man she appealed to stared back at her white-faced and -hesitating. The woman beside him clung to his arm in fright. " Do not leave me! Do not leave me!" she cried. "I can't let you be drowned, too! Oh, I am fainting! It would kill me to let you go!" In another moment, in an impulse of cow- ardice, Harold Sturge turned from the heiress. drowning girl and gave his attention to the

• • • • • It Was • is s i n"or guardian's arms that Theresa opened her eyes. It was he who carried her I first to shelter, and then conveyed her back the party. to Wildwych without alarming the rest of It with every was he who encompassed her Was and then waited, fuming, n audienc e till the hour came when she could give him se. Sir Edward knew his own heart now, and worse now h so did iheresa know hers. For better or for prayed that h would know his fate, and he Cr heart had not been already given to her cousin. When the rest of the party, returned late in the evening, full of enquiries as to what more than had happened to Miss Garnet, 'they learned One piece o news. They learned that Miss Garnet was really Miss Theresa Garnet Ilkworth, the heiress of Carden Hall; they learned that she had been almost drowned that afternoon; and they learned lington. f that she was now engaged to Sir Edward El- The only one of the party who said no word to her on learning these items of news, was Mr. Harold Sturge, who, in an execrable state of mind, made up of shame, self-re. " Oh, tell me quickly—though it is too late now," she declared. " I think he meant my own self, sweet- heart, and it is not too fate. You have seen 'the ousted heir,' and you do not love him. Now your father's friend, your 'old guar- dian,' tells. you he worships you, and you say v°2! All is I.llglTr'N'it sAgt whis- pered joyfully. " Harold Sturge will have hie heiress, and I have the man I love best in the whole world. It was worth nearly drown- ing to learn my own heart."

LILIAN QUILLER-COUCH (Author of " Man," " A Spanish Maid." " The Romance of Every Day)" etc.).

The big carriage rolled on and on in the twilight over the broad road which, led to Carden Hall; until at length the white track which to the coachman's eyes had been urt- rolling itself like an endless white ribbon in the dimness, was blotted out by the shadow of the tall leafless trees of the long avenue. Inside the carriage a slim girl lay back among the cushions and fur rugs, and the ' lamp which shone down on her shewed her face to be white and weary, and her eyelids closed. In the library of Carden Hall Sir Edward Ellington walked to and fro between the hearthrug and the still uncurtained window. He was a man with a plain face but a good presence; and the restlessness which seemed to possess him on this evening was quite un- usual with him. As the hands of the clock upon the mantel- piece moved on towards seven, Sir Edward al- ternately gazed down into the blazing coal. or strained his eyes through the window- panes to the now dark outside world. In his heart a half,nervous impatience was ming% ling with a kindly pity. " This is the first and last time I accept a guardianship," he thought with a rueful smile, 'if it means hanging round other person's houses on chilly nights waiting for unknown wards. Hullo! that's the carriage!" Hurrying from the library Sir Edward made his way across the hall to the wide open door, at which several men and women servants were already gathered. With s. broad sweeping curve the coachman drew up his horses on the outside gravel, and the lamp shewed to the waiting eyes an eager white face at the carriage window. "Welcome to your home, Miss Ilkworth," said Sir Edward going forward and. taking the small gloved hand held out to " htm. "It is kind of you to be here, said the girl with real feeling in her voice. "I sup- pose you are—?" " I am your guardian, yes," he replied with a smile. " I came over from Hayes just to give you a greeting. You must be very tired, He led the way up the broad steps to the coming so quickly." hall. _ "Yee," ‘ she said with a pretty laugh. "I've come all the way from Spain without stopping. And this "—she looked round upon the warm, bright hall with its soft carpets and glowing lights—" is my home. And these —she did not finish her sentence, but she smiled with kind, trusting eyes upon the waiting servants, and their hearts were won. . I don't know," she said, turninglaugh- ingly to Sir Edward, "whether it is your place to invite me to dine, or my place to invite you, but please let us dine together. I know that I must have inconvenienced every- one by coming so unexpectedly in the end; but I should like to explain things a little." A quarter of an hour earlier Sir Edward was heartily wishing the meeting with his ward well over, and, himself well on his way back to Hayes Castle. Now, however, a plea- surable anticipation filled him as he listened to Miss Ilkworth's hospitable suggestion, and he wt':s as eager to stay as he had before been to go. "You must not trouble yourself with ex- planations," he said. "Be assured that everyone concerned was eager to have the mistress of Carden Hall in her own home at last. I confess I had not thought of sharing your meal; indeed, I felt sure you would be glad to be alone, to rest in your own room; and I had intended riding back to Hayes, when once I had seen you in good hands. at if you are sure you are equal to a guest to- night, I shall be most happy to stay." - I do not want more solitude," replied Miss Ilkworth, rather sadly. "I have had too much of myself these past months; and even on the journey I have been chiefly sitting , still seeing other people happy. I shall be thankful to talk and be talked to. Shall we say dinner in an hour's time ?" 'An hour's time." seemed to be agreo- able to everyone, and Sir Edward watched his ward follow the trim maid up the broad stairs of the home which she had now entered for the lirst time; then he, himself, went back to the library to pass the hour in thoughtful recollections of the past and plea- sant anticipations of the future. " So that is old Ilkworth's daughter," he mused. "It is early to judge yet, but I hinc she has the old boy's good heart, and his rower of winning the hearts of other pee- Before the hour was over Miss Ilkworth ea ~e back to him; and whatever the quality of her heart might be, there could be doubt , he charm of her presence. Her white ' ks had gained colour now that the dust A : weariness of travel were gone. She wore •osa, trailing gown of soft black silk, ,-,, g fly open at the neck and sleeves, with ate laces to relieve the sombreness. And • , pr, tty throat and hands were white as

_ You will like me better when you have 112, something to eat," she declared, coming a:.:ls him with a confident smile which •.v-ed that she had no real fears of his dia. ..4ir Edward smiled back with quick under- 'ding of her mood. " I daresay you are he admitted, " for I shall know you • 11...,r by that time." Dinner is served," announced Helmer at th 400 r. And resting her hand upon Sir Ed- w. i-d's proffered arm, the new mistress of Ce rden Hall walked for the first time into the ' 'stately dining-room of the home of her ace estors. It was quite a gay meal which ward and o.na, %Han took together in the cheerful oasis in t. eve micldle of that spacious room; and not until they were left alone at the conclusion, to da fly over their dessert. did Miss Ilkworth attem pt to make any of her promised expla. natiot s- " Sir Edward," she began with half-sad gravity " later on I want to ask your advice and he. 'ear Miss Ilkworth—" Oh, lon't do that!" she interrupted im- isively. Do wl bat ?" "Don't call me 'Miss Ilkworth,' " she ex- plained. " You are my guardian, you know, and my fa filer's friend.' " But—" lie stammered a little confusedly, at the une: tpected turn of the conversation. " I have sc: ircely realised your name—is it— Theresa i" „„" Yes. tesa. The girl was silent for a few moments, and her eyes were misty as they rested thought- fully upon the table, and sho slowly drew her pretty finger round the edge of her fin- ger-glass. " My father was all the world to me," she said at length. in a low voice. " I don't re- meinner my mother. You, very likely, know much more about their marriage, and her ac- cident than I do. My own passionate adora- tion of my father made me understand some- thing of his worship of my mother. But of their married life I have only guessed that they loved Spain only second to one another —that my lather, a handsome, heart-free man, met my mother in Spain when he was no longer young; that they married and for- got the world; that soon after I was born my mother was thrown from her cauiagt

anti kitten, and tnat my heart-broken tather never came back to his home." " I do not know much more than that," he said gravely. "But I knew your father all my life until he went away for the last time. He was about twenty years older than I was, but we were firm friends, and he was my hero. He was so handsome and brave. I had barely come of age when he left Carden, so I think you will understand that I felt both surprised and honoured when I learned that he had appointed me his daughter's guardi- an. I was deeply touched. The blow of his death was a terrible one for you." I am afraid," she said softly, "that for months I was utterly, selfishly despairing. I forsook the old house in Corovian, and I wan- dered in new places, caring for nothing, heeding no one. At last, in my sorrow, I re- membered what I had been 4rongly forget- ting, I remembered that ray father had ex- pressly begged me not to mourn—to be sure only that he was happier than he could ever be on earth, that, if his faith told him the truth, the longing of seventeen years would be satisfied at last, that he should be with my mother. He had said many loving things in his care for me, and now in a flash I re- membered that he had bade me go home to England, to his real home. On that day when I roused myself from my grief, and remem- bered his wishes, I resolved to lose no more time, and I came at once. You were very let- ting me ele me aasll lthoseiked mlonetoliistid Sirne tEdw haveardb, elrente- , compulsion then, I think." ' I knew you were suffering, he said quietly. Not o many w would have let me havel nleyn weany, d yi gtuhaaosrugaihnaZu s, " he said, with a friendly smile, " and I am glad to have you under my own eye at last." " I want to stay here at Carden for a while, very quietly," she said, throwing off something of the sadness which had shad- owed her soft eyes, and smiling back at him. "I don't want a lot of people to know yet that I have come from Spain. And then— later—l want to tell you of a plan which has occurred to me; a plan by which I think I can carry out my father's wishes, and do the best with my new possessions." "Don't count too much on my prudence." he laughed. "I've never been an adviser be- fore."

" Oh, I'm sure you are the best of guar- dians," she declared laughingly. " You let your ward do what she likes, so sensibly. Yon will be greatly in demand as a caretaker, I'll ' be bound, when once I have sung your praises to the world." When Sir Edward rode home to Hayes Castle that night, his heart felt as young and ' happy as a boy's. " She is a charming cora- pa.nion," he thought as he made his way over the hard, dry roads. "But I wish she didn't ' guardian me quite so much. It makes a fellow seem so old and severe—and, after all, I'm neither really." It was some time, however, before Miss Ilkworth spoke of the plan which she had in her mind. Days slipped into weeks, and the longer the words remained unspoken, the less did she feel inclined to alter the present state of affairs. Rids, drives, long talks made the hours slip by so happily that for a time nei- ther guardian nor ward questioned the reas- on why life had become so pleasant. It was Sir Edward who drew himself up with a jerk at last. " I—l believe I love her," he said half- dazedly to himself. "I'm behaving unfairly to her. Her father didn't trust her to. me that I might shut her up in the country. I must set about getting a younger chaperon for her than old Mrs. Bodges, I must send her away—" Next day Sir Edward tried to do his duty. " Well,'' he said, as he and Theresa sat in the old window seat in Carden library, "now that spring has come I ought not to let you stay vegetating here. You said one day that you had a plan you wished to carry out. Tell me how I can help you. For a while Theresa sat silent, then, " I want you," she said, "to help me to marry my cousin, Harold Sturge; the man who would have had Carden if I had not been born." Sir Edward felt thankful at that moment that the shock which a heart may feel does not show outwardly. " I did not know you knew Harold Sturge," he said with strained quietness. "I don't know him. That's why I want you to help me." "Have you heard that he is calculated to be the kind of husband you wish to have ?" All, don't let us joke about it," cried Theresa. "I will tell you just why I have this plan. I know nothing about my cousin, but when my father was dying we talk.ed of many things, and I realised two things very deeply, first.' how truly he loved the English home which he himself had forsaken, and , second how much he feared the burden of it upon the shoulders of myself a ioung girl, who had never even known English life. Then bit by bit he told me of the boy who had been his heir for so many years, when everyone had thought my father was a con- firmed bachelor, and he spoke with sympathy of the boy's disappointment." She paused. That was surely not a reason that you—" " No," she continued, " but on the last day, when his voice was weak and his mind wandered at times, I heard him say over and over again, as if in distress, It is too heavy for a young girl—alone. And he is a good man. Will you marry him, Terry—but only if you love him, Terry, only if you love him.' Then I would question him. How can I make you happy, father ?' And he would re- ply, scarcely realising me. Yes, it would make me happy. He is a good man. Marry him, Terry.' I listened, longing for the name to be uttered, for I would have promised any- thing to give him rest, but—he never spoke again." 'Do you know that he meant Harold Sturge ?' asked Sir Edward, with a new lightening of the heart. " No; but he had been talking of him and of the estate. Who else could it be ?" Sir Edward rose and paced the room medi- tatively. " Why don't you say something ?" asked Theresa impatiently. I beg your pardon. Tell me what I can do to help you. " " Well, she blushed hotly. and hesitated. You must surely understand," she protest- ed, "that I cannot besiege my cousin and ask him to marry me. But, after my fa- ther's words, I would like to meet him with- out letting him know that I am the cousin who ousted him, the owner of Carden. I want to like him, I admit; but I want to meet him, and let him meet me, free from any embarrassment of heirship or relation- ship. Can you help me to that, Sir Edward ?" " Yes," he said gravely, "I can and will." ' Thank you, she said. But there was no pleasure in her voice; and she felt, though she did not understand, the suggestion of sadness in his.

It was at Wildwyeh Manor that Theresa Garnet Ilkworth first saw, as Miss Garnet, her cousin, Harold Sturge, and saw him ab- sorbed in paying impressive, though half contemptuous court to a shrewish, unattrac- tive heiress, Miss Tuggs. It was a lively country-house party into which Sir Edward had introduced her as the orpnan daughter of an old friend, scarcely out of mourning for her father. Mr. and Mrs. Stairedge to whom he had confided Theresa's true name, were glad to welcome her for Sir Edward's sake. But when her guardian had left her Ther- esa, felt suddenly and unreasonably lonely, far more so than when she had first arrived, alone and strange, at her big, unknown home in England. ‘VildWych Manor was full of guests, but there was no really friendly face there, and gradually she realised that she missed her guardian at every turn. "He is so good, so understanding," she told herself. Here, everyone seemed occupied with some }hallow and trivial, or, even less worthy ob- lect, to kill time or gain a selfish end. "Harold Sturge doesn't care a pin for that girl," declared Mrs. Stairedge one evening to a few of the party gathered round the hall fire. Harold and the heiress had just strolled away to the billiard room. " And I wish Percy hadn't asked him down this month. I don'tience like ."having mercenary marriages op my cousc

div.head: BOILED MILK CONTROVERSY.
div.p: BOILED MILK CONTROVERSY.

Foreign Royal ladies are showing as much interest in aviation as members of our own peerage. The Grand Duchess of Mecklenburg- Schwerin—a niece of Queen Alexandra, and daughter of the Duke and Duchess of Cumber- land—went up in an aeroplane at Nice a few days ago. It has become the fashion for society ladies to accompany aviators on flights at Hen- don on Sunday afternoons. Lady Drogheda, Lady Eileen Vivian, and Lady Eileen Knox, were among the first to venture with Mr. Gra- hame White. Lady Victoria Pery has several times looped the loop in an aeroplane with Mr. Gustav Hamel.

div.head: Royal Matchmaker.
div.p: A Royal Matchmaker.

The Grand Duchess of Mecklenburg-Schwerin has, not undeservedly, earned a reputation— among her husband's family—as a matchmaker, for she was chiefly instrumental in bringing about the marriage of her brother, Prince Ernst of Cumberland, with the only daughter of the Kaiser. The Duchess Owns a villa in the Enga- dine, and there the Crown Princess Cecilie often came, accompanied as a rule by Princess Vic- toria Louise. By a series of strange coincidences —which the Grand Duchess and the Crown Princess alone could have explained—Prince Ernst of Cumberland was invariably on a visit to his sister when the Kaiser's daughter was ex- pected. Thus a woman's wit found a way to reconciling the hostile houses of Hanover and Hohenzollern.

A Nonagenarian Woman Novelist, Novel writing would seem to be a rejuvenat- ing occupation, for women at any rate. Several of our successful lady novelists have long since passed the allotted three score years and ten, and are still devising plots, creating characters, and writing books. Miss Katherine S. Macquoid!' who has written numerous stories and other books, has just celebrated her ninetieth birth- day. Despite her advanced age, she is brisk and alert, and keenly alive to events and ques- tions of the day, and is busily engaged on a new story which will shortly be published. It is interesting to note that Miss Macquoid considers the girls of to-day superior to those of her youth.

div.head: Tango at the Vatican.
div.p: The Tango at the Vatican.

A. French dancing master has commenced an action for damages against a certain Cardinal who denounced the Tango, and placed it under an episcopal ban. This caused the dancing teacher the loss of several pupils, and otherwise injured him in his profession. The Pope, how- ever, has released the Tango from ecclesiastical censure. As introduced to his notice at a Special performance at the Vatican, his lloliness seems to have thought it more depressing than morally dangerous. " You take your amusements very sadly," be said to the dancers, and Pius X. is clearly of opinion that the Tango will soon die of its own inanity.

Sterilised Milk Useless as Food. Whether or not bovine tubercular bacilli can be communicated to human beings, it is largely at the instance of the medical profession that the public have adopted the practice of boiling milk as a precautionary measure. We are now told that there is very little, if any, more nour- ishment in a glass of boiled milk than in a glass of water. That is Mr. Robert Mond's opinion, after conducting exhaustive experiments with milk as a food in infants' institutions, and it was endorsed the other day by Dr. Vincent at the Cheshire Milk Producers' annual dinner at Crewe. Boiling milk, it is declared, destroys the various bacteria it contains, which are of vital importance to its food value, and it is • added that the only thing which saves babies fed on cooked milk is that the sterilisation is very often only partially effected. Seeing that this opinion is put forward on scientific authority, it is a matter of great importance that the public should know whether or not it corresponds with the facts. It clearly calls for a Government expert inquiry, for, if boiled milk is really food spoiled, there is an enormous amount of mischief
being done which in the public interest should be checked at the earliest possible moment.

rhe Return to the Natural Figure. The new silhouette, which Dame Fashion has decreed shall reign during the spring and sum- mer, deserves a warm welcome, for it follows the natural lines of the human figure in a much greater degree than any of its immediate prede- cessors. The dress of to-morrow is to bring out the softness and suppleness of the natural figure, with its harmonious and graceful lines, and there are to be no exaggerations. Or so say the prophets! Nothing stiff, or boned, will be per- mitted, and the minaret or wired tunic is conse- quently doomed. Only heavy embroidery at the edge will be allowed as fullness. Hips will still be wider than shoulders, and where nature fails in this respect, draperies, frills, or slightly puffed and graceful little panniers, will suggest the required width. Only a trifling line will mark the waist, but the natural tapering from hips to ankles is to be carefully followed. The bagginess that now distinguishes corsages, more especially for evening wear, is to disappear, and ' softly drooping draperies take its place. There is, however, a decided tendency towards effects at the back of dresses, such as the grouping of flowers, and the little apron 7 of draperies, that unpleasantly suggest the bustle. But this may tone down as the season advances, and it is hoped that such will be the ease. Bargains in February Sales.

The winter sales are by no means over; in fact, in some instances they are beginning, and going on throughout the month of February. The White sales come somewhat later than the others, and these are now in full swing. Those women who appreciate dainty lingerie may now indulge in hand-made nightdresses and French. knickers, charmingly trimmed with Torchon lace and muslin insertions, which are offered at ridiculously low prices. The white lingerie blouses, shirt blouses, the former prettily tucked back and front, are to be had at a quarter of the usual cost. White 'cotton crepon shirts, well cut and finished, offered for a little over a couple of shillings, should certainly be secured. They could not possibly be made for the money. Those who ha ye delayed making their purchases I until the eta of the sales will this year be gainers rather than losers. Gloves, too, are unusually cheap this season. For evening wear there are twelve button mousquetaires in good kid at less than half the price these usually ; command.

KABIR, THE WEAVER MYSTIC. Kabir was a weaver, a simple and unlettered man, who earned his living at the loom. Like Paul the tent-maker, Boehme the cobbler, Bunyan the tinker, Tersteegen the ribbon- maker, he knew how to combine vision and in- dustry; the work of his hands helped rather than hindered the impassioned meditation of his heart. Hating mere bodily austerities, he was no ascetic, but a married man, the father of a family; and it was out of the heart of the common life that he sang his rapturous lyrics of divine love. Here his works corroborate tradition. Again and again he extols the life of home, the value and reality of ordinary exist- ence, with its opportunities for love and renun- ciation: pouring contempt upon the professional , sanctity of the Yogi, who "has a great beard and matted locks and looks like a goat," and on all who think it necessary to flee a world pervaded by love, joy and beauty—the pro Per theatre of man's quest—in order to find that On° Reality Who has " spread His form of 1O" throughout all the world."—Miss Evelyn Under.; hill, in the February "Contempore.ry P..wievr."

div.head: Four German Multi-Millionaires.
div.p: Four German Multi-Millionaires.

According to the latest computation, the Kaiser is richer than any man or woman in his dominions. His forest lands and farms are valued at more than twelve millions, to which must be added other possessions worth not less than seven, making the respectable total of nearly twenty millions. The Duke of Meeklen- burg-Strelitz comes next, with nearly eighteen millions. Frau Krupp von Bohlen has at least sixteen millions, and Prince Albert of Thorn and Taxis not less than fifteen Million pounds. These are the four richest people in Germany.

For 400 years the village inn at Lamberhurst, near Tunbridge Wells, has been in the hands of a family named Beech, and on Saturday the licence was transferred from the landlord to his son, Mr. Edwin Beech.
