div.head: BATHS AND TRAMS.
div.p: BATHS AND TRAMS.
Councillor Pemberton Discovers a " Scandal " at the Public Baths.
SUNDAY REST FOR TRAM MEN.

There was some straight talking at the War- rington Council on Tuesday about the delay in Life completion of the Baths extension and also on the topic of allowing the tramway employes one Sunday free of duty in every four. Councillor PEMBERTON raised the Baths ques- tion by asking when they would be finished. , Alderman BOLTON said the extension would be finished as 600/1 as possible, and they would be clean and nice. (Laughter.) Councillor PEMBERTON said they were now asked to spend over ..k970 extra on the Baths. Actually the committee were going to build the ,baths without a boilerhouse, chimney and laundry. Nobody but the Baths Committee would have made such a mistake. (Laughter.) The whole of the work had been so neglected by the com- mittee that it amounted to a scandal. Alderman BOLTON denied this, and thought when the Baths were re-opened everybody would be satisfied, and Councillor Pemberton could then get " a jolly good wash." (Laughter.)

div.head: TRAM MEN'S ' REST DAY."
div.p: TRAM MEN'S ' REST DAY."

Dr. JOSEPH, the Deputy-Hayor, moved the pro- posal in regard to giving the trabaway employes one Sunday off duty in the four.' Alderman BrIITON would not like to stand in the way of anyone having a Sunday. off, but the arrangement proposed seemed bad. It gave only a half-hour service on the Latchford and Stockton Heath routes, 20 minutes on the Ceme- tery route, and 15 minutes on the .Longford route upon Sunday mornings. The route that, did not pay got the best service; that of LOng-
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 7, 1914.

div.head: FINE VARIETY AT HIPPODROME.
div.p: FINE VARIETY AT HIPPODROME.

No one can cavil over the entertainment pre- sented at the Hippodrome this week. The pro- gramme is well balanced, varied and intensely interesting. The Musical Johnstons give a turn of the best and prove that they are truly masters of the xylophone. The music is most effective. Smart jugglers are The Venettas, with an un- usual fund of humour. Miss Irene May is a talented soprano, and Mr. Percival Williams satisfies with his rich baritone voice. Herr Doring's trained pigeons are particularly inter- esting, and exceptional variety is found in the dancing turn by the Spinette Quintette. All the other items are excellent.
" WHAT HO! RAGTIME" NEXT WEEK.

At last it has come our way. Next week Warrington folk will be busy engaged nightly reviewing the revue. The visitor is " What ho! Ragtime," one of the best and most catchy of these merry pieces now on the road. The fact that it is being travelled by one of Mr. Austen Hurgon's companies is the halltmark stamp that it will be presented in the best manner the wit of the stage art it+t can devise. There are smart scenes, catchy chat, daring dancing and lively singing, and the whole goes with 'a swing and vim which must commend itself to the audi- ence. A first-class company of star artistes pre- sent the revue, which will be given twice nightly.

div.head: VARIETIES AT THE THEATRE ROYAL.
div.p: VARIETIES AT THE THEATRE ROYAL.

Fitzgerald's Juggling Girls give a clever turn with the clubs at the Theatre Royal. They o,re a smart troupe. Lyndon and Stokes supply a first-class dramaHc sketch. Miss Nancy Hanks' Merry Maids are clever vocalists and dancers, and the Sisters Cody are smart shots. The other turns and pictures are good.

div.head: ALADDIN'S VISIT TO THE ROYAL.
div.p: ALADDIN'S VISIT TO THE ROYAL.

Pantomime will hold sway at the Theatre Royal next week. The theme is 'Aladdin," and this will be told in an attractive way by a bevy of clever artistes. The songs, gags and dances are of the best, and a treat is in store for lovers of this type of amusement.

ford. (Hear, hear.) It would be more eqnitable if the Latchford and Stockton Heath routes got the 15 minutes' service and Longford the half- hour. He suggested a2O minutes' service on all the routes on Sunday mornings.

div.head: NOT SATISFACTORY.
div.p: NOT SATISFACTORY.

Alderman BOLTON said the proposed serviees were not satisfactory to the public. The Cor- poration had driven the 'bus services from the streets, and now they had created a monopoly they wished to starve the traffic by cutting down the facilities on Sunday mornings. He thought they should run the trams as usual and take on more men in order to give the others a Sun- day off duty:' Phe tramways belonged to the public, and they had a right to expect every facility. To give that was only a simple matter of employing a few additional men. Otherwise they were placing the public in the bands of the taxi drivers and similar people. (Laughter.) Councillor PEMBERTON : The public can walk..

div.head: CURTAILED MORE DRASTICALLY.
div.p: CURTAILED MORE DRASTICALLY.

Councillor LINDLEY said Alderman Bolton had not attended to his duty, else he would have known that one car on the short Longford route could do the double journey in 15 Minutes, while on the Stockton Heath and Latchford routes it took half an hour. The committee thought such a service would carry the traffic, as there were only a small number of Passengers between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. on Sundays: The MAYOR would have preferred haying the service curtailed even more drastically. If in a great city like Bradford the Sunday tram ser- vice did not start until 2 p.m., and gave satis- faction to the public, the people of Warrington would. not be in such great difficulties over the proposal. He would support a half-day service on Sundays.

- Councillor PEMBERTON thought the public would only be too pleased to walk, in order to give some of the tramway employes a holiday on Sundays. Dr. JOSEPH said a half-day service was pro- posed, but it was rejected. The new scheme was approved.

div.p: TOWN PLANNING.
A Warrington Scheme Withdrawn Through Unexpected Opposition.

div.head: ALTER THE BY-LAWS.
div.p: ALTER THE BY-LAWS.

Alderman BOLTON seconded. It was no use talking about town planning, because the Cor- poration by-laws said the Corporation should give so much yard spape and air space. If they complied with the by-laws they -complied with every regulation made \by the Corporation in They must alter the by-laws r town planning, as it was nar- row a condition that there was Ile did not see why th matter should be rushed. He did not see why there should be all this waste of Corporation property. When they had altered the by-laws there would be nothing for the Town Planning Act to do in Warrington.

div.head: ALDERMAN BENNETT HURT.
div.p: ALDERMAN BENNETT HURT.

Alderman BENNETT, who characterised the 1 Town Planning Act as the best measure passed by the Government, and a very noble measure, ' said that kind of debate made him despair. His optimism was being knocked out of him, and he should go down to the grave a dispirited old man. A great deal of time had been devoted to these questions, week after week, month aftm month, and year after year, and every member of the Council knew all about them. They had been confirmed by the Council on three or four occasions, every landowner affected had been consulted, and the whole matter had been re- ported to the Local Government Board. Now the Chairman of the Health Committee, for- sooth, suggests that all their work should be undone, and that the moment the committee took a practical step they should go back. Upon my word, he said, it absolutely hurts me to think that at this stage, after so much discussion, that any member of the Council should take an action so retrograde as that taken by Alderman James Evans. A Proposal to Call in Additional Expert Advice Rejected by 20 Votes to 7.
LIVELY DEBATE AT THE TOWN COUNCIL.
The controversy over the alleged delay in the re-construction of the Warrington Bridge entered upon another phase at the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday.
The Special Committee of Inquiry wanted an- other expert to be called in, and although defeated in the General Purposes Committee, the proposal was persisted in at the Council.

A heated discussion ensued, and " scenes" were almost the order of the night. The Mayor often had to ring his official bell to maintain peace, and in the hope of soothing tempers Ile gave the members permission to smoke.

After a debate of over two hours, during which matter, relevant and irrelevant, was discussed at length and with heat, a vote was taken, and the Inquiry Committee's scheme to call in an expert was defeated by twenty votes to seven.

The fun over the bridge began when Councillor Pemberton arose to move the recommendation of the Inquir3i Committee that an Ashton-under- Lyne engineer be called in to give expert evi- dence, and to expedite the work. This proposal was contained in the private agenda.

After Councillor PEMBERTON had reviewed what the Inquiry Committee had done, he asked the ruling of the Town Clerk as to whether it was competent for the General Purposes Committee to refer back their recommendation without first rescinding the resolution of the Council on the terms of their appointment?

The MAYou: If the minutes of the Bridge Inquiry Committee are passed by the Council, that will be an end of it. The consideration of the proceedings of the General Purposes Com- mittee will not alter the effect in any case. Councillor PEMBERTON : It is a very unfortu- nate position to be placed in.
The MAYOR: If we take the decision,of the Council and it is passed by the Council, that is final.

Councillor PEMBERTON : I have never had such insolent treatment as that I had at the General Purposes Committee. Nobody would dare to say at a public meeting of the Council what was said at that committee meeting. I resent such treatment very much.
He then moved the adoption of the Inquiry Committee's proposal to call in an expert.
Councillor LASHFORD seconded.
ALDERMAN BENNETT'S VIEWS.

Alderman BENNETT moved that the minuteg of the Inquiry Cominittee, and particularly that part about calling in an expert, be not con- firmed. He did so, said the Alderman, with regret, as he wished to give all credit to the Inquiry Committee for the sincerity with which they had approached the work entrusted to them by the Council. He was, however, bound Ito say he did not think they had taken the right course in the matter, or a course likely to secure the end they had in view—the completion of the bridge. They had not made out their case, they had not been able to advance any substantial evidence of neglect._

No member of the Council had said a word of criticism of the bridge itself, of the design, or of the way in which the work had been done. If when the work was finished, they had reason- able ground for complaint, if they thought the work had taken longer than it ought to have done, the matter was in the hands of the engi- neer. He could adjudicate as to whether, in view of the difficulties and extra work involved, the 'time taken was excessive,•and the Corpora- tion could, if necessary, recoup themselves out of the retention money. If there was a dispute between the contractor and the committee on that question, and if they could not settle it in .a friendly way, the remedy was provided—they could go to arbitration.

and now I speak I think it is most unfair to interrupt. Time and again the engineer has been before the Council and failed to make him- self clearly understood. Alderman BENNETT : Because you treated him with no courtesy. (Hear, hear.) Several members said Councillor Osborne WaS not in the Council at the time. thor_Cixdoguie6n,6c woiasltltior OSBORNE : We were first told the to cost £14,310. That was increased

Councillor WILKINSON: £16,604! Be correct. cOUlleillOr OSBORNE : I am correct £16,602 2s. 7d. (Laughter.) Now the sub-committee have been told it is to cost £lB,OOO or £19.000, and if we go on for another month it will have jumped up again.

COST NOT THE SUBJECT. * Councillor ROBERTS: Were you appointed to I go into the question of cost? Councillor °norm: Yes, we were! Councillor Roman (sharply): I think not Alderman SMETHURST: Only the delay. Councillor ROBERTS: You are going outside the purview of the committee's powers. The MAYOR: To inquire into and report upon the delay. Councillor OSBORNE said the Inquiry Com- mittee had kept strictly to the point, and he proceeded to read from a private and confiden- tial report, when he was subjected to a series of interruptions. Councillor OSBORNE (sharply): These inter- ruptions are quite irrelevant and uncalled for. Councillor ROBERTS: If the interruptions are irrelevant, that is caused by your statements. Councillor PEMBERTON (turning to Councillor Roberts angrily): We didn't interrupt you!

div.head: Right Resentment.
div.p: Right Resentment.

He did not wonder that an engineer of such eminence should strongly resent the suggestion that another engineer should be appointed to criticise his work and have access to all his docu- ments. It was an attitude which any 'profes- sional man would take up in the circumstances. Before they could appoint Mr. Garside, the other engineer, without Mr. liVebster's sanction, they would have to dismiss Mr. Webster. That would mean paying his full charges, and very likely exposing themselves to the risk of an action. Costly litigation, which could not be of any advantage to the Corporation, and which would be vexatious to Mr.- Webster, would prob- ably ensue; and it would tend to delay, instead of accelerating, the progress of the bridge. They had the assurance of the engineer that the bridge would be completed by the end of the year. Those who had visited the works frequently had noticed that the progress was really highly satisfactory. He had heard it suggested that the progress hdd been accelerated since the appointment of the 'comrdittee, but that was absolutely. misleading and contrary to the fact. Alderman BOLTON: I second and reserve my speech.

div.head: SECURITY AND STRENGTH FIRST.
div.p: SECURITY AND STRENGTH FIRST.

Councillor ROBERTS supported the amendment for several reasons. The security and strength of the bridge were the first things that should be secured at any cost, and under any condi- tions. If there had been what appeared to be unnecessary delay, it was not a fault without its redeeming side. In concrete work time was of essential _importance.

It had been said that," they should never swop. horses in crossing a stream." The resolution, if carried, meant that they were going to swop horses, because the engineer had stated definitely and emphatically that he would not submit, under the advice of his lawyer, to the intrusion of any other engineer, and he was fully justified. (Hear, hear.) There was no charge against him —except a general ebarge of unnecessary delay in the construction of the bridge—nor was there any suggestion as, to his work being unsatisfac- tory., Why, therefore, want another engineer? They were treating their present engineer .ex- ceedingly unfairly, and he had attended meetings of the Bridges Committee when he had not been treated quite as kindly as he might have been treated. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: SCENE NUMBER ONE.
div.p: SCENE NUMBER ONE.

Councillor Ossonxx rose to support the ap- pointment of an expert, and the first scene started. The Council, he said, had missed the chief point. What the sub-committee were ' asked to do was to try to find out the reason of the delay. They were not asked to consider the professional abiliTy of the engineer. They were satisfied that a delay had taken place. It seemed to him that in the interests of the public they should, as far as possible, rid their minds of sentiment.
A MEMBER: Sentiment, nonsense! Councillor OSBORNE : I have listened patiently,

div.head: HIS SUPPER THERE.
div.p: HIS SUPPER THERE.
The MAYOR: Those who interru.pt you, Coun- cillor Osborne, cannot make a speech. (Laugh- ter.)
Councillor PEMBERTON : They don't want to hear the facts. Alderman BOLTON: Nonsense' Councillor OSBORNE : The more interruptions, the longer I go on.

Councillor WILKINSON: I'm going out if you go on much longer. (Laughter.) The MAYOR: Then go out, if you don't want to stop. (Laughter, and hear, hear.) Councillor OSBORNE : If you keep quiet I'll get through my speech all the quicker. Alderman BOLTON: I'll have my supper here. (Laughter.) The MAYOR (ringing the hell): Will you 'kindly give order, Alderman Bolton? Alderman BOLTON: I'll go out! Councillor OSBORNE, who was subjected to fur- ther interruptions, thought they should have another engineer called in, but if the Council said "No," that ended the whole of the matter so far as the Inquiry Committee were con- cerned.

div.head: WHO SELECTED THE COMMITTEE?
div.p: WHO SELECTED THE COMMITTEE?

Alderman BURTON said some had complained of the strong language used. He had been sub- jected to that kind of thing, and so strong was it at times that he thought he might get his coffin ready. (Laughter.) They had not as a Council heard a word of complaiht about the character of the work on the bridge. Councillor Pember- ton had chosen his own committee. He chose a legal man, and lae put that legal man on as chairman. He meant Alderman Forshaw. The MAYOR: No, the Council did that. • Alderman SMETHURST : No, no! Alderman TINNIoN : No, they didn't. The MAYoa : Councillor Pemberton read the ' names out.

Alderman Txxxiox : It was done illegally. Alderman BURTON said he was informed that, on the question of calling in another expert, the committee had gone against the legal adviser altogether, and that they wanted the Council to do the same, which seemed to show there was something more behind it. (" No, no.") Alderman SMETHURST feared Councillor Pem- berton was leading the Council into a litigation ' which would lead to a tremendous expense to the ratepayers. He wished the Council would ' sanction the publication of the private repart and let the public have the truth about what had actually taken place.

div.head: LIVELY EPISODE.
div.p: A LIVELY EPISODE.

Councillor BROADHURST said there was no in- tention on the part of the committee to "swop horses," as had been hinted. If the senior members of the Council, such as Alderman Tin- nion, Councillors Roberts and Wilkinson, had constituted the committee, their recommenda- tion would have been carried. The Deputy- Mayor had said that the committee named the second engineer before they went into the matter. There was no truth in that statement. Dr. Jossen (the Deputy-Mayor): I beg your pardon:_ I made no such statement. _ "'

. - The MAYOR: Dr. Joseph said the committee knew nothing about the bridge. Councillor BROADM*RST : He said we ought to have made this appointment afterwards. The DEPrTY-MAYOR Nothing of the kind. I made no such statement. You are dreaming.

Councillor BROADHURST : If he had any objec- tion to the chairman we appointed, and to our not having appointed Alderman Smethurst— The DEPUTY-MAYOR : Nothing of the kind. Will you try to tell the truth, if you can? Councillor BROADHURST : I believe I can tell the truth, even with yourself, sir. The DEPUTY-MAYOR : Well, you are not telling it now. The MAYOR : Dr. Joseph said •he did not respect the committee through their leaving Alderman Smethurst off. lam on the com- mittee, but I know he didn't mean me. (Laugh- ter.) Councillor BROADHURST : What I say is this: One month ago he had an opportunity of moving an amendment to the appointment of the com- mittee as proposed by Councillor Pemberton, Alderman TINNION: No, he had not.

div.head: DR. JOSEPH INDIGNANT.
div.p: DR. JOSEPH INDIGNANT.

- - The Dseurt-MAYon : I ask your protection, Mr. Mayor. It is a determined personal attack by Councillor Broadhurst upon me, Councillor Bnommunsr : Not at all. 1 The DEPVTY-MAYOB : It is not the first time he has done it. I ask your protection. Councillor BROADHURST : One month ago, when Councillor Pemberton moved certain names to constitute the committee, Dr. Joseph had the opportunity of suggesting any other names he thought fit, and there would not have been the slightest objection to that. The MAYOR: Dr. Joseph says he left the meet- ing before the names were brought forward. Councillor BROADRGRST : A good many did the same thing. The only member who rose to pro- test was Alderman Tinnion, who immediately resigned. from the committee.
Councillor WILKINSON : The way you are going onjou're.wasting time.
Councillor BROADHURST : going to have ray say in my own way, Councillor Wilkinson. Councillor Wuxi:caw : And it's nothing but a lot of twaddle and nonsense.

COUDCMOT BROADHURST : Well, your opinions don't count for much in the Council. Alderman TINNION : IT is disgraceful. Councillor WiLxissoN: I shall propose a time , limit to speeches. The MAyoa: Bring it up at the next meeting, land shut up in the meantime. (Laughter.)
TO MAKE IT. A BEAR GARDEN. Councillor BROADHURST : If I am going to have these interruptions, I can assure you I shall

make this Council into a bear garden. I want to pay every respect to the chair, but if these members persist in the interruptions I shall shout down every opponent who is here to-night. That is what I intend to do—even if you have me removed, sir. I have attended hundreds of meetings in connection with trade unions. Alderman TINNION : This is not on the agenda. Councillor BEOADHL7R3T : These members to- night who say they are gentlemen—well, I am sorry for them.

Alderman BOLTON: We are not gentlemen. Councillor Wiumisobr said that two-thirds of the work had been completed at the bridge, and they had paid two-thirds of the cost. They had plenty of money left. Alderman SmErurasr : We have £ll,OOO in hand now. He was astonished to hear that the com- mittee went dead against a legal gentleman of Alderman Forshaw's ability on the question of calling in an expert. Councillor BROAD/WEST I rise to a point of order. There is no truth in that statoment. Councillor OSBORNE : Alderman Burton was wrong in making the statement and Counoillor Wilkinson is wrong in repeating it. - Alderman BURTON: It came from good authority.
Councillor PEMBERTON : It is quite wrong. We were unanimous.
The MAYOR : I was at the meeting, and I quite agree that Alderman Forshaw was in accord with the committee. It was unanimous.

"TWADDLE AND RIGMAROLES." Councillor IlAwmoax said it was unfortunate that so much heat had been introduced. The proposal of the Inquiry Committee was a serious one, which, if passed, would involve the Cor- poration in considerable litigation and expense. Alderman TINNION said they knew the cause of the delay. Were they going to expedite the work by continuing the fishing expedition? He thought not. Whatever possible good could have arisen from the appointment of the•com- mittee had already been secured, but the calling in of another expert would be calculated to nul- lify. it. ,

_ Alderman BOLTON was surprised that after the decisive vote at the General Purposes Committee the Council should be kept there, hour after hour, listening to "twaddle, opinions and rig- maroles," that would be a disgrace to the Coun- cil of any town, let alone of Warrington. (Laughter and aftplause.)

"HOUNDED FROM PILLAR TO POST." Councillor Pumnitros, in reply, said: If every- thing is all right and beautiful, why fear an inquiry, as it 'would all come out that you are right? I think it is well known to the whole of Warrington that no man has suffered more for his public utterances than I have done. I have been persecuted and hounded about from pillar to post. While I am here I will work in the interests of the ratepayers, and if I cannot stand it any longer I will get out, but while I am here I shall work for the whole of the inter- ests of the ratepayers. Councillor WitHnisoar: And so will other people, and they will look after their own busi- ness as well. This bridge will now cost thou- sands more. C' Vote.") Councillor PEMBERTON : My business is the business of the ratepayers. Councillor WILKINSON: Get out. (Laughter. and cries of "Vote, vote.")
A DECISIVE VOTE. The rote was a decisive one. The scheme to engage the services of a -second expert was de- feated by.. 20 votes to seven.
The division showed that the members voted as follows:

For the Amendment of Alderman Bennett— Aldermen Bennett, Smethurst, Bolton, Tinnion, Burton and James Evans; Dr. Joseph, Dr. Fox, and Councillors Wilkinson, Shaw, Roberts, Jen- kins, Taylor, Dickenson, Hawthorn, Lindley, Archer, Chrimes, Craik and Locker-20. Against the Amendment—Councillors Gough, Broadhurst, Pemberton:Lashford, Cunnington. Osborne and the Mayor—seven.

div.head: ALCOHOL A RACIAL POISON. A Doctor's Statement to the Band. of Hope Union.
div.p: ALCOHOL A RACIAL POISON. A Doctor's Statement to the Band. of Hope Union.

Lady Barlow, President of the Lancashire and .Cheshire Band of Hope and Temperance Union, speaking at the yearly meeting of the union at Manchester on Saturday, said they were at the beginning of great things in the world of ton- perance. As to the consumption of strong drink, they had to admit that there had been an in- crease. These figures now stood at £161,500,000, but they might take this-rauch comfort to them- selves—the increase had not been in proportion to the increase of the trade of the country; that I it could be now shown that trade could increase, and with it the prosperity of the country, with- out, necessarily, an increase in the consumption of intoxicating liquor. (Applause.) Some of them thought the time had come when they should cry "Halt !" in the matter of the expen- diture on armaments. They were under the impression that they were being forced by trusts, which were working under the surface to secure the sale of implements of war, that they were being impelled by unseen forces to spend more and more money in this direction. After all, the great sum we had to find in this matter— and Lady Barlow admitted it was a huge sum and preposterous—it was only ..t51,000,000, as compared with .X 161,500,000 for drink. There was a great outcry up and down the country against any increase in the Navy Estimates. They wanted to raise an equally loud cry against the drink bill. "It is not by our armaments that we stand or fall as a nation," Lady Barlow said, "but by the character of our people." (Ap- plause.) In their own particular area they had to face the fact that there was in 1912 18,000 first convictions of men and women. Their great hope lay in work among the young. Dr. C. W. Saleeby, of London, gave an sfldress on " AlcohoL; A Racial Poison." He said that it was a well-established fact that, apart from any injury alcohol might do to the individual it attacked, it injured also his offspring. Alcohol- ism was recognised by all authorities to be the most active agent not only in spreading venereal race poisons, but also in making worse the action of that disease. The action of alcohol was to produce not the actual idiot or the actual epilep- tic in the next generation, but a lowering of health and power of resistance in the off4pring. Lady Barlow was unanimously re-elected Pre- sident of the union. Mr. J. S. Highaan, M.P., 1 of Southport, was re-elected honorary treasurer, and Mr. Herbert Knott, of Wilmslow, chairman,

div.head: CHARTERED
div.p: CHARTERED
A MOMENTOUS SESSION.

Few- -Paii-iiiineirt.ai; Sessions have presented such a vista of momentous results impending as that which will open on Tuesday. Before it closes, the Home Rule Bill and the Welsh Dis-1 establishment Bill will have been brought safely into tort; the Plural Voting Bill will have passed --through the penultimate stage of its progress under the Parliament Act; and there Is every reason to hope that an important measure of educational reform will have been placed upon the Statute Book. Mr. SAMUEL has already intimated that, during the next Session, the Government will also •bring forward its proposals for reconstituting the Second Cham- ber on a democratic basis. Naturally, the Opposition view this prospect in a very lugu- brious spirit, cheered only by the hope that they will be able to make "something happen" to bring the Session to a premature conclusion. The political corresPondent of the " Evaiing Standard" has made a very naive disclosure of the "compelling reasons" for some kind of a stroke to bring this about. If the Opposition can force the Government to dissolve before the Home Rule Bill is passed in June, then, he ex- plains, the Bill will lose the benefit of the Par- liament Act. The Bill would have to be brought in agaih, and carried through the House of Commons in three successive sessions, and it could hardly survive this labour of Sisyphus. So much for the pretence of the Opposition that all that is needed to clear up the Irish Question is another General Election! We are now told that if the Government were to go to the country and wiin, the Lords' would still refuse to give way, and Ile Bill could only be passed under the Parliament -Act, as if there had been no General Election. There could be no clearer proof that the Opposition's demand for the Bill to be "referred to the people" is nothing but a conspiracy to reduce the Parlia- ment Act to a nullity.

THE SAD CASE The ease of the Tariff Reform Farmer g OCS REFORMOvFi R T . TARIFF . from bad to worse. At a meeting of the Bishop's Stortford Chamber of Agriculture n . January 22nd, Mr. R. G. PAOBY, the prospective 0,. Unionist candidate for the Saffron Walden Divi- sion of Essex, presiding, the following resolu- tion, quoted in the "East Anglian limes" of January 24th, was passed That this meeting considers the present proposals of Tariff Reform would be most injurious to the agricultural interest, and hopes they will be withdrawn from the pro- gramme of the Conservative party at the next election. The CHAIRMAN, in a generous endeavour to outline. his policy as an ardent upholder of the Edinburgh programme, gave an unconscious demonstration of the pitiable plight to which 1 these conscientious observers of varying 1 methods of procedure are reduced. According to the journal quoted above, he said that: As a candidate he was pledged, if sent to Parliament to vote against any proposed food taxes. lie would tax certain articles, but not if the tax would affect agriculture. Feeding-t 5 should certainly be exempt. That Is what Australasian .politicians would call the "No—Yes" policy. . ~.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 7, 1914.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 7, 1914.
THE PASSING WEEK.
LEFT BY THE TIDE.

Mr. Page Croft, who has been stumping the country on the prospective blessings of Tariff Reform, reached Warrington by last week-end, and inflicted on the small audience that assem- bled in Parr Hall some of the discredited and rejected arguments that were set in motion by Mr. Joseph Chamberlain a decade or so ago. It is a lasting testimony to the grit that resides in the Englishman that he never knows when he is beaten. That Mr. Page Croft or anyone else could be found seriously to pretend that the flag which Mr. Bonar Law hauled down to half-mast is still flying, would be subject for admiration, could one in the circumstances keep down one's feeling of commiseration. To-day we publish an article on our industrial expan- sion by Mr. Parker, covering the period of the Tariff Reform agitation at its height, and in its decline up to date. There was, it will be re- , membered, a great to-do about our inability, for instance, to cope with foreigners in the motor and kindred trades. Since Mr. Chamber- lain spoke, Mr. Parker shows our exports of carriages, motors, cycles, &c., have increased by 215 per cent., to a total in 1913 of £11,373,000 a year, while our imports have increased 475 pericent. to a total of £7,417,000, a trade gain of .R 1,644,000. Other trades shown have —but they have gone up. And Lancashire and Yorkshire, chiefly concerned with cotton and wool, stand stubbornly—a stubbornness born of self-interest—by Free Trade that found them poor and has made them rich.

THE Irusit EXCURSIONISTS. Those who took the Irish semi-circular tour a few days ago, and their friends, have been frantically endeavouring to make people believe that they have spread " consternation " in the ranks of the Radical party. It is, we suppose, a kind of Tariff Reform consternation, that we are incapable of comprehending. The public will note the intent with which the deputation was sent forth, and the fact that they have been fighting fiercely on the defensive ever Since they came back. When they have finished laughing at the fiasco, the public will be able to say where the " consternation " has been at work.

To-day" the twelve," or thirteen, have written us a feeble reply to the article we published last week from ," An Ulster Protestant." It will be noticed that they deny that their report is against Home Bute in principle, but only against the particular measure now before Parliament. Then why all the babbling about ';liome Rule a crime," "Local Liberals denounce Home Rule," and the rest of it?

div.head: TIRING PARTY.
div.p: A TIRING PARTY.

One would have thought that with all this excitement about Home Rule being a crime, and Mr. Ebenezer England, the Liberal, writing to the Tory meeting, apologising for his absence, there would have been a tremendous crowd at Parr Hall last Friday night, but there was the poorest attendance seen at any " great " political meeting in the same place for years. It is estimated that 800 attended, so that there was plenty of room. Was it because Tariff Fteform is dead? Or because Home Rule is settled? Or because Mr. Harold Smith has somewhat tired his friends? Or was it all three combined?

div.head: WHY?
div.p: WHY?
Yesterday <£so—five £lO notes—was handed to an otTicial of the Warrington Union to go to- wards the relief of the poor rate. The name of the giver was not divulged.

A CURE FOR SNOBBISHNESS. James Welch tells an amusing story of Corney Grain in this month's "Strand Magazine," which should do a vast amount of good in all parts of the country, by exposing the snobbish- ness—and perhaps checking it somewhat— which still survives in spite of the democratic tendencies of the age.

Talking of meals, says the writer, I must pause for a moment to tell you a beautiful story of Corney Grain, even at the risk of your knowing it. He had gone to give an entertainment at the house of a "nouveau riche" down in the country somewhere. There was a dinner o. When he got there, to his amazement, he was shown into the servants' hall to wait. Their dinner was just on the table, so he accepted the butler's invitation and sat down to it with them. After the meal, at which he was parti- cularly bright, he went all through his pro- gramme for the benefit of his hosts, the servants. He had hardly 'done when he was summoned to the drawing-room, to find the guests there solemnly seated in rows, waiting for him to commence. "Commence?" he asked, with his gland smile. "Commence what? My little entertainment? Oh, I see. Very sorry, but—it's over. I gave it, as I always do, where I dined. Good-night."

OUR SUNDAY CARS. The scheme, ai outlined in this column Last week, by which it, is proposed to give tramway employes a Sunday off every month, was approved by the Council on Tuesday night. But will there be further deputations and further rescindings? The arrangement seems to be unsatisfactory because partial and differentiat- ing, and not final because it does not meet the wishes of the men.

A FALSE START ON TOWN PLANNING. On Tuesday evening the attempt of the Council to make a start upon the Town Plan- ning Act scheme for Warrington was rudely checked. The minutes contained a reference to the contemplated erection of houses in Chester New-road, and an entry showing that a letter had been sent out to local architects and builders, stating the number of houses to be allowed to the acre in future. An interesting discussion arose upon the motion of Alderman James Evans, who asked that the minute re- ferring to the chester New-road be referred back. lie gave several reasons, but Alder- man Bennett saw in the whole of them sufficient to make him despair. Usually Most militant in tone, Mr. Bennett confessed that he was I really "hurt," and the quiver in his voice showed that he was greatly upset by the fact that after three years of hard work in corn- , mittel members of the Council—" and Alderman Evans, the Chairman of the Health Committee, forsooth"—should still be in need of enlighten- ment on this important scheme, and wanted a fresh start. Alderman Evans had given the impression that he objected to builders being limited to 20 houses to the acre, but when Alderman Bennett said that this number was the maximum to be allowed in other towns, where inquiries had been made, Alderman Evans denied that he had said whether there should be 20 houses or not. But ho had cer- tainly warned the Council that they themselves might become builders of houses, and would then find themselves " tied " by their own action to 20 houses to the acre. Of course, his strong point was that we should not commit ourselves until the authorities on the outskirts of the town have committed thernselves to a definite policy. That is quite right in its way; but those who want to see steps taken to save the town itself from further overcrowding will, like Alderman Bennett, begin to despair if years are allowed to pass and nothing can be done hut "refer back." "Although it was passed by the Liberals," said Alderman Beinnett, "I give them credit for having passed/a noble Act and taken an enlightened step "—a sentence which, com-1 ing from a Conservative, ' showed up the grudging attitude of some Liberals In ralher a had light. The minute was withdrawn "for further discussion."

div.head: BRIDGE.
div.p: THE BRIDGE.

There was a full-dress debate on the state of the work at the Bridge, at the Council on Tues- day night, but the issue was somewhat clouded by unfortunate wrangling. It is a question that demanded calmer treatment and fuller con- sideration. The interruptions to which Coun- cillor Osborne was subjected were altogether uncalled for and quite unnecessary. As a mem- ber of the Sub-committee, he was entitled to j place his views before the whole of the members j and that they were not in agreement with those I of the majority is no excuse for refusing him a fair hearing. The assurance was given that the Bridge will be finished this year.
GRAMMAR SCHOOL AND EDUCATION CommirrEE.

It is understood that the Grammar School, the Education Committee and the Board of Education are still being much exercised con- cerning the need for a new Grammar School building. As we have previously explained, the local authority are de,sirous that any altera- tions at the Grammar School should be consid-1 ered in conjunction with the provision of another Secondary School for boys, which would leave the present Secondary School available for the girls of the town. The Governors of the Grammar School have not been able to see any attractions for them in this suggestion, and efforts to come to close quarters have so far been unavailing. lb I would appear to be of 111-omen that at the recent Old Boys' dinner the local authority was for- gotten by the whole of the speakers. We regret that if it reflects any spirit of towards the Education Authority on the part of the Governors. It may be hard for the latter to consent to part with traditions, but people have to be guided by the logic of facts in these increasingly democratic days. The facts connected with this little controversy can be told in a few words. The Board of Educa- tion will not allow the school to remain on its present site and draw Government grants. Thereupon the Governors agree to go elsewhere, and without saying a word to the local authority, go in quest of the site. The Educa- tion Committee, who have undertaken to meet the annual deficit in the accounts of the school to the extent of £4OO were never consulted. The position of the Education Coinmittee is that if the Governors want to retain their school intact they may do so—but pay for it. At the present time the impresslon in town is that the Governors wish to retain the denominational character of the school, although it IS partially maintained by public funds. now

div.head: LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
div.p: LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
The Teachers Show Themselves to be very Active Trade Unionists.
A QUEER LABOUR ARGUMENT.
BY "A WORKER."

The tramway employes are to get one Sunday off duty per month. This has been found pos- sible by curtailing the service on the Sunday mornings. The original idea was to delay the starting of the trams for two hours on Sunday morning and thus give a day off once a fort- night, but this was withdrawn at the request of a deputation, and now the Tramways Committee have substituted the monthly day's rest. This is something to be going on with, but surely in these' enlightened times Sunday labour could be even more curtailed. Of all the Corporation servants the tramway employes have the longest hours, and they are well worthy of some reduc- tion. l'erhaps a way of giving a Sunday free of duty each fortnight may be devised. A Teachers' Strike.

For the first time in its history the National Union of Teachers are involved in a strike to secure better conditions for its members con- cerned. The venue is in Herefordshire, and the Education Committee there cannot say they have not been warned about what was to happen. For six months the Union has been striving for improved conditions in vain. The conditions existing are shameful. Experienced head masters, who have spent large sums of money upon their training, are paid at the rate of £9O a year, or a wage worse than is paid to the men who roll the roads in this county of cider and low wages. If the committee think they can rule the salaries of the teachers on the same basis as they can rule the wages of dis- organised farm workers, they labour under a I' great mistake. 1 Organist as Well. _

-With the teachers every trade unionist must have full sympathy, for they are only fighting a battle which most of the older unions have passed through. What will surprise trade union- ists more than the strike is the poor wages paid in some parts to the teachers. There are scores of artisans in Herefordshire who receive better pay. One head master and his wife jointly re- ceive £ll5 per annum—the man £9O, the wife A:25. A weaver in a cotton shed would refuse such a wage as that paid to the school mistress, and not mince words over her refusal. In some places the .1:90 a year schoolmaster has to play the organ in the parish church free of charge for this "handsome" salary. These are said to be common cases in Herefordshire, and it there- fore seems that the National Union of Teachers have every justification for calling upon their members to strike. That a substantial victory may await them must be the wish of every organised worker. That Conference.

I have often wondered what use the Labour party's conference is, and after the recent meet- ing at Glasgow I am still left wondering. The Labour members were attacked by the "direct action" group for not running Parliament on their own. The M.P.'s retorted that they did not get sufficient support from the workers, and covered up all by their anniial attack on the Government, one delegate stating that the Liberals were worse than the Tories. I hold a brief for neither political party, but I just ask this: Had the Tories been in power, would the Trades Dispute (No. 2) Bill become law? We know that Boner Law, Wolmer, and others have promised the capitalist federations to repeal this Act as soon as they come into power, and yet we find some Labourists anxious to see the party who have given Labour the best measure of this decade turned out to let the Tories in, PO that the Act may be repealed. I cannot, and I do not, think any intelligent working man can grasp this queer line of argument.

div.head: ST. ANN'S NEW REREDOS.
div.p: ST. ANN'S NEW REREDOS.
Striking Dedication Service by Archdeacon Spooner.
PRESENT-DAY LACKINGS.

Thursday was a memorable day amongst the members of St. Ann's Church, Winwick-road, for a special service was held to dedicate the new reredos and communion table and to re- open the church, which, for the past six or seven weeks, had been undergoing a transforma- tion at the hands of the decorators. The Yen. Archdeacon Spooner performed the service of dedication, whilst the Vicar, the Rev. J. Davies, conducted the remainder of the service. Special hymns and Psalms were sung.

div.head: REMARKABLE SUCCESS.
div.p: REMARKABLE SUCCESS.

Archdeacon Spooner took for his text I. Chron. xvi. 29, " Worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness." He prefaced his remarks by saying that he rejoiced with their Vicar and them- selves at the remarkable success which, under God's blessing, had rested upon their endeavours to make their church, that sanctuary of God, more beautiful and more worthy for his wor- ship. He hoped it would be a continual source of the greatest Possible comfort and gratifica- tion. They met together that night by a solemn act of dedication to ask God to accept, sanctify and bless the new holy table and the reredos, with which there were tender ties.

div.head: Present-day Lackings.
div.p: Present-day Lackings.

It had been said, and he thought with very great truth, that one of the lackings of the pre- sent day was a due sense of what worship meant. There were nny people who went to their churches or chapels having very little idea as to what it was meant for. The word worship was of Anglo-Saxon origin, and implied render- ing to some person or object fitting respect and reverence, and it was the worship of God, the paying to Him of due respect and due regard in an appointed manner, which was referred to in the text. Paying to God was a great object of their worship.
Human Idols.

They knew men set up in their hearts various i idols, which fell down n these days, just as they did in the days of David. There were the idols of wealth, of position, and. the dominant idol of the twentieth century—of pleasure—and having set up one or other of the idols in their hearts, bowed down and worshipped them., Some sought wealth, others were fired by ambition, desiring not a position by which they could worship God, but one to command the attention and the subordination of their fellow men. How many, and this included all classes, were setting up idols of pleasure and living simply for pleasure. In God's worship it as quite possible to set up a wrong object.

Worship Through the Eye. They might desire to worship through the eye, and be attracted simply by what was external. The beautiful buildings and adornments were right in their place, but were not the objects of their gathering together. Then again, there was worship through the ear; he did not depre- cate music, for he was very fond of it, but it was not music they had to worship. The object of worship was God. Worship God in the beauty of holiness. There was the material aspect. There was a reason for building beauti- ful churches. People in the present day, as in the past, loved to surround themselves in their homes with that which was artistic. That was quite right, and, speaking to parents, he spoke of the benefit to their children of beautiful sur- roundings. If surroundings made such a change there was no reason why they should not try to make their churches as beautiful as they pos- sibly could. The architecture of the church had its_teaching...

They should remember that symbolism was perfectly right so long as the truths which were symbolised were truths of the Gospel and accepted by the Church, and it only became wrong when it directed them contrary to the teachings of the Church. Those connected with that church had ample scope to do work among the large population of 10,000 people who lived in that VicillitY•

div.head: INDUSTRIAL EXPANSION.
div.p: INDUSTRIAL EXPANSION.
A Twelve Years' Record under Free Trade.
BY CHARLES E. PARKER.

It may be of service to readers interested in the industrial expansion of this country to study the oversea exchanges in relation to certain trades as shown in tile Board of Trade returns. In the comparison instituted below the period covers a dozen years, 1902-1913, inclusive. It was in 1903 that Mr. Chamberlain made that sudden change of front from Free Trade toProtec- tion. It has always been a mystery to me how anyone possessing such intimate knowledge of economic conditions, being acquainted with in- dustrial affairs, not ouly as a manufacturer, but also as a statesman, should so misread the in- dustrial conditions existing in 1902 as to be led into making such gloomy prophecies of coming disaster: And further, that he should recom- mend Protection, or, as it got to be called, Tariff Reform, as the only means of evading the ruin he imagined he foresaw. Enough has been said of the particular trades which would "go," and which have gone ever since, but not in the sense Mr. Chamberlain implied. His Imperial proposals are now re- duced to an attenuated and emasculated residuum. The Colonial Preference part is in- definitely postponed, and Protection, naked and unashamed, is all that is left of a discredited political and economic blunder. My present purpose is to take a group of trades, the development of which has engaged my atten- tion, because for one reason or other, they were prominently to the front in the strident ding- dong of this Tariff Reform controversy, which is now happily subsiding.

- - - It will be seen each of these trades have made very substantial progress during the time in question, and that they have as a whole made very much more rapid progress in their exports than the imports of goods which are classed under the same head. It is well to remember that it does not follow that because goods im- ported and exported are included in the same section, and possibly under the same name, they are the same goods. In almost every case such imports have some special character which we cannot profitably give to them in this country. Before dealing with the special trades, we give the figures for the goods classed under manu- factured goods as a whole. The rate of increase beats all records.
EXPORTS. Wholly or malnly manu- factured goods 1913 411,572,145

It is only right to say that part of this in- crease is due to rise in price; this is most marked in raw material, probably 7 per cent. would cover the proportion over the exports and imports of manufactured goods. No one can accurately estimate this proportion, as the char- acter of the goods is constantly changing. which makes it impossible to make an abso- lutely correct comparison of the years in ques- tion.

New Curate of St. Paul's. At the Bishop's Palace, Liverpool, on Monday, the Bishop licensed the Rev. Edward Downham to the curacy of St. Paul's Church, Warrington.
Fire in a Stable. In the early hours of Wednesday morning the Warrington Fire Brigade were summoned to an outbreak of fire at the stables of Messrs. Rich-
....- ardson, coal merchants, in Old-road. The motor engine was soon on the spot, and, owing to the promptitude of the brigade, the damage was limited to a very small sum.

"History of (Mester." At the meeting of the Wycliffe Y.P.S. held on Thursday night, the Rev. T. T. James in the chair, Mr, J. W. Sansom read a paper upon " The Iliktory of Chester." A vote of thanks was passed, on the motion of Mr. E. Jeffery, seconded by Miss A. Wallington.

Buckley-street P.S.A. Society. The usual monthly meeting of the above was held on Sunday. There was a fair attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. Fairhurst, and Mr. 3. Robinson, of St. Helens, was the speaker. The soloist, Mrs. E. A. Sanders, admirably ren- dered "Into Thy hands." Mrs. and Miss Green sang two duets, "What a meeting of the loved„ ones" and " The future lies before me." .31r. 11. Woolley read the lesson.

The Antiquity of Man. br. W. P. Gowland, Liverpool University. will lecture, on Monday, on "The antiquity of al,,,an in the light of recent disnoveries," in the ro-street flail, under the auspices of the Literary and Philosophic Society. There have lie, en many discoveries of late which, have made "le story of man's development more fascinating ever. One of the most important was the Tiding of the Piltdown skull in Sussex, which, is claimed, makes the antiquity of man date '"lndreds of thousands of years further back than was warranted by previous knowledge.

. An open meeting will be held to-morrow after- noon. The speaker will be Councillor Millar, of Widnes; the chairman the Rev. T. T. James, and the soloist Miss E. Hewitt.

div.head: IVarrington Market Prices . •
div.p: IVarrington Market Prices . •

At Warrington market on Wednesday the prices were: Wheat, 4s. 6d. to 4s. Bd. per 701 b.; oats, 28. 6d. to 2s. 9d. per 451 b.; wheat straw, 275. per ton; oat straw, 28s. 6d. per ton; XX flour, 235. 3d. per 2401 b.; bran, Is. 4d. per 201 b.
Mr. W. B. Forshaw a Commissioner for
Oaths.

The Lord Chancellor has been pleased to appoint Mr. W. B. Forshaw, son of Alderman W. J. Forshaw, a Commissioner for Oaths in the Supreme Court of Adjudicature. Mr. Forshaw has been in partnership with his father, under the style of Forshaw and Forshaw, for the laat six years.

Hibernian Appoininents. At a meeting of the local XAcient Order of Hibernians, held on Sunday, Bro. E. Handley was elected President, in place of Bro. D. Currie, who has received an appointment in Birmingham. Bro Currie's departure is greatly regretted by all the members of the Order in Warrington. Bro. John Ryan succeeds Bro. Handley as treasurer.

Team Changes: Jolley Unable to Play. Late last night it was announced that several changes would be made in the Warrington team to go to Leeds to-day. Jolley is unable to play, as he is not fully recovered from the effects of the match at Wigan last Saturday. Daintith will take his place; Tranter will be brought out of the pack to play centre threequarter, and Harmer will take his place in the forwards.

Rylands' Staff Dinner. The twelfth annual staff dinner of Messrs. Rylands Bros. was held in the Lion Hotel last evening, when about 80 were present. Mr. W. P. Rylands presided and proposed the Royal toast. Mr. W. H. Venal)les proposed the toast of the firm and spoke of the good relationship between the management and the staff. Mr. T. Leslie responded. Mr. J. Blackly proposed the toast of " Mr. W. P. Rylands," who later sub- mitted "The Staff," to which Mr. T. Wadsworth replied. A number of excellent items were given by Messrs. T. Humphrey, J. Babbitt, and Senior Angel Blanco (Mr. W. Moores).

div.p: New Punishment Methods.

tiett.33 eeting of the Borough- LicensingJus- a s on Monday the following resolution, which has been passed by the justices in Liverpool and large towns, was adopted: "That, in the Of the justices, the time has now come w°oPthhienenri°,nue less in the interests of justice than of the saving of both time and money, the limita- tion of forty shillings at present imposed in cases of simple larceny and the like, and the limitation of .0 imposed in cases of wilful damage should be abolished by the Legislature, and the powers of the justices extended so as to enable them in their discretion, and with the consent of the accused person, to deal with all such eases, with suitably extended powers of punishment."

div.head: AVonders of East Africa: Philornathic Lecture.
div.p: The AVonders of East Africa: Philornathic Lecture.

On Wednesday evening, at the Old Parlour, Cairo-street Schools, Mr. J. E. 0. Thompson lec- tured to the members of the Warrington Philo- mathic Society and their friends on " British East Africa." After describing the Protectorate, Mr. Thompson gave a graphic account of the exploration of the interior. He next dealt with the Vganda Railway, revealing some of the diffi- culties and exciting hazards which attended its construction. His portrayal of the native tribes proved especially interesting. He con- cluded with an account of the big game of British East Africa, in the course of which he disclosed many surprising zoological facts. The lecture, which throughout was marked by a comprehensiveness and lucidity that gripped the audience, was admirably illustrated with lantern slides, Mr. Hedley H. Taylor operating the lantern. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded Mr. Thompson. Mr. J. Walsh presided.

div.head: Crosfield's Band and Charily.
div.p: Crosfield's Band and Charily.

Always to the fore in the cause of charity, Crosfield's Band added further to their reputa- tion for this good work by giving a concert in the Hippodrome on Sunday afternoon in aid of the Nursing Association. They gave of their best and delighted the audience. Two new works were presented from the pen of Mr. Josef Holbrooke, who came to Warrington specially to conduct the rendition of his two specialities. One, "April Fool's Day," was a tuneful, if airy, triple, and it met with approval. The other was a march, "Romance and Reality," which did more justice to the composer's capabilities than the first. Many old favourites figured upon the programme, and these were played as only Crosfield's Band can play them. Mr. W. Halliwell skilfully controlled the band, and two first-class solos were given, one on the trombone by Mr. J. E. Hacking, and the other on the cornet by Mr. W. Ellison. div.head: Tanning Outlook: Prices High, But
div.p: Tanning Outlook: Prices High, But
Trade Strong.

It is not my purpose to pose as an alarmist on trade matters, says the Warrington correspon- dent of the "Leather World," but I cannot help feeling convinced that a very difficult time is ahead for the leather trade generally, when record prices will reign for both raw and finished goods. There is not much room for doubt now that there is a shortage of hides which is likely to be very severely felt as the season advances. Several tanners with whom I have discussed the point refer to the way in which live stocks have been depleted by the enormous slaughter of calves, and aver we shall see hides touching a figure which has hardly been dreamed of before. As evidence there is already a worldwide upward move; home markets are rising, the Continent is demanding advances all round, and in America we see advances being made, although the hides were only "poor mid-winter quality." Of the two chief branches of our trade it will be the manufacturing side which will likely feel the ! pinch most severely, for generally they have ' been playing a waiting game, but have probably waited too long, as any considerable weight of stuff is not to be had now except at increased figures. Tanners, on the other hand, are fairly well covered for all they have to deliver, and, taking alarm from the outlook, are itrongly disinclined to take on any further obligations.' Turning to the immediate present, I find trade much stronger, and leather of all classes moving more freely; the home demand is still mainly confined to " hand-to-mouth " orders, although these are growing in size, but there is a full inquiry for export, and as this section calls for ,a minimum of negotiation, no fuss or com- plaints, and asking prices freely paid, it is a factor of which our home consumers should take serious heed.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 7, 1914. " EXAMIPER" AND "THE TRIP."
Trinity Church Social. The annual congregational social evening will be held in Patten Hall next Thursday.
New School.
The Education Committee invite competitive plans for the proposed new school in Lovely- lane.

Cheaper Bread. The local Master Bakers' and Confectioners' Association announce that they will reduce the price of bread id. per 41b. loaf from Monday. Protecting Wild Birds. The Warrington Borough Council make an important announcement concerning the pro- tection of wild birds, and particulars will be found in the advertisement on the front page.

div.head: Life and Death.
div.p: Life and Death.
There were 35 deaths in Warrington last week. giving a rate of 24.5. Births numbered 41, giv- ing a rate of 29.4. There were 11 new cases of scarlet fever, and there are 66 cases now in hospital.

The Warrington Infirmary. The Honorary Treasurer, Mr. Roger C. Parr, gratefully acknowledges a contribution of £2l from Mr. W. A. Savage, "Zillah," Appleton, in respect of which Mr. Savage becomes a life governor of the Institution.

div.head: Catholic Evidence Lectures.
div.p: Catholic Evidence Lectures.

Important lectures will be given under thc auspices of the Catholic Evidence Lectures in St. Mary's, Buttermarket-street, on Sunday, 15th .February, and during the week. The lecturers will be Fathers Downey and Crea. On Sunday the lecture is at 6.30 p.m. and on loriday and during the week at 8 p.m.

div.head: "The Old Guard."
div.p: "The Old Guard."

The famous conric—o-p—era—,-;71`1; Old Guard," is to be presented by the Crosfield Amateur Operatic Society in the Royal Court Theatre during the week commencing 2.3 rd February From what we know of the capabilities of the society, Planquette's masterpiece will get a great rendering. Bumper houses should be the nightly rule.

Captain Crosiield and the Junior Liberals. The long-promised debate on National Service will take place at the rooms of the Junior Liberal Al4sociation, Horsemarket-street, next Tuesday evening. The affirmative will be taken by Captain Crosfield, and the negative by Mr. George Toulmin.

div.head: Museum Lectures.
div.p: Museum Lectures.

To-night the first of a series of popular lectures to be delivered at the Co-operative Hall, under the auspices of the Ogden Trustees, will be given by Mr. B. ff. Mullen, M.A., Curator of the Pub- lic Museums, Salford, who will speak on "How to enjoy a good picture." There will be lantern illustrations. No charge will be made for ad- mission.

Spring Cleaning and the Poor. Miss Hroadbent, The Hollies, Latchford, writes:—" Now that the time of spring cleaning is coming round, may I remind your readers how grateful I am for old magazines, books, or work materials of any kind, for the inmates of the Workhouse Hospital?. Any parcels left at the Workhouse Lodge addressed to me will be safely delivered, and the contents turned to good account."

div.head: Land Reform Demonstration.
div.p: Land Reform Demonstration.

There will be a great land reform demonstra- tion in Parr Hall on Saturday, February 21st, in support of the Government proposals, undei the auspices of the Junior Liberal Association. The speakers will include Mr. G. Hay Morgan, LC., M.P., Alderman F. W. Raffan, MT., Dr. Charles W. Hayward, prospective Liberal can- didate for Eddisbury, and Mr. J. B. Martindale. prospective Liberal candidate for Widnes. Mr Arthur Crosfield will be in the chair.

Why the Opposition Withdrew. At the meeting of the Warrington Rural Dis- trict 'Council on Wednesday it was decided to allow the Surveyor, Mr. Newcomb, .270 for the use of his motor car, which be used whilst fol- lowing his duties. There was at first some opposition to such an amount, but when it wae stated that special sub-committees were con- veyed in the car to transact Council work the opposition was withdrawn.

Child Killed by Lurry. An inquest was conducted on Thursday by Deputy Coroner F. A. Jones on Emily Tierney, 13 months old, who resided with her parents at 47, Lythgoes-lane. The child was on Wednes- day afternoon playing on the footpath, when the Mother went into a neighbour's house, and soon afterwards she heard a scream, and found her child lying a few yards from the footpath. The girl had been run over by the front wheel of a lurry in charge of William Burgess, of 34, Cyril-street.—A verdict of " Accidental death' was returned, the driver being exonerated from all blame.

Unpopular—A Bachelor. Asked to write down and hand in what they deemed the most unpopular thing in the world, a Legh-street Primitive Methodist audience, at a lecture on Thursday night, got much merri- ment out of the incident. One paper—suspected to be the work of some fair maid—described the most unpopular thing as "a bachelor." The fun was all the more merry from the fact that the lecturer was outside the ranks of the bene- diets. The lecture was entitled "The most un- popular thing in the world," and the lecturer was the Rev. J. Watkin, Birkenhead. His defini- tion of the most unpopular thing was "work." He treated the subject in a humorous way, and the audience were much entertained.

div.head: Opposition Make a Brave Effort to Save
div.p: The Opposition Make a Brave Effort to Save
Their Face—But Fail.

It is increasingly clear that the way in which " The Examiner" exposed the Tory trick that was intended to delude the public into the idea that " Local Liberals denounce Home Rule," has caused not a little dismay in the Opposition camp.

At last Friday night's Unionist demonstration Mr. Harold Smith, M.P., hard pressed for some way of getting his friends out of a tangle, drew attention to two printer's errors that have appeared in "The Examiner" in the course of two years. His system of logic would appear to produce the following result:—" The Examiner" two Years ago had a word misplaced, and a week ago a picture out of place; therefore the " Liberals " who went to Ireland were really Liberals. So far as we are concerned he .is welcome to the logic, and so far as the Liberal party are concerned he is welcome to the "Liberals." He certainly appears to know

more about them and their claim to the title than Liberals do. If Mr. Smith will look nearer home than "The Examiner" office he will find a much richer quarry for his exceptional gifts as a snapper up of usually unconsidered trifles. We have already read his " organ " a lesson on the inadvisability of throwing stones on the part of those who live in glass house*. If our gifted contemporary desires to return to the charge, either directly or from behind Mr. Smith's sheltering form, we shall not fear the net result. But we shall not need to trouble about such minor matters when we are able to show our readers such things as are embodied in the following. The first column contains the criticism of ourselves by the "Observer," and the second the criticism of ourselves by the "Guardian." As will be seen, there is a strik- ing similarity :

div.head: "LIBERAL CONSTERNATION."
div.p: "LIBERAL CONSTERNATION."

To the Editor of "The Examiner." Sir,—The measure of Liberal consternation at the results of Lady Greenall's Party is to be found in the frantic efforts made to discount their repo& "An Ulster Protestant" is the latest who tries his hand. I will just deal with one of his points. Intimidation. He says: "Did the deputation find that in all the most important Catholic towns many of the largest business men were Protestants who were depending entirely upon Catholic customers for support? If the Nation- alists and Catholics of Ireland are intolerant, would such a state of things exist?" It is quite true, and in many cases the Protestants are almost the only people, by reason of their thrift and industry, who do the trade of the place. The Nationalist deals with them simply because there may not be a grocer or baker of his own persuasion' who meets his requirements pro- perly. But toleration! The following resolution speaks for itself : " Resolved : That we. the members of the A. 0.11., , Sligo Division (No. 23), strongly dissent, andl place on record our united protest !igainat the, conduct of a number of local Piotestant roar.'

chants who, whilst liviog in a community which is ninety per cent. Catholic, and on whom they are almost entirely dependent, publicly state their disapproval of the Home Rule scheme for Ireland on the alleged grounds of finance, and that we hereby call on all the Divisions of the Order in the country to note the signatories to this treacherous document to whom Home Rulers' money must be as equally objectionable as Home Rule itself.
" JAMES COLLERY, " HENRY MONSON."

These men are only to be "tolerated" while they "keep their heads shut." If they want peace they must abandon the elementary right of free men, the right to express their opinion upon political matters. H. S. NEALE. Union Defence League, Westminster, S.W., February 3rd, 1914.

div.head: MR. ENGLAND AND MAJORITY
div.p: MR. ENGLAND AND MAJORITY
TRAGEDIES.
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

- Sir,—Referring to Mr. C. E. Parker's article of last week, which is couched, as is usual from him, in courteous terms, may I say that though it raises some excellent debatable points, yet his arguments are somewhat "academic." lie impugns the Liberalism of part of the deputation. In doing so he might as well impugn the Liberalism of the men of Ulster, the great majority of whom are Liberals, and have been so for generations. But what. is more to the point is that the Government —a Professedly Liberal Govern- ment—have in this Home Rule Bill scattered to the winds some of their great Liberal principles. How, for example,, do they reconcile the fact that 42 Irish members under the Bill are to sit at Westminster and legislate on English, Scotch and Welsh Bills, and yet at the same time the House of Commons will have no power to legis- late on Irish affairs? Is this Liberalism? No, it is an absurdity, and a ridiculous privilege as well. . . _ _ _

Then, again, this Liberal Government pro- fesses to be a Free Trade Government. Is not this so? And yet under this Bill they allow the Irish Parliament to legislate and fix duties on manufactured goods imported into Ireland, and also excise duties on articles produced in Ire- land. Another great Liberal principle gone— though this went some time ago. The fact of the whole matter is that this Government—ostensibly Liberal—is, after all, a "Coalition Government," and the United King- dom is now called upon to pay its price. Mr. Parker very naturally raises the "major- ity" principle. There happens, however, to be in Ireland practically two races of people, the minority being in Ulster. This minority has demonstrated in all that counts that is best in life as being the superior race of the two. That cannot be gainsaid. The people of the North, despite greater difficulties than have been ex- perienced by the men of the South, have left them far behind in most of the arts and manu- factures of civilisation. _ _

However, no seriously minded or deep think- ing man will allow everything to be dominated by the ' principle of majority." The world has witnessed too many tragedies already by bow- ing to the will of the majority. "When the people were asked, 'Whom is it that I shall release unto you—this man or Barabbas?' the people cried Barabbas!' And Barabbas was released, and the other man went to the Cross." No, it is not majorities that must prevail, but reason—for the majority of to-day may easily be the minority of to-morrow. It is in the name of "Reason" why Ulster. realising that under this Home Rule Bill will be under the rule of the Nationalists, has, like Cromwell of old, taken up the sword in the defence of her civil and religious liberties. E. ENGLAND.

div.head: ON THE DEFENCE.
div.p: ON THE DEFENCE.
"The Deputation" Reply to "An Ulster Protestant." " PRINCIPLE " OF HONE ROLE NOT
INVOLVED.
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—The representatives of the local Liberal party must surely feel thankful to "An Ulster Protestant" for coming to their aid and at- tempting, at any rate, to reply to the report of the recent deputation to Ireland. We might reasonably have declinedlo deal with an anony- mous correspondent, but we feel that full dis- cussion cannot fail to be of service in the present crisis; and we content ourselves with expressing the hope that "An Ulster Protestant" will dis- close his identity, so that we may know to whom we have the privilege of responding. It is perfectly easy to justify the whole of our conclusions up to the hilt. Suppose we take items seriatim:—

div.head: ' I.—Rates and Slums.
div.p: ' I.—Rates and Slums.

The report said that in the places we visited, where Nationalists had the control, the rates were high, and the conditions unsatisfactory. In the principal Nationalist centres we I visited the rates were given to us as follows: Dublin, 10s. 3d. in the ; Sligo, us. Id. in the :..e; and in Longford the figures are very little less.

With reference to Sligo, we would draw atten- tion to the report of the auditor of the Local Government Board for the year ending March 31st, 1913, which contains some scathing critic- isms of the administration of the town, particu- lar reference being made to the large amount of uncollected rates, which include arrears of not less than ..C2/3, which were owing by Nation- alist members of the Council at the close of the audit.

As to the Dublin slums, the report is not con- tested, the age of the city apparently being urged as the excuse. No answer is made to the charge of "filthy streets." for which the repre- sentatives responsible for the government of the city must certainly be held responsible. Contrast the above with the clean and pros- Perous condition of the Ulster towns we visited. Enniskillen, where the•rates are about 4s. 6d. in the X; Omagh, Cs. &I. to about is. 4d. in the Portadown, is. 4d. in the ..C; and Belfast, 7s. id. in the 11.—Intimidation.

- Many proofs of intimidation and boycotting can be provided. In Longford and Newtown Forbes, the cases of Mr. Michael McCann and others will doubtless be familiar to your corre- spondent, and it is definitely asserted that cases of boycotting were met with which were en- tirely due to religious or political reasons, some of the boycotts resulting from refusals to sub- scribe to the funds of the United Irish League. In Sligo, recently, several of the business men of the town actually had the audacity to sign al statement criticising the present Home Rule Bill solely on business and financial grounds, and the reply of the League to this daring ex- pression of opinion was to issue a manifesto, calling upon the people of the district "to assume in all matters an altered attitude to- wards the gentlemen concerned," and "request- ing that they be deprived of every privilege they were heretofore welcome to enjoy." A report in the "Irish Times" of the 12th January, 1914, will amply confirm this state- ment. 111.—Land and Housing Reform. We are glad that it is admitted that the Land Acts are effecting a peaceful revolution in Ire- land. No one will wish to withhold any of the credit that may be legitimately due to those who are now clamouring for Home Rule, although their methods are open to much criticism; but it must be remembered that the Acts were passed under the British Parliament sitting at Westminster, whose statesmen (mainly Union- ists) framed the Bills, arid, through their repre- sentatives, largely administered the Acts. Can it be claimed that such splendid progress would have been made under a separate Parliament, openly hostile to this country, the avowed aim of many whose advocates is complete and final separation?

Bees your correspondent desire us to give him evidence of this fearful and disgraceful dis- loyr.lty; of episodes such as the rejoicing over Boer victories, the erection of memorials to men fighting against our soldiers, the spitting on and burning of the Union Jack, the open cam- paigning against recruiting for the British Army, and the like?
Unfortunately, the evidence is only too abundant.
I V..—Ulster Prosperity.

. . There is again no attempt made to criticise this clause of the report. On the subject of emigration one has to look much further than the present measure of Rome Rule to find an explanation, for even in " com- fortable and prosperous England," alas! the emigration figures are extremely disquieting.

- - But as an index to Ulster's general prosperity, your correspondent might have mentioned the poor rate, which is much lower in Ulster than in any of the other provinces of Ireland. Inquiries were made with regard to wages in Belfast, and the trade unionists among the deputation found that the standard was some- times as high, and sometimes higher than in the corresponding branches of similar trades in England. The average set down by your corre- spondent is obviously unfair and misleading, as it is necessary to ascertain exactly the propor- tion of women and girl workers included in each comparison before it can be of any real use. V.—The Rights of Self-Government..

The reference to South Africa, as an aid to your correspondent's argument, in view of recent events, is somewhat surprising, but with this we are not immediately concerned. Again there is no denial of the conclusions in the re- port, and we would particularly ask our fejlow townsmen to note the serious attention devoted by your correspondent to our statement as to the "sincerity and grim determination" of the Ulster Unionists. He, at any rate, does not repeat or support the opinion that Ulster is bluffing, to which time after time, month after month, you have given expression in the columns of " The Examiner." He does not even refer to wooden guns! And your correspondent, who presumably re- sides in Belfast, has had many opportunities of forming an opinion. May we venture to call your attention to the words which appeared in last Monday's "Daily 11 News " : "The Ulster Position.—Those who know best the state of affairs in Ulster know ' that at this moment it is a very dangerous one. There should certainly be no more speeches on the Ministerial side about • Bluff.' It is con- ceivable that if there had been fewer of such speeches in the past the position now might have been easier." Will your readers accept that? VI. Your correspondent, in his last paragraph, opens out a great field for controversial matter. What does he mean by "legitimate National aspirations"? Can he deny the evidence of desire for complete and final separation from this country? Is this a legitimate National aspiration for Ireland? Has he read the in- scription on the Parnell monument in Dublin, erected less than two years ago? Even the reality of the demand for "Home Rule" by such an overwhelming multitude of the people of Ire- land, which is always urged as a convincing reason, is at least a matter of argument, and we had many evidences of the fact that there is a large body of public opinion in Ireland, which, if it only dared to find expression, is entirely hostile to the scheme.

Let your correspondent note that our inquiry was not into the principle of Rome Rule, but as to the position with regard to the Bill which is now before Parliament, and which is, we are told, to be thrust upon the sister country, if necessary, at the point of the bayonet. The conditions have to be taken as they at present exist. Our conclusions were based on these, and we submit that they have not been weakened in any way whatever by your correspondent's reply.
We can, however, thank him for the spirit of serious attention which he has been gr.- enough to give our report, because we )-
