div.head: CLAIM OF ULSTER
div.p: THE CLAIM OF ULSTER
AND OF THE
WARRINGTON DEPUTATION
DICTATE NATIONAL POLICY.
By CHARLES E. PARKER. In the report of the local deputation to Ireland, Section 4, we have the followirg words: " In Ulster there was every sign of increas-

ing industry, comfort, and -prot-iperity." No one denies that North-East Ulster is the most prosperous part of Ireland, although the relative prosperity has been much exaggerated. But I fail ,to see that the four counties in the north-east corner of Ulster, even whpn backed by a Warrington deputation, have the right, because of their wealth, to say to the remaining 28 counties that these are not to have Home Rule because they are not so well off.
_ PRESENT CONDITIONS RESULT OF THE PAST.

It is well that we should understand the causes which have resultea in the relative mate- rial welfare in this small corner of Ireland, in which the linen trade is the chief i3ol.lres of the prosperity. You cannot divorce human affairs from their past- Present conditions in -Ulster are the result of this past. The two principal causes which have produced these results are.:—

First, the oppression of the Catholics, parti- cularly by means of the penal code. Second (bound up with and a part of the first), the strangling of the industrial develop Anent the trades of Ireland which were in the hands of the Catholics, and the encouragement of t.he linen industry in the hands of the Ulster Orange section. The latter was composed mainly of people from Scotland and England, who were planted in Ireland during various reigns on estatea confiscated from the original Catholic inhabitants.

div.head: PENAL LAWS.
div.p: THE PENAL LAWS.

The penal laws against Catholics debarral them from education and from stations of in- fluence. Their lands and property were conas- cated and distributed to various new-created lords "upon the express condition that such should plant a certain number of English families on his own estate, and that he should not suffer any Irish to rent, or otherwise occupy any part thereof." As late as the latter part of George the Third's reign no Catholic (al- though the persons professing that religion numbered five-sixths of the entire population) was permitted to carry arms in his own defence, to acquire property on land, to lend money on mortgage, to vote in the election of Members to Parliament, to act as guardian to his own chil- dren, or to have the least share in the manage- ment of the country, or parochial affairs of the district to which he belonged. Catholics' lands were confiscated and handed over to settlers from England and Scotland, or to those who turned from their faith. There is no country in Europe in which the confiscation of the land has so often been repeated as in Ireland. Apart from laws the history of Ireland may be described as that of a series of sanguinary wars • fomented for the purpose of confiscation. CATHOLIC INDUSTRY CRIPPLED.

In industrial development the policy of England as against Ireland has been equally cruel and unjust. The whole Anti- Irish policy of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries was simply a process of protecting English production against the com- petition of their fellow-subjects across St. George's Channel. English statesmen strove to suppress, as far as possible, every species of enterprise in which the Irish competed. Ire- land was kept in primitive penury in tho inter- est of the predominant partner. Nor was this action purely economic. Strafford fostered the Irish linen trade of Ulster while deliberately repressing the rise of the woollen manufacture, which was almost entirely in tho hands of the Catholics. Nor was this policy confined to manufactures. After the Restoration a Bill was passed to prohibit the importation of Irish cattle, sheep, swine, beef, and pork into Eng- land. As a result the Irish sought markets abroad, and foreign exports of wool and the manufacture of woollen fabrics considerably developed. The Irish competition in foreign markets was soon felt by English woollen manu- facturers, and Parliament was induced to put a 20 per cent. export duty on Irish broad-cloths, thus handicapping Irish export. Later a Bill was passed absolutely prohibiting the exports from Ireland of any goods made or mixed with wool. The wool trade was thus effectually crippled. In connection with the strangling of the wool trade there was, as a set-off, an engage- ment that the linen and hemp trade centred in North-East Ulster would be encouraged, and as a result the flax trade in the Ulster district became firmly established. It is true in later years there was a duty almost prohibitive for a time put on linen goods from the North of Ire- land, but, unlike the woollen trade, Ireland was still allowed to export linen goods, thus giving a preference to the Ulster trade.

For about two centuries England used Ireland, and especially Catholic Ireland, solely for the benefit of English manufacture, crushing any trade that competed; consequently, at the rebel- lion of 1798, the time of the Political Union, there was left a torn and exhausted Ireland—all except North-East Ulster.

I have no brief for the Catholics as such. The times in which these deeds were done were cruel and selfish. The Protestants were top dogs, and they made the under dog suffer. It is no answer to say that when and where Catholics were in power they were equally intolerant It is not ray purpose to weigh the merits or discuss ' the effects of the two faiths .upon their followers. f3,' purpose is to show the reason why the condi- tions of N.E. Ulster and its industry is one of prosperity. lam quite ready to admit that the people of Ulster may, as a mixed race, be better skilled in the art of making money than the Irish pecple as a whole. Many of them are of Scotch origin, and having been reared in that country myself I know something of the qualities in this people which make for material success. But the present success in Ulster could not have been achieved without the favourable treat- ment granted to them and denied to the rest of Ireland.

EFFECT OF PREFERENTIAL TREATMENT. But the effect of this preference has not been altogether good.' It has developed the spirit of boasting and ascendancy. The pampered Ulster men now say to the world in general, and to the Warrington deputation in particular, "Look at us, how rich and prosperous we are, and how comparatively poor and unenterprising is the rest of Ireland." They swell themselves out and claim their prosperity to be the outcome of their superior intelligence and business capacity, and the deputation innocently believe it all— and so they say in paragraph number five of the report

"The vast majority of the people of North-East Ulster are convinced that Rome Rule would ruin the industrial development of the province, and be of no practical benefit to the rest of Ireland, and with that conviction we are in agreement."

And so it comes about that this small minority in North-East Vster; four counties out of the 32, are to determine and dictate a policy not only for themselves, but, forsooth, for the whole of Ireland, and this Warrington deputation, in- cluding a number who still are pleased to call themselves Liberals, are in entire agreement with this presumptuous and undemocratic claim.
ON THE DEFENCE—continued.

that the more discussion there is upon the sub- ject the more the British people will begin to realise the overwhelming strength of the case for the rejection of the present measure, which will assuredly bring "not peace, but a sword." Yours, &c., GEO. IT. SMITH, WILLIAM HEALEY, W. H. BELLIAN, EDWARD WILLIAMS. RALPH DONE, GEO. RAVENSCROFT, JAMES H. ALLEN, J. B. J. McDERMID, J. E. WARREN, R.! ALBERT REGAN, E. ENGLAND, , ARTHUR BENNETT. Wexrinetto, Cth February. 1914.

div.head: STRIKES AND POLITICS.
div.p: STRIKES AND POLITICS.
" Ignorant Revolt Instead of lntdiigcnt Adaptation."
To the Editor of "The Examiner."
Sir,—Persist as I may, I cannot get Mr. Dukes

to discuss_the thing that really matters. • He is quite prepared to write about Rip Van Winkle, or any mortal thing; but give a sensible explan- ation of his own attitude he will not. In like manner do I refuse to hide his position behind the closed doors of a trade union. Also do I reserve inyself the right to criticise whom I like, and where I think, best. In spite of the immo- bility of my mind I might say that my mental activities have act become so restricted that my criticisms cannot extend beyond what I think

_ about Liberal and Tories, National Service, &c., but if I think that the actions of those whose activities are supposed to be solely confined to raising the material basis of the working class are wrong, I shall criticise; and Mr. Dukes and his marionettes can draw whatever conclusions they like. I do not wish to flash signals to the "enemy." But I do wish to be particularly energetic with those persons who, under the guise of "fighting" far the working class, advocate nostrums that look like putting their particular selves upon a pedestal. I say, and Mr. Dukes has also said, that poli- tical action has done little more than put work- ing men upon a pedestal, and also supplied them with more material wants than a wreath of olive leaves. Also the same with industrial action. The workers are beaten through superior knowledge and a greater stock of life's necessities every time. Why not let us admit it Why delude ourselves always that it is this that is wrong, and it is there where lies the mistake; any and everywhere but the right place? If the working class were as intelligent as the employing classes they would soon grasp the fundamental mistake that underlies great wealth and great poverty. The only thing that keeps a pig satisfied with a life in filth is that it has not the mental capacity to conceive of any- thing higher. It will not make things any the better by first saying the worker is poor because he has not as yet got sufficient gumption to organise his labour power, and he must refuse to produce commo- dities unless he gets a certain wage for doing so. Mr. Dukes ought to know that wages do not mean anything but a certain measure of mate- rial comfort. Then the workers are told, after being battered in an unequal struggle, that cessation of production is not progress, but a policy of pulling down, and we must "go in" for political action. That is, the working class must send men of superior intelligence, drawn from their own class, to a legislative and admin- istrative body to look after the business of the worker. Now, I ask, is not that hero-worship with a vengeance, and also an admission that the working class are incapable of looking to their own affairs? In both political and industrial action the work- ing class leaders are beaten by the very people for whom they are working. They cannot get the backing needed. The occurrences in South Africa are the logical outcome of the policy of the workers wanting something, and not know- ing how to get it. In South Africa the workers have sent affew men to Parliament to ask the capitalist air better conditions. That is what is known as moral force. Appealing to the capitalist's humanity and common-sense to give them a decent livelihood: a little may come from that source, I admit. In South Africa they have also tried to force better conditions by means of the strike. This puts the capitalist to use all his means of forcing the worker to work under the capitalist conditions. And the capitalist does it by using armed force.' But does not Mr. Dukes see that all this asking for better conditions admits the principles that the capitalist is supreme? It is something like me asking Jack Johnson, after I have given him my purse, for a shilling. I will try to persuade him with unanswerable arguments and flowery language if possible, but if I cannot get the shilling by that means, I say I will force it out of him. In the case of persuasion I might get something out of him, but in the case of force I get what I deserve for being so stupid. Such is my opinion of political and industrial action, and that is what I mean by saying that the workers are always prepared for igaorant revolt instead of intelligent adaptation. One is fighting for better conditions, the other is asking for them. Both are ridiculous. Fight- ing the capitalist will get the worker all the bruises he deserves; and asking for better con- ditions might get a little good. But if the worker wants to live the life that he is rightly entitled to he must understand first the economic laws controlling life. And Ido not think that the mass of the people will deliberately under- take to study fundamental economics. Some of us may, and I suppose we must pay the -penalty for doing so by having our body and soul constantly tortured by the very enlighten- ment that ts-hould have proved our blessing. The mass of the people will, in my own esti- mation, be dragged along by force of economic circumstance. And the basis of the working class improvement is, in- my opinion, the co- operative movement. Whilst' Socialists have been raving about public bread supply, &e., the "Stores" have done it. But why I believe that "Stores" are going to be the instrument for working class emancipation is because it appeals to the ..e e. d. side of the worker. If there is any trut,h in the assertion that co-operative pro- duction and distribution eliminates all unneces- cost in production and distribution, then the "Stores" ought to beat the capitalist easy in the price of commodities. One illustration, and then I have finished. At

div.head: CHAMPIONS OF THE OPPRESSED.
div.p: CHAMPIONS OF THE OPPRESSED.
What the Missionaries Have Done for Nations Abroad.

"By the law of God there can never be oppressed people in any nation without the effect of their oppression re-acting upon the masters." Such were the words of the Rev. H. Ogden,i stc Church o uwrho, Sunday evening,preachinguatGolbo tookrne-st for tßahpi- ts subject "The emancipation of the slave." He chose for his test, "Go ye therefore and teach all nations," and "Lo, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world." Dealing principally with missionaries, and particularly the' work of tho Baptist Missionary in Jamaica, the preacher said the Missionary had always been the eman- cipator of the people, and the champion of the oppressed. It was very true that a "thousand years in God's sight are but as yesterday, or a watch in the night," but 100 years was a very far cry in human life. Between the beginning of Carey's work in India and the centenary of that work much water had passed beneath the bridges. He ventured to believe that between Carey's work—more than 100 years ago—and the present representations of India on the Viceroy's Council there was a close cOnnection. Probably many people would assign the reason to -work such as Annie Besant's, but a little investigation would reveal that the most intelligent social Students in India were Christians.

div.head: Emancipation Bound to Follow.
div.p: Emancipation Bound to Follow.

Emancipation was bound to follow the preach- ing of the Gospel, and equally so was that true of Jamaica. In 1814 the work of the Baptist Missionary Society was begun. At the time when Columbus discovered America the aborigines of Jamaica were Red Indians, strangely christened by the Spaniards as "Red. Demons." Columbus established that the world was round. His Church established that by tyranny and oppression, and by vice and cruelty, the native races could be wiped out. In , less than two centuries the work of destruction ' was completed. By 1814 the reins of govern- ment had passed from Spanish hands to English hands. The Englishmen established the curse of all time in Jamaica. They determined to secure the amount of work for the minimum wage. The negroes were brought from Central Africa and from the Coast. The "Black Hole, of Calcutta" seemed to have been paradise com- pared with the holds of these slave ships. Chained and huddled together, the slaves died in hundreds, and the putrefaction, dirt, filth and darkness were indescribable. When any were fortunate enough to arrive at Jamaica they became the brutalised slaves of the English ranch owners. By the law of God there could never be oppressed people in any nation without the effect of their oppression reacting upon the masters. The submerged tenth was always a menace to the swimming population. The East End of London was not too far from the West for the West End to feel it. The- planters and white overseers set aside their lawful wives and took unto themselves negresses as mistresses. One had only to read "Uncle Tom's Cabin" to discover how such vice reacted upon the families of the white people. It was a general truth that a.good master made a good servant and the tyrant produced a villain. The great work of redemption, namely, the emancipation of slaves was wrought by William Knibb and Thomas 1 Burchell. About 1814 the Baptist Missionaries focussed a large proportion of their income upon the island. One-fourth of the revenue was sent to Jamaica, and the effect was now seen in the fact that there were 60 Baptist negro pastors, 150 churches, and 35,000 church members. One of Knibb',s reports stated that he himself barely escaped prison. He stood by one of his coloured workers whilst the negro was flogged for wor- shipping God, and it was not strange, when they read the history of all emancipation, to find that Knibb's most terrible antagonists were his own countrymen. "Scratch the pocket of any man, white .or 'black, and you will catch a tartar." In 1833 Knibb came to England. On the one hand he was met by indifference, and on the other by determined opposition.

div.head: Must Speak the Truth.
div.p: Must Speak the Truth.

On one occasion, when speaking, he was advised not to mention Jamaica lest he imperilled the income of the Baptist Missionary Society, but he said he must speak the truth, as he felt it within him. The country was at last roused—such honoured men as William Brock. of Norwich, making great sacrifices on behalf of the cause. By 1838 the country had become converted, and £20,000,000 was expended for the freedom of 800,000 slaves. Eight hundred thousand people for the first time tasting liberty would be a menace to any community, but Baptist pastors were ready, churches were formed, and now, in 1914, Jamaica not only sup- ported all their own churches and pastors, not only educated the children on the island, but Missionaries were sent to the Congo to tell the story which had wrought such social redemption in one century amongst the coloured people of Jamaica.

the ,present there is a scarcity of houses here in Warrington. Rents are going up- Now, the Co-operative Society could build houses and rent them cheaper than the private owner. Higher rents are forcing the workers to build their houses. And so we might go on. It may be a poor consolation to some of us who want letter conditions. But burking facts will not bring them, any more than idolising men and sending them to Parliament will. It is all fiddlesticks Mr. Dukes saying that he is not ambitions to get to Parliament. Why all this activity of him- self and his colleagues? I was certainly amused by Mr. Dukes saying that we understand each .other perfectly and are only writing to create interest, &c. STOeKTON HEATH.
Dukes: They would be able to see better. (More laughter.)--The matter was left in the hands of the Lighting Committee.

Active Liberalism.—There has been much activity in the ranks of Liberalism in Stockton Heath recently, and several effective meetings have been held. Now the hour of the social function has arrived and this takes the form of the annual tea to be held on Thursday evening in the Providence Schoolroom, Chapel-lane. The tea will be under the auspices of the Stockton Heath and District Women's Liberal Associa- tion. After tea an important meeting is to be held. The chief speaker will be Miss Shaw, a London lady, who has ,done much good work foi Liberalism. Mr. P. M. Oliver will also address the meeting and the chair will be occupied bY Mrs. Henry Roberts. The entertainment will be given by Mrs". Sanders and Mr. H. M. Ashton, two well-known and popular artistes. The entertainment and meeting starts at 7.30 pia.

A Rabbit Tale.—Arising out &I the report of the Sanitary Inspector on a case of infectious disease at the Parochial Committee Meefing on Tuesday, Councillor Dukes said that it seemed the cause of the infection in Derby-road was the dampness and the stagnant water. The matter had been raised at four monthly meetings, but each time it had been put off. Something ought to be done. The walls were covered with mil- dew.—The Clerk lam pleased to say the con- tract has been signed and work is pikeeding.— Councillor Whitley, addressing Mr. Dukes : TT:we you heard that at the house from where the affected children were taken there were about twenty rabbits in the yard, and that gave a verY offensive smell.—Councillor Dukes: I did not know about the rabbits. I thought that the disease was more likely to have occurred through the stagnant water than from the menagerie—(laughter)—in the yard.—Councillor Clark suggested that the contractor should be asked to remove the cause of the water first, and the committee. approved of the proposal.

div.head: TOWNSHIP TITTLE-TATTLE.
div.p: TOWNSHIP TITTLE-TATTLE.

Did the plans for cottage property Frighten the Councillors on Tuesday night? They wore the look of pure alarm. * What will next happen to the scheme? The Fire Brigade are to practice to-day. "John Bull" should be asked to attend ' To see that they are not what he said Our local fire-fighters were a few weeks ago. Out of 200 letters sent to the local Property owners to ask their views About improved sanitation in the parish ' Only about 50 troubled to send a reply. Of course, property owners are nowadays so - Very poor they can't afford a penny stamp, And notepaper also costs a bit of money. A new terror awaits the town of Warrington. The Council are to be asked to take up The trouble over the Swing Bridge question. Warrington has already one bridge trouble in hand. Will it tackle still -another bridge problem? The street nameplates are so battered By stone-throwing imps of youngsters That the names of streets can't be read. A Councillor suggests that the names should be Affixed to the lamps, inside the glass. .Then he jocularly added that the self-same Stone-throwers would have more light by which They could see to hit the target, and perhaps Then we might also complain of a "Glass-go." What do the Heathens think about the sug- gested Half-hour service of trams on Sunday morn- inn; • To miss one means a thirty-five minute wait. Another injustice by Warrington some will say.

Members Present.—At the monthly meeting of the Parochial Committee on Tuesday the follow- ing members were present; Councillor G. Pilling (in the chair), and Councillors H. J. Westbrook, F. Warburton, j McDermid, C. Hallows, C. Dukes, F. Rose, J. Whitley, G. F. Clark and F. Pearson.

Dearest in Britain.—According to recent statistics on tramway matters, the lid. fare from Stockton Heath to Warrington, just over li miles, is said to be the dearest tram ride in Great Britain. In some towns passengers are carried five or six miles for the same fare, on one Manchester stage they are carried four miles for the penny.

Wesleyan Church Renovation.—Rapid progress is being made in connection with the renovation and re-decoration of the Wesleyan Church and school, Stockton Heath. The work will be com- pleted within the next few weeks, and then the Wesleyans will have one of the prettiest churches, so far as internal appearances go, in the district.

and Mr. P. M. Oliver. the No Election Picture Posters.—ColonelSykes, the Unionist M.P. for the Knutsford Division, prospective Liberal candidate, have arranged that no picture posters shall be displayed in the division at the next election. Referring to this matter at one of his meetings, Mr. Oliver said the absence of pictures and posters of an objectionable character would mean a saving in their pockets and would also prevent bad blood in the division.

Ashbin Troubte.---The question of repairingaslibius was again raised at the Parocniai Com- mittee meeting on Tuesday night.—Councillor Pearson said that he had seen the blacksmith as to whether ashbins and pails could be repaired, but naturally'The man said he could not say until he had seen samples of damaged bins.—lt was agreed to send a few pails and bins for the blacksmith's inspection.

Postmaster-General's Desire.—At the Paro- chial Committee meeting on Tuesday it was stated that the Postmaster-General was seeking permission to erect telegraph posts and lay an underground line in Stockton Heath. The Council's Surveyor recommended that the con- sent he given, so far as the streets were con- cerned, provided the posts are fixed and, the underground lines laid to the satisfaction of the District Council's Surveyor. This was agreed, after some discussion. ,

Dumb Men Wanted.—At the monthly meet- ing of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee on Tuesday tenders were opened for the empty- ing of ashbins and pails. Cduncillor West- brook suggested that the contractor would undertake to employ dumb men—(laughter)— because some of them created quite a noise at 12 o'clock Midnight by shouting to one another. —lt was decided to accept Mr. Spensley's tender, by which be agreed to do the 'work for .242.0 per annum, with an addition of „.e4O per annum per ashhin, and a deduction of £4O upon every pail which was substituted by the water-carriage system. .

Housing Question.—It was reported at the Parochial Committee meeting on Tuesday that the Sanitary Inspector had made a tour of the district on January 31st, and found that there were only eight unoccupied houses.—The Sur- veyor submitted plans of proposed buildings at Northwich and of houses which have actually been erected at Taunton.—Councillor Duke. thought it was a mattes which should be sub- mitted to a special committee, and after some discussion Councillor Westbrook proposed that the matter be left in the hands of Councillor-. C. Dukes, J. McDermid, P. Warburton, J. Whit- ley and P. Rose.—This was unanimously carried.

A Fresh Temptation.—A practical suggestion with regard to the naming of the streets was submitted by Councillor C. Dukes at the Paro- chial Committee meeting on Tuesday. He thought it would be better to have the names of the streets on the lamps at the corner of the streets. Young boys had been throwing at some of the other name-plates, and at night it was impossible to see the names. Ile suggested zinc plates inside the lamps.—Councillor Whitley: ,That suggestion, if carried out, would tempt boys to throw at them. (Laughter.)—Councillor

div.head: STILL TIIE " SIGH " BRIDGE. Should AVarrington Be Asked to Assist the " Heathens " on Bridge Question?
div.p: STILL TIIE " SIGH " BRIDGE. Should AVarrington Be Asked to Assist the " Heathens " on Bridge Question?
The Swing Bridge is still the " sigh " bridge, and now it is suggested the aid of Warrington should be invoked to get the alleged grievance removed.

At a meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee on Tuesday night a letter was read from the Manchester Ship Canal Company in reply to the Committee's Communication, em- bodying the resolution pahed by the Committee at its last meeting. The company acknowledged receipt of the letter and resolution, and said they had given full consideration to the matter, but in view of the responsibility which would attach to them in the event of anyone receiving injury through being allowed to pass through the gates and on to the bridge before it had regained its ordinary position after having been swung, the company could not, as stated in pre- vious communications, Permit the gates to be opened for road traffic before the bridge was "in situ." At the same time the company's servants would continue to give the best possible attention to the traffic. ,

Council t it was Warrington's matter more than Stockton Heath's. It was an AWON MATTER. ior Clark WARRINGTON important matter for Warrington, and he thought it would be advisable if they could join with Warrington and see the Ship Canal direc- tors and explain their grievances. They had had the gates opened during the last 20 years as soon as the bridge was almost in Place, but that custom was all at once stopped. There had been no complaint or injury at Stock- ton Heath. He thought the reply was unsatis- factory. Councillor Westbrook agreed that Warrington should help them, but he hardly thought Stock- ton Heath should act conjointly with them. and They should t Councillor Clark : In our agreement with the company the clause says the time of opening the independently- says thirteen minutes. It was eventually decided, that the Chairman (Councillor bridge should with t i ) Warrington unreason- able, whilst theagreement Filling) and the Clerk (Mr. Ashton) form a deputation, and that they should attempt to arrange with the Warrington Corporation to join them.

div.head: IMPROVING SANITATION. Many Property Owners Ignore the Committee's Inquiry.
div.p: IMPROVING SANITATION. Many Property Owners Ignore the Committee's Inquiry.

- At the monthly meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee held on Tuesday night, the Clerk reported that lie had sent out com- munications to 200 property owners with refer- , eneeto the conversion of the privies to the water carriage system. Out of this number he had received replies from 16, who were agreeable to , the conversion, and to pay half the cdsts. ! Twenty-six had replied stating they were ' opposed to the scheme, whilst 27 intimated they had already the water carriage , on their premises. system installed By this the committee would ' see that there was a big majority who had not replied. / ' It would thus seem that they would have to look at the question as though they were to pay the whole cost.

It was decided that the approximate •cost should be obtained, so as to arrive at the amount they would ask the Local Government Board to allow them to borrow. Councillor Clark said they should ask at Irilat rate they could borrow the money, and for how long a time. The time would make a great difference to them, and he thought the Local Government Board should assist them in !hat direction, as the Board seemed to be trying to make improvements; Councillor Rose asked if they could not also get an expert to tell them how many extra gal- lons of water would be required for the system. Councillor Whitley thought the sewers were inadequate, and there would be the.difficulty of the syphon on the canal. Couribillor Westbrook: That is a matter for Warrington.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.
LINES FROM LYMM.

The Primitive Methodist males smiled When the ladies set out to make a Record in the way of "At Homes." The mere males thought the last word Had already been discovered in that direction. The ladies have, however, proved different. Mere man still smiles, but it is Reported to be the grin of pleased surprise. The ladies have taken their triumph merci- fully. The Baptists had a merry tea party. Such functions make life all the more happy. The Rev. H. Ogden charmed with his telling address.

Sad Occurrence.—The weekly half-holiday in Lymm was marred by a sad occurrence. A youth named Jack Johnson, of Brookfield-ter- race, Lymm, and employed at the Co-operative Stores, was engaging in a game of football on the ground of the Lymm A.F.C. After the game concluded he began wrestling with a youth named George Iteaditt, of Cherry-lane, they both fell on the ground, with the result that John- con's ankle got broke. He was conveyed to Mrs. Treathcote's residence in Pepper-street, where Dr. Thorpe was soon in attendance. He had him removed afterwards to the Warrington In- firmary, where he is progressing favourably.

Congregational Social.—The annual meeting and social of the Congregational Christian Ser- vice Band was held on Monday evening. The Rev. J. A. Penaliggon, the pastor, gave a very good address to the younger members, advising them to be true to their convictions. The officers for the ensuing year were elected as follows: President, Rev. J. A. Penaliggon ; secretary, Mr. A. Thomas; treasurer, Mr. J. Hewitt; register secretary, Miss Egerton. Sacred songs were given by Mrs. C. Lewis, Miss Rowles and Mr. Flewitt. Refreshments were partaken of, and the testimony of the meeting was that a very good feeling had been fostered in the band dur- ing the past year, several of them becoming members of the church.

Independent Methodist Social.—The members of the Independent Methodist Church, Cherry- lane, spent an enjoyable social evening on Wednesday. Refreshments were provided by Mesdames H. Hewitt, T. Hewitt and T. Readett, and the blending of dainty edibles. songs, dialogue, reading, games, &c., combined to en- sure a happy time. Mr. R. Hewitt presided, and songs were contributed by Miss Nelson, Mr. A. Mercer and Mr. H. T. Mercer, whilst another vocal contribution was the duet by the Misses Readett and Witter. A capital dialogue was given by Mesdames T. Hewitt and A. Mercer and Miss P. Mercer. Other acceptable items were thg. pianoforte solos of Miss Eva Pearson and Mr. S. Mercer, and Mr. W. Mort's Lanca- shire reading. A number of suitable games were also indulged in.

Baptist Annual Tea.—On Wednesday the an- nual tea at the Higher-lane Baptist Church took place. There was quite a representative gather- ing to partake of the good things provided by the members of the church. At the evening meting the Rev. 11. Ogden, of Warrington, was the speaker, and his address was very much enjoyed; his words were distinctly encourag- ing, and the church's workers felt it to be an incentive to further effort. The chair was taken by Mr. Edward Clarke, of Cadisheqd, an old and faithful friend of the Higher-lane society, who was very warmly welcomed, and his speech much enjoyed. Miss Rigby and Miss Tanner, both of Warrington, gave great pleas- ure with their songs, as also did Mr. Boscow, who made his first appearance before a Lymm audience. Miss Jessie Holt and Miss Bessie Wright played pianoforte duets, and, as on pre- vious occasions, were warmly applauded. The Pastor, the Rev. G. E. Lovell, in his address, briefly reviewed the past year's work, and ex- pressed his pleasure at seeing so many friends pthent ; he hoped that as a church they were commencing what'would prove to be a very suc- cessful and prosperous year, and he thanked most heartily all those friends who had so kindly helped them on this occasion.

div.head: PRIMITIVE METHODIST "AT HOMES."
div.p: PRIMITIVE METHODIST "AT HOMES."
Unique and Most Successful Gatherings.

When the ladies of the Primitive Methodist Church announced their intention of eclipsing all their previous efforts in the way of "At homes," the mere males smiled indulgently, but discreetly hid their thoughts beneath a multi- tude of words, and smiled some more. Yet the ladies made good their boast, and took their triumph with that modesty.:which is the crown- ing glory of the sex. Sometime between Monday morning and Wednesday evening, artistic per- ceptions, skilfully interpreted by busy hands, transformed the main schoolroom into an ideal reception hall and drawing-room combined. Cosy chairs and inviting lounges replaced the usual sitting accommodation; prosaic windows hid their familiar feature, behind tastefully ar- ranged curtains; choice pictures adorned the walls; stately palms and other foliage plants, singly and in groups, contrasted pleasantly with the prevailing colour scheme.

In an alcove, commercialism was represented by a stall of useful and fancy articles, which found ready sale amongst the guests; a buffet at the other end of the room also receiving its share )1 attention. No. 3 vestry was the aTiode of weird shadows and slow music, and the atmos- phere was heavy with mystery, for here the curtains of the futui!e were withdrawn, and for the modest sum of is. Madam Zenana would reveal the joy.s and sorrows of the days not yet. After comparing notes visitors have come to the conclusion that longevity is on the increase, and one of the great questions of the future will be, What shall we do with our parents? Comedy was represented by'a humorous scene from Edwin Drood, "Mr. Edwin Drood to see Miss Rosa," and Miss Armstrong has previously shown us that she is the possessor of histrionic abilities of a high order, and her delineation of "Miss Rosa" was worthy of her high reputa- tion. as we have never seen the part of Dickens' volatile maiden in such good hands. Mrs. Priestner as "Miss Twinkleton " had but a small part on this occasion, but what little she had to do was well done. Mr. Arthur Appleton was responsible for the representation of Edwin Drood, and caught the correct spirit of the character from the commencement, and it is no flattery to say he did exceptionally well.

Well-chosen Amusements. The onerous task of providing change of pro- gramme for Wednesday, Thursday and Friday -evenings was admirably carried through by Miss Welford and her committee; the large company present on each occasion finding delightful re- creation in listening to the artistes, partaking of the ample and choice variety of refreshments, joining with their friends in the search for hidden trfasure, &c. A charming assortment of Tongs was contri- buted by the Misses Harwood, Kirwin and Riley, and Messrs. Gough and A. B. Edwards. Clever instrumental music was afforded by the violin solos of Miss F. Holt and Mr. B. Hargreaves; autoharp solos of Mr. Ball; and the proficient pianoforte selections and accompaniments of Miss J. Holt and Messrs. F. Champ, E. A. Ed- wards and Kirwin. Variety was given in the form of some excellent recitals by the Misses Wild, Coleman and Rushton. The humorous items of Mr. Humphreys were also enjoyed. Another attraction was that of the Pedlars' Parade, undertaken by the Misses M. Champ. W. de Jong, F. Holt, G. Littler, M. Lloyd- and M. Priestner. . nomemig,

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

Wesleyan Church and Missions.—ln connec- tion with the Wesleyan Church special services were held on Sunday. The preacher in the morning was Mr. R. H. Sutton, and the Rev. H. Middlewood preached in the evening. On Thursday the annual home missionary meeting was held in the church. Mr. Frank Hickman presided. The deputation was Mr. William Norwell, Connexional evangelist, supported by the Revs. J. Gunnell and H. Middlewood. and Messrs. J. Watson and J. Carman (society stewards). Mr. Middlewood gave the yearly re- port, which was considered very satisfactory. Mr. Norwell, who is well known in many parts of the country for his pleasing personality and effective preaching, had the congregation spell- bound as he instanced case after caWe—how he and others had been used of God, by their mis- sionary work, in reclaiming some of the lowest possible degraded men, and, what was more, that some of them were to-day .doing very effec- tive work in connection with Christ's Church_ The collections amounted to nearly XS, an in- crease on last year of over £2.

Right of Way Question.—At the monthly meet- ing of the Warrington Rural District Council it appeared from the minutes of the General Pur- poses Committee that after an interview with the agent of Captain Hughes it was decided that no steps be taken in the Fiddler's Ferry foot- path controversy until the return home of Captain Hughes, who might be absent ttntil July.—The Clerk said he was in receipt of a copy of the Public Rights of Way Bill, the second reading of which had passed the House of Commons in three successive sessions, and which might pass a Committee cif the House of Lords in the ensuing session. The Bill would remove the uncertainty and' ambiguity of the law on the point.—The Council passed the fol- lowing resolution: "lii the opinion of this Council it is imperatively necessary that the law in regard to the proof of public rights of way should be simplified, and the expense of litiga- tion reduced, in view of the frequency with which disputes arise in regard to such ways, and in order that this may be brought about the Council urges upon His Majesty's Government the importance of providing facilities for the passage of the 'Public Rights of Way Bill,' which the Council regrets has not yet been placed on the Statute Book."

div.head: WIN WICK.
div.p: WIN WICK.

A Sewage Question.—At the monthly meeting .of the Warrington Rural District Council, held on Wednesday, considerable discussion arose on the report of the deputation which attended the Winwick Asylum to inquire into the assertions made by the authority that the Council were still permitting untreated sewage matter to flow into the Asylum drains. The Clerk to the Asylum Visiting Committee further stated in his letter dated January 9th that he was now instructed to request-the Council to take steps to treat the sewage by septic tank. or other approved means, before the same entered the Asylum land; failing this, his committee would seriously consider the question of taking such action as they may be advised to maintain their rights.—The Surveyor produced samples of water which had been obtained on the day the deputa. tion visited the Institution. One bottle, which appeared to be clear, was said to be a sample of the water as it left the Council's land, and an- other bottle of very dark and evil-smelling water was alleged to have been taken from the drains after it had passed through part of the Asylum's land. It was point out that thewater fiats to left the Council's drains, looked almost drink, but the doctor said that perhaps it was the most infectious.—lt was decided to send the samples for analysis.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

Wesley Guild.—The monthly devotional meet- ing of the Guild was held on Monday evening, when short but excellent papers were read by three young members, 'Messrs. A. Proffitt, G. Ball and W. Farrar. Miss B. London sang as a solo "Light of the 'World.' The roll was called by Mr. H. Tomlin. The Rev. E. Morgan presided and congratulated those who had read Papers upon the success of their efforts.

Motor Car Burnt Out—While Frank Timms, a motor dealer, of Lord-street, Leigh, was driv- ing a motor car at Padgate on Monday, a flame appeared under the footboard, caused apparently through a leaky petrol pipe. Touching the. exhaust pipe it ignited the petrol in the tank, and the car burst into flames. Despite the efforts of several farm labourers, who threw huge quantities of soil upon the car, it was destroyed. The damage, which is estimated at £llO, is cov- ered by insurance. The driver escaped injury.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY.

Parochial Tea.--The members of St. Mary's Church held their tea party in the Sankey schools, when there was a record attendance. The ladies of the church were in charge of the tables, and looked after the company in their usual good style. After tea dancing took place in the large room, Messrs. Ray Bros. supplying the music. In the smaller room a concert was given, the Rev. J. R. Jones (the vicar) presid- ing. The artistes were as follow: Miss Murray, Miss H. Hall, Mr. and Mrs. Gibbs, Mr. 0. John- son, Mr. Platt (of Crewe), and Mr. Dawson. The artistes proved themselves excellent enter- tainers, several being heartily encored. The M.C.'s for the dancing were Messrs. W. S. Fur- ness, F. C. Newbold and B. Ray. Miss Jeans was the accompanist for the concert.

div.head: MOORE.
div.p: MOORE.

Mr. Oliver's Visit—Liberalism in Moore is a promising element, and fresh interest has been aroused in the People's Cause by the forthcoming visit of Mr. P. M. Oliver. who, along with Coun- cillor J. Kendall, will address a meeting in the Infant School on Friday evening next, at 7.30. On the Thursday night the same speakers •*ill be at Antrobus.

div.head: RISLEY.
div.p: RISLEY.

Independent Methodist Church.—A concert was held in the school in connection with the above place of worship on Saturday, when various songs and recitations were given. Mr E. Barton occupied the chair. A dialogue wai given which caused much laughter. Mr. P. Lythgoe and Mr. W. Seed created a great deal of fun by their antics. Miss Barton's song •was well received, as also was Mrs. Andrews' " Daddy" and "Our Father." The character sketch by the Wesleyan friends was loudly ap- plauded. " The Night in a Dormitory," by. Masters G. England and j. Monks, caused much merriment. The dialogue, " Hardup's Rivals," by, A. Jackson, E. Monks and E. Higham, was a source of some good fun, and received great ap- plause. "The six little nurses" (wee mites), who must have given a great deal of trouble to Mr. Slater to train in the able way he had done, quite realised his expectations, for nothing less than an encore would satisfy the audience. A vote of thanks was given to the Viresleyan friend( who had helped, proposed by Mr. W. Hughe seconded by Mr. J. Higham. Risley Independent School.—Open Sunday wk. observed in the above Sunday school on Sunday. lost, a fair number being present. Songs an recitations were given by the adults and chi dren, an a helpful afternoon was spent.

PETER RYLANDI3.-111.
Life at Westminster.

div.head: In the Larger Field of National Politics.
div.p: In the Larger Field of National Politics.
BY ARTHUR

There is every evidence that Parliamentary life was congenial to Peter Bylands. At once he was in the midst of things, making speeches that revealed clear thinking and comprehensive study. There was no period of painful apprenticeship. Already in the Town Council and upon the plat- form he had become a debater and an orator. In his 50th year, and with a business life cover- ing nearly 30 years, his view of things was eminently practical. From the first he distin- guished himself in debate upon matters that touched finance, and from the first be found a subject for criticism in the wasteful expenditure that marked the spending departments of the State. National waste jarred upon him, and the House of Commons had many uneasy moments under his fiery and pointed criticisms.

div.head: SOCIAL SYMPATHIES.
div.p: SOCIAL SYMPATHIES.

Along with a passion for economy and for business-like methods of Government went a strong passion for social reform and betterment. He was Chairman of the Warrington Brawn of the National Education League, a member of -the Committee of the Land Reform Association, a Vice-President of the National Union for the Suppression of Intemperance, as well as of the Licence Amendment League. That he should have prominent association with Temperance Institutions was in harmony with life-long sym- pathy and habit. Early in life temperance interests had awakened, as it had in many War- ringtoniang, at the voice of the pioneers of total abstinence. When a youth, he had given time and eloquence to the advocacy of total abstin- ence. The grandfather of the present writer, who was born in the same year as Peter Rylands, has often told of• laborious Saturdays, when, after the labours of the week, they trudged to- gether along the canal bank to Runcorn and Widnes, or visited Lancashire and Cheshire villages to address temperance meetings.

EFFORTS FOR LICENSING REFORM. In the. larger sphere which had now opened he delighted to give his strength to a movement which he had served, perhaps no less effectively, in his native town for more than thirty years. In the sessions•of 1870 and 1871 he was one of for the prohibition of the promoters of a Bl the sale of liquors on Sunday, and his able advocacy in the House of Commons awakened the admiration of temperance workers. His support of the Permissive Bill drew from Sir Wilfrid Lawson the playful statement : "I should have really liked not only to pay you a seeing the wonderful town which, visit, but also with a public ' in every street, yet returns an MY. who votes for the Permissive Bill !" He supported, too, the woman's cause by efforts in favour of the Woman's Disabilities Bill, and iva a member of the Royal Commission upon the Contagious Diseases Act, against which Mrs. Josephine Butler fought a strenuous and suc- la ttle. ed t o a the in cessful ha The sy eaars Radical, that 1 lay betweenra pidly advanced o and dissolution of 1874 were strenuous years indeed. leading place in the ranks of advanced thinkers, and there were many who looked to him as a future Radical leader.

div.head: REJECTED AT .WARRINGTON; ACCEPTED
div.p: REJECTED AT .WARRINGTON; ACCEPTED
AT BURNLEY.

When he sought re-election- in Warrington in 1874 he had won his place at Westminster and was in the front rank of social reformers. But, like many other ardent and progressive men, Ile was rejected at the polls. It was a season of Tory triumph, and Mr. Greenall secured a majority of 180. An invitation was given to Mr. llylands to contest South-East Lancashire, which only a very hopeful and courageous man would have accepted. He faced a second contest, to suffer a much greater defeat. For two years Ile was excluded from Parliament. Then in 1876 an opportunity occurred to become candidate for Burnley. He entered the conflict full of vigour and secured a notable victory.

div.head: CRITIC OF BEACONSFIELD..
div.p: CRITIC OF BEACONSFIELD..

- -- With the Conservatives in office, Mr. Bylands felt himself under no restraint in the matter of criticism. Wherever he detected jobbery or waste his attacks were made with a fiery and indignant eloquence that was seldom tempered with mercy. Lord Beaconsfield he distrusted utterly, and lie attacked his foreign policy with masterly and unsparing eloquence and know- ledge. Four years spent in Opposition were as strenu- ous as the years spent on the other side of the House. With remarkable mental energy ho mastered subjects of intricate and national interest, and the election of 1880, which brought Mr. Gladstone to power, found him looking to the future with eager hope and the confident

My informant was at the time associ- ated with a certain Yorkshire hydro, and one day a member of the proprietor's family was accosted in the street by a young man, who wished to be directed to " Cornwall," Admiring , the pluck of one who could comfortably face such a protracted walk, the gentleman entered , . into conversation with him, and ultimately landed him at the hydro for a meal, and, fur- ther, enlisted the sympathies of the housekeeper, a .Scotswoman, for a distressed countryman. ' The man said he belonged to the Shetlands, had received injuries to his eyes and face from the explosion of a ship's boiler; he had walked from Aberdeen, and was on his way to an uncle in Cornwall. The tale, given' in a particularly ' straightforward manner, with convincing earnestness, the production of a letter of invita- tion from the uncle, and the man's seeming re- luctance to accept assistance, won the hearts of his audience (a portion of the hydrO staff). A collection was made, some good clothes were fur- nished, and after consuming a hearty meal with evident relish, tho sportive young Scotsman, with a bundle of food, another of clothing, the sum of 30t.\., and a letter of recommendation to a Leeds eye doctor Wiese interest bad been en- listed by telephone), was safely bestowed in a train to Leeds, and—lost to sight! Assuredly this was none other than the notorious Angus, who when last I heard of him was making his way to Bridlington, and prior to that was in search of Dawlish in Devonshire! He always spins the same old yarn, and for that, if for no other reason, ought by this time to be as well known as the infamous and elusive Spanish treasurer swindlers. Yes. indeedy (as one of the old American humorists used to phrase it), "This is where the Guild of Help comes in."

div.head: MOUNFIELD.
div.p: MOUNFIELD.

expectation of seeing great things done for the people. But the labours of ten years in Parliament had reduced his physical powers. His best work had been done, though neither he nor his friends had yet realised it. Keen disappointment waited for him under Mr. Gladstone's Premiership. The Midlothian speeches had inspired hope, but events depressed him slowly but surely. Mr. Gladstone's man- agement of Egyptian affairs filled him with annoyance. Life at Westminster became dis- tasteful, and lie found his 'confidence in his leader sadly diminished.

div.head: ALIENATION FROM LIBERALISM.
div.p: ALIENATION FROM LIBERALISM.

To the Land Bill he gave earnest support, but the Coercion Bill almost drove him out of the Liberal ranks, and brought him to his feet in the House of Commons in a strong and sincere Protest. Alarmed at the embarrassment he seemed likely to bring to Mr. Gladstone, his con- stituents covered him with wholesale remon- strance, and Peter g.ave way. He supported, by his votes, a measure which he detested in his heart, and the volume of wrath which might have found vent in protest and criticism remained to embitter him against his chief. That he was genuinely attached to Burnley and Burnley people is quite manifest, and their influence held him to the Liberal cause much against his will through days of stress and tension. He was ready to break away, but hardly ready to be a leader in a cleavage which would have brought upon him the denunciation of his own constituents.

Mr. Chamberlain repeatedly urged him to vote against the Coercion Bill, telling him that both he and John Bright.were strongly opposed to it. Mr. Rylands replied: "Our constituents will say to us that if Bright and Chamberlain, whose Liberalism is beyond question, can Sup- port Mr. Gladstone on this question, surely they may expect us to do so. If you and Bright will resign we will not hesitate to support you, but we won't sacrifice ourselves."

div.head: CLEAVAGE COMPLETE.
div.p: THE CLEAVAGE COMPLETE.

Dislike of Mr. Gladstone became almost a mania, and to it was added a severe dislike of the Irish party, whose conduct and obstructive tactics were making Parliamentary life wean- some to to him. Dislike changed to disgust when Mr. Parnell advised the Irish electors of Burnley to vote against him at the contest of 1885, and Mr. Rylands found himself at Westminster with a twin-passion of dislike for the Irish and for the Statesman who was about to bend his great strength towards a solution of the Irish problem.

"THE SWORD WEARS OUT THE SCABBARD." Pew will quarrel with us if we say that the Member for Burnley was not able to view the Irish problem with an unprejudiced eye. Twenty years before, or even half a dozen years before, it would have been different; but strenuous years, and the working of an abnormally active brain, had exhausted his physical resources. Intellectual vigour failed with the drooping of bodily powers, and Peter Rylands was no longer himself.

His opposition to Mr. Gladstone and the Home Rule Bill was not a surprise to his intimate friends. Yet to the multitude it was, among many surprises, the greatest of all. To many of the Whigs who were looking for an excuse to join the Tories it was, as Mr. Gladstone after- wards said, " a positive Godsend." But Peter Rylands was regarded universally as an advanced Radical.

div.head: LAST CONTEST.
div.p: THE LAST CONTEST.

- - - -•- • -- • • To his friends at Burnley it was a great shock, and when the election of 1886, fought upon Home Rule, was thrust upon them, it was with mingled feelings that they took sides against a Member whom they had come to regard with no common affection.

To Peter Rylands the contest must have been a peculiarly trying one. With old friends ranged against him, and with new and strong prejudices to fight, the courage of the strongest might have failed. He fought as he had never fought in a contest since the famous days of 1868, and he won a narrow victory. His last visit to Warrington was made just after the struggle and the victory. He called upon old friends and talked of earlier and hap- pier days. But the old elasticity was gone, and there were tones in the voice that suggested a man grown prematurely old. His day of public service was almost over. The last battle had been fought and won. Strength slowly diminished in vigour and be passed away, unconscious and free from pain, on the morning of February 4th, 1887.

The World's Tribute of Interesting Items of News.
QUAINT AND AMUSING.

There has recently been installed in a com- mittee room of the New Zealand Parliament a newly-invented automatic voting machine which is said to merit comparison with the totalisator for accuracy. It is claimed by the patentees that in addition to saving both labour and expense, the machine declares the voting list the instant the last voter has left the booth.

Electrical Cure for Deafness. Remarkable results in curing the partial deaf- ness that comes from inflammations of the middle ear are reported from Brunswick, where Dr. Hamm, an ear specialist, has been testing a device invented by Professor Penkert, of the Brunswick Technical High School. This is called the ototherm. It is a tiny electrical in- strument, which is introduced into the outer ear, and there, by means of a high frequency current, sets up a heat that is said to cure the deafness in course of time.

Nose4:tubbing. Maori women of New Zealand know nothing about kissing. Nose-rubbing is their form of salutation, and when two friends meet they hold each other by the hand, bend their heads until their noses touch, and then rub them gently from side to side. This form of greeting is not confined to the women, but is practised by the men; they seldom meet without rubbing noses. In times of lamentation the Maori women will sit for hours with their hoses touching and moan for the loss of some chief, whom they have in all probability never seen.

The World's Largest Apple. A few weeks ago it was announced that the "Largest Apple in the World" was grown last summer at King's Acre, Hereford. The variety was Gloria Mundi, and the specimen weighed VA ounces. "The above claim," writes the " Sydney Morning Herald,„ „will not stand. Two years ago an apple was shown in Sydney, which was grown by Mr. Frank Clarke, Wood- side,Rylstone. It was a Lord Russell variety, and weighed 331 ounces, or an ounce more than atliec apple referred to above. At the time it was claimed to be the heaviest apple ever grown, and apparently it still holds the record."

div.head: Origin of Shaving.
div.p: Origin of Shaving.

It has been conjectured that the practice of slelaad vring originated from its being found that the afforded too good a hold for the enemy in This is the cause assigned for the origin of shaving among the Greeks about the time of Alexander. In other countries the practice was first adopted by military men. Historians men- tion the alarm in which some Roman emperors battle.b lived because of the fear that their barbers might cut their throats. For the sake of conceal- ing a scare on his throat, the Emperor Hadrian wore a beard. This fact brought the custom again into fashion.

div.head: Marinetti's Dicta.
div.p: Marinetti's Dicta.

here are some maxims of Marinette the Futurist : Woman is an obsession. Alen only love women who are extravagant. Futurism is based on the development of sensibility. Love has lost its absolute value. The fanatic is the person who offers to-day what will be the platitude of to-morrow, and so is the Futurist. Such is progress. Poetry is no longer in favour. Why? Because it does not deal with life as it is. It is like a stage-coach lumbering along when motor cars and aeroplanes dash by at lightning speed.

div.head: Fashion and Accidents.
div.p: Fashion and Accidents.

I Half a century ago, crinolines were responsible I for many accidents to life and limb. Nowadays I hobble 'skirts and high heels contribute to an increasingly large number of injuries sustained by women while getting on and off trains and , mounting and descending stairways in stations on the Pennsylvania Railroad. A careful record kept for the three months ending October 14th of all injuries sustained by women due to slip- pig,t stumbling, or falling while on the railroad property, indicates that these accidents are be- coming more rather than less frequent, despite the fact that the railroad has repeatedly called the attention of its women patrons to the num- ber of accidents caused by hobble skir and high heels.

Human Element in Boiler Explosions. Boiler explosions may not he more common than heretofore, but they are certainly more numerous than they need be (says "lover "). Many users of steam boilers do not know what an immense a)mount of energy is contained in even a small boiler, and they therefore take risks and compel others to take risks that are fre- quently entirely needlesS• Further, the men who pay the bills are not usually around the boiler very much, and the danger is even less i real to them than it would be f they were where they could hear escaping steam and see the hot fire under the boiler. They, therefore, compel the man whose bread and butter depends on his ability to hold his job to take the risk. Fre_ quently he does not dare say very much, u i because he would be likely to lose his position if he did.

Earthquakes Form Hole in Bottom of Sea. A hole nearly a mile deep was formed in the bottom of the sea off the coast of Panama by the recent Central American earthquakes, accord- ing to apparently authentic reports. As a result of these earthquakes a submarine cable was broken, and a cable ship was sent out to make repairs. The ends of the cable were found to be off Los Santos from the mainland, and is about half a mile wide.—" Popular Mechanics." under enormous masses of material; and, where the Government charts, published in 1904, showed found a depth f 5 oof1;000 t. ,) soundingso the cable shill) ,000 ft. Moonlight Makes Fish Putrefy, The observation that the rays from the moon favour putrefaction detracts from the romance .:11sproceeding, and there is eonblink," a temporary blindness said to be due to sleeping the moon- which has long been associated with moonlight. It is an old tradition that to sleep in the moon's in such'. N%a-as tliinadan g as ge! light of tropical climates (says "The Lancet"). There is even quoted a death the cause of which was officially stated to be exposure to moonlight. Apparently the food most seriously affected by the moon's radiations is fish, and 'seemingly trustworthy statements have been made as to the ill-effects produced in persons who had par- taken of fish which had been freely exposed to moonlight.
Coal in the Antarctic.

In the opinion of Professor D. W. E. David, Of the University of Sydney, Australia; the scientific discoveries of Captain Scott's ill-fated Antarctic expedition may prove to be of great practical importance. At the head of Beard- more Glacier, Frank Wild, of the Shackleton expedition, discovered seven seams of coal crop- ping out of a great cliff of sandstone and shale, and with his ice-pick chopped out small speci- mens that, when analysed at Sydney, showed the coal to be of workable quality. This vein Messrs. Griffith, Taylor and F. Debenham, the geologists of Captain Scott's party, traced to a point about 650 miles north of Beardmore Glacier. Professor David believes that it may prove to be one of the largest unworked coal- telds DI the world.

div.head: WORLD OF LETTERS.
div.p: THE WORLD OF LETTERS.
New Books.
Notes on Politics and History. A University Address. By Viscount Morley, O.M. London: MacMillan and Co., Ltd. 2s. 6d. net.

It was a happy thought of Lord Morley's to recast and amplify the address which he de- livered as Chancellor to the University of Man- chester in the summer of 1912, into the book which be has now published. Nothing could well be more suited to such an occasion than the high thought and subtle criticism, the brilliant literary quality and the penetrating insight into affairs, contained in these hundred odd pages. There is nothing of the attitude of the "superior person" in Lord Morley; he speaks as a student to students. He makes some wise and much- needed observations on the political habit of mind, the interpretation of the signs of the times, and on the national atmosphere and char- acter. He has a high estimate of the place and importance of universities in the world, though he does not forget that in the past universities have not always been mindful of their true function. "Universities," says Lord Morley, "have been boldly ranked by competent his- torians, with trial by jury and Parliaments, among leading institutions of the Middle Ages. At any rate, in England the power of universi- ties and.the public schools that feed them, has been immeasurable in the working of other in- stitutions. They have been main agents in moulding both our secular and ecclesiastical politics. They have worked too often for dark- ness as well as light. Too often and too long have they been the mirror of stolid prejudices and childish conventions; the appendages of old social form and institution, rather than great luminaries, dispensing knowledge, and kindling that ardent love of new truth for which youth is the irrevocable season. Power of this high dimension is not likely to be missing in our new universities, though its forms are undergoing rapid revolution. Well was it said, ' C'est toujours le beau monde qui gouverne le monde.' That is still a great deal more true than people think, even in countries like our own, where aristocratic polity has in large degree gone down. But the privileges of the fine world of social class must yield henceforth to the forces that shape temper, judgment, and range of public interest, in educational centres such as yours." In an illuminating consideration of the influ- ence of nationality in politics, Lord Morley con- trasts it with the advance of science, which has a tendency directly opposite. "Science works not at all for nationality or its spirit. It makes entirely for cosmopolitanism. In multifarious congresses in every capital of the world nation- ality is effaced. Parthians, Medes, Elamites, meet on common terms, and liberty, equality and fraternity all prevail, without intermixture from diplomatic sophisteries. Science, besides all else that it is and does, is the strongest uni- fying agent of the time, especially if we include the inventions that science makes possible and the commerce that inventions stimulate and nourish." . .

Some of the great questions raised in this little book are: What is progress? Is it a spon- taneous force? What is the effect of Western contact with the Eastern races? What is the State? and so on. On all these matters—as on a host of others—Lord Morley brings to bear a keen, penetrating mind, richly endowed, with a wide range and an almost unrivalled historical knowledge and long political training. we commend these " Notes on Politics and History" to all who are interested in fine literature, and in particular to those who take their politics seri- ously-. In publishing this address, Lord Mor- ley has paid the highest compliment within his power to the university of which he is the dis- tinguished Chancellor. The get-up of the book is altogether admirable

div.head: "WE WHO WRITE BOOKS."
div.p: "WE WHO WRITE BOOKS."

Mr. Clement K. Shorter, the distinguished editor and critic interviewed in " Great Thoughts" for February (Smith's Publishing Co., 6d.) has much that is interesting to say about modern novels. "We who write books," he says, "suffer from the immense num- ber of books now published. There were 13,000 books published in 1912, and, when the accounts come to be made up, it will, no doubt, be found that as many have been published in 1913. It is impossible to have half of these books re- viewed, while the great majority of those that are reviewed will receive very perfunctory treatment. That is why criticism of literature is a very much poorer thing to-day than it was thirty or forty years ago, although reviewers, as a rule, are paid much more for their work than was paid in those days Successes are made by incidents of personality aml are often most mysterious. Three out of the four most popular novels published this season have owed their success not in the least to the'reviews, but entirely to the generally circulated statement that they have been banned by the libraries. The fourth, which, in my\ Judgment, has very little merit—l refer to the fiction of Mrs. Barclay—owes its success to forces quite remote from criticism. I think it must be the gossip of the dinner tables that raises certain books above their fellows. Commonplace books find their glorification in commonplace minds. As deep calls to deep, so shallow calls to shallow, and the one or two i critics who desire to take a high standard fulminate n vain." The Editor has a fine description of Oxford. There is an • interesting sketch of Joseph Conrad, and a ! delightful article on Lady Ritchie, by Rowland ' Grey. The articles on the " Craftsmanship of Writing" will be very useful to young writers. Among the illustrations in this number is a facsimile of one of Browning's love letters.
AMERICA'S MOST POPULAR AUTHORESS. The February Number of the "Woman at Home" contains the opening chapters of a new romantic serial, " Laddie," by Mrs. Gene Stratton-Porter._

It will possibly be remembered that not so very long ago the authoress of this new serial created a furore in America, where some of her best known works, as " The Girl of the Limber- lost" and " The Harvester," each ran well into six figures. Mrs. Stratton-Porter lives at Geneva, Indiana, U.S.A., on the edge of the great Limberlost Swamp, which plays so pro- minent w part in her books. Here she is very close to the heart of things in the great world of Nature, and, as will be seen by a perusal of one of her novels, cities with their light and glamour have no attraction for her. In our hearts we can well envy her perfect and peaceful yet satisfying mode of life. Mrs. Stratton-Porter knows that happiness is akin to goodness, and as we read the first instal- ment of '` Laddie" we feel the uplifting influence of this exquisite love-story. In " Laddie" we find idealism of the highest type, poetry, romance and that intense love of Nature that opens up to many of us an entirely new world of beauty.
Miss Victoria Monks, the musk-hall artiste, was badly bruised in a motor car collision on Putney Heath on Saturday, when driving from London to Surbiton.

div.head: Literary Gleanings.
div.p: Literary Gleanings.
THE HUMBLE BEE.

There is something friendly, something homely about the humble bee which is entirely lacking in the more specialised honey-bee and in the ' rather terrifying wasp. Perhaps it is the popu- lar delusion that they have no sting which endears them to us. Nevertheless, this is a delusion, for both the queen and the workers have stings and ocasionally use them., .but the poison is weaker than in their allies and the pain inflicted correspondingly less. On the other hand, certain advantages rest with the humble bee; it does not, like the honey-bee, lose its sting when used, but can withdraw it, and use it again another day. Unless handled or mis- used, however, the queens do not sting human beings, though if the nest be disturbed in an unmannerly way the workers will often strike out. The economy of the household is also more attractive to the average man than is that of the bee-hive. It is less ordered, less specialised, and is carried on more on the lines of the comfort- able city firms of a century ago and less on the lines of an up-to-date trust or syndicate. Few trusts or syndicates awake our deeper affections, and as Bagehot said about Political Economists, " No one really mourns when they die."—Pro- fessor Shipley, in "Country Life."

THE DOGGER BANK. Accidents happen in this little town at sea, and sometimes bad accidents, for the work is rough, and often the success of a man's task depends entirely on his timeliness and dexterity. Miscalculation brings disaster on him. The human machine, not being an affair of cogs and gear, of mathematical exactitude and automatic precision, is sometimes a little too soon or a bare fraction short in its duty, and smashes badly. A trawler is fitted only for the use of healthy and even vigorous life. Such a small ship is, in ' winter, almost always in quick and uncertain movement. The man maimed in such a situa- tion has to endure horrors; and though it is possible that a hospital ship of the Deep Sea Mission may be near;yet even so the imagina- tion shrinks from contemplating the transfer of a victim. It is significant, too, bow many of these deep-sea fishermen are unable to swim. The mate of our ship could not. "1 don't want to know how," was the way lie put it; "the sooner it's over the better."

This digression gives time for the trawl to come near. Looking overside, when the pocket of the net is close, one can see the gleaming mass of fish comihg up through the water. It is swung in over the deck, pouring with water and slime, and the bottom of the pocket is deftly unfastened. The mas.s falls, the living fish writhing and scattering in all directions; had- dock, cod, plaice, halibut, soles and hake, prin- cipally. You are warned not to handle speci- mens carelessly.. A hake can give a nasty bite, and a weever,with its poisonous spines, does even worse. There is a litter of starfish, crustacea, and weeds with it all, strange forms of ocean plasm more attractive to the naturalist than to the fisherman. Sometimes the trawl brings up what had better been left at the bottom, the men will tell you; but they have no opportunity to elaborate such gruesome affairs when the catch is on deck. That has to be cleansed, and sorted into boxes. I saw it done in winter. It was cold, with a bitter and searching wind, and there was a lumpy sea running; and with those deep cuts on their finger joints, common to most of the crew, which the brine kept raw, whatever the reward of the men, it was not great.---From "Off Shore," a Londoner's cruise to the Dogger Bank, in the "Pall Mall Magazine."

SEVILLE. To the visitor from northern lands, Seville is the embodiment of all his dreams of the sunny South. Pleasantly situated on the banks of the navigable river Guadalquivir at the sea-gate of a large and fertile valley, close to the meeting of the waters of the Atlantic and of the Mediter- ranean, blessed with a climate that permits one to live almost perpetually in the open air, sur- rounded by palms and fragrant orange trees, with the romantic memories of the ancient Moorish dominion penetrating the atmosphere like a rich perfume, and inhabited by a pleasure- loving and contented people, the city has been aptly compared to a lustrous sultana in all her finery. A well-known writer, Calvert, says : " There is a charm and compelling fascination about Seville which produces in the traveller visiting the city for the first time a sensation of physical ecstasy. George Borrow shed tears of rapture as he beheld Seville from the Cristina Promenade, and listened to the thrush and nightingale piping forth their melodious songs in the woods, and inhaled the breeze laden with the perfume of its thousand orange gardens. The Moors left their beloved capital in the height of its prosperity, in the full flower of its beauty . . Seville lives. Cordova is dead, and

Granada broods over her past. These are ceme- teries of a vanished civilisation. Alone among the ancient seats of Moorish dominion, Seville has maintained her prosperity." Valdes says: "Seville has ever been for me the symbol of light, the city of lop and joy." But with all this joyous appearance, Seville has another side, a practical one. It is the headquarters of the Army in Andalueia, an im- portant seaport, and the terminus of three lines of railway. In addition, there are many choco- late, soap, match, cork, cloth, and cotton fac- tories, an arsenal, and an immense Government tobacco factory, which employs 6,000 women. Close to the gipsy suburb of Triana is the Cartuja, an ancient monastery, now an impor- tant porcelain factory employing 2,000 persons As the city lies barely ten metres above the level of the sea, there used to be always trouble in times of flood, but in 1904 an elaborate system of defences against the rising of the Guadal- quivir and its tributaries was successfully estab- lished. The temperament of the people is differ- ent from that of the inhabitants of Madrid or Barcelona, being gay and light-hearted, and the city has always had the reputation of loyalty to the throne. The picturesque street life with its vivid cos- tumes suitable to the sunny climate has often been described and set to music, as in Rossini's " Barbiere di Seviglia," Bizet's "Carmen," and Mozart's " Figaro," and "Don Giovanni." Seville is the home of the famous dance, the bolero. During the past thirty years the popu- lation has increased from 133,000 to upwards of 150,000. The history of Seville is a page of romance. Tradition says that Hercules founded the city, and that Julius Coesar built the walls, but his- tory is certain that there was an important Plurnician, and later, a Roman settlement, within a few kilometres north-west of the pre- sent site, in early times. Under Augustus, the city of Italica, as it was called, became the capital of Baetica, one of the then three pro- vinces of Roman Spain. It is said to be the first Latin-speaking town founded outside of Italy.— From "The Theosophical Path."
