CONUNDRUMS.
Why are children whose parents are dead like worn-out shoes?—Because they are left-off-tins (left orphans).
Why is the letter A like 9 inches P—Because it is the fourth part of a yard. . _ _
_ _ Why is a boy doing his sums like a serpent on end?--Because he is an adder up.
GAME OF VOWELS.
A member of the party asks a question of his right-hand neighbour. The answer given should be brief, suitable, and prompt, but must not include the vowel interdicted by the questioner. For instance :
George—" Do you like skating, Harry? Answer without an E."
Harry—" I was always fond of it, and I am now."

Harry—" With whom did you go to church yesterday, Fred? Answer without an A." Fred—" With my mother's sister," answers Fred, cautiously, knowing that if he said "aunt" he would have to pay forfeit. The game continues until a number of for- feits are collected.
A FELLOW'S MOTHER. " A fellow's mother," said Fred the wise, 'With his rosy cheeks and his merry eyes, "Knows what to do if a fellow gets hurt By a thump or a bruise, or a fall in the dirt.
"A fellow's mother has bags and strings, Rags and buttons and lots of things; No matter how busy she is, she'll stop To see how well you can spin your top.
"She does not care (not much, I mean) If a fellow's face is not always clean; And if your trousers are torn at the knee She can put in a patch that you'd never see.
" A fellow's 'mother is never mad, But only sorry if you are bad, And I tell you this, if you're only true She'll always forgive whate'er you do.
" Pm sure of this," said Fred .the wise, With a manly look in his laughing eyes. "I'll mind my mother, quick, every day— ' A fellow's a baby that don't obey."
THE TWO LITTLE KITTENS. Two little kittens, one stormy night, Began to quarrel, and then to fight; One had a mouse, the other had none, And that's the way the quarrel begun.
"I'll have that mouse," said the biggest eat, "You'll have that mouse?". we'll see about that; "I will have that mouse," said the eldest son. "You shan't have the mouse," said the little one.
I told you before 'twas a stormy night When these two little kittens began to fight; The old woman seized her sweeping broom, And swept the two kittens right out of the room.
The ground was covered with frost and snow, And the two little kittens had nowhere to go; So they lay them down on the mat at the door, While the old woman finished sweeping the floor.
Then they crept in again, quiet as mice, All wet with snow, and as cold as ice. For they found it was better that stormy night To lie down and sleep than to quarrel and fight.
HOW THE GIRL SAVED HER FRIENDS. It was a fine sunny day in the month of July. A girl of fourteen was kneeling beside a railed-in grave in the quiet "field of rest" close to the highway._

Down the road came a troop of soldiers. The girl on seeing them sprang to her feet with a cry of alarm, then dropped down behind a yew- tree as they passed, and so escaped unnoticed. Then she thought quickly. The soldiers would soon reach her home, the Chateau de Saint Croix; they would find no one but servants (her parents were both dead); after taking the chateau they would ,surround the village. What would she do to prevent this? Why, ride to Roneevoux and order out the squadron kept in readiness for border raids. But all the horses were in the stable, save Grand-pas, her father's favourite hunter, the fastest horse in the country-side. He was 'in the pasture. After a moment's deliberation, the girl deter- mined to ride him. She had ridden bare-back before now, but as she saw the huge animal lift- ing his glossy black neck from the grass, her heart sank. After several attempts, however, she succeeded in mounting him. Then, by gently pulling his hair, she managed to guide him on to the highway. She had ridden many miles when dusk was beginning to descend, still she urged the splen- did animal onwards. She had lost her way, and was almost beginning to despair, when Grand- pas whinnied softly, and came to•a standstill. The girl slid down and saw through the dark- ness the outlines of a street. She knocked at the first door she came to—an inn—and, as it turned out, the meeting-place of the local hunt. To the landlord she explained the situation. The alarm was raised, and a body of troops was despatched just in time to save St. Croix and the village. Grand-pas had found his way to his dead master's usual halting-place, and so saved the situation.

In his report to the Whines Licensing Ses- sions on Tuesday Inspector Bannister said the district contained 98 licensed houses, viz., 70 public-houses, 16 beerhouses " on," 7 beerhouses "off," and 5 other licensed houses. The popu- lation was 37,833, giving one licence to every 380 persons. The six registered clubs appeared tia have been well conducted. The justices' intim- ation to licensed victuallers respecting back-door trade had received attention, and the long-pull Practice had almost ceised. The police had paid 1,270 visits to licensed premises and, with the exception of a few irregularities, they were found to be well conducted.

A STIRRING SATURDAY.
Two Men Who Created a Lively Time in Warrington.

The police of Warrington found Saturday afternoon rather a stirring time. Two men, were responsible for this, and they had different ways of making things lively. One's ambition took flight in the direction of a breezy argument upon Home Rule, but whether he was to argue it from the Ulster standpoint or not was not made clear, although this debater was prepared to fight if necessary. The other's ambition was to pulver- ise the police force of the town. . . . . _ _

Each in his little way created a full meed of stir, although when they appeared at the Police Court on Monday they were more than penitent.. The first to appear in the dock was a man named McTigue, who had no settled abode. He was charged with being drunk and with assault- , ing Police Constable Dickson. The Mayor pre- sided over a full Bench of magistrates.

div.head: TO ARGUE HOME RULE.
div.p: TO ARGUE HOME RULE.

The officer's narrative was that on Saturday afternoon he saw McTigne in a drunken state in Market Gate, and as ho was in personal dan- ger from the street traffic he advised McTigue to go away. I asked him where he lived and his answer was, "In the West End." McTigue refused to go away, as he was going to argue the Home Rule question. On the way to the Police Station the man became disorderly and assaulted the officer. Mr. Lockett, of 9, Suez-street. came to the assistance of the constable, and McTigue was with difficulty taken to the lock-up. The magistrates imposed a fine of 10s. and costs, with the option of 14 days in prison. Mr. Lockett was complimented upon the willing and courageous way he went to the assistance of the police. "TO PULVERISE THE POLICE."

Sergt. Clough was called to deal with Edward Baker, of 22, Haddock-street. said to be a wire drawer. He went to the Raven Hotel in Fennel- street, and refused to quit, because he was act- ing in a drunken and disorderly manner. Mr. Brooks, the' licensee, said Baker started to wrestle in the tap room, and to kick break- fast cans about. He took the drink away from him, and When be asked Baker to leave he re- plied that it would take the Chief Constable and all his force to get him away. Sergt. Clough single-handed managed to get him to the lock- he Chief Constable said his attention was directed to Baker by his remark that he would pulverise the police, and lie found that Baker was not an ordinary drunken man, but lie was mad drunk.
If we had not taken notice of this man, said the Chief, jocularly, this building might have been laid in ruins.
Baker was ordered to pay 10s. and costs or spend 14 days in prison.

div.head: ST. HELENS POLICEMAN DIES ON DUTY.
div.p: ST. HELENS POLICEMAN DIES ON DUTY.

"He was the cleanest policeman and one of the most straightforward, obliging and transpar- ently honest men I have ever met," was the tribute paid by the Chief Constable of St. Ilelens to Police-Constable Grundy, who had been a member of the St. Helens Police Force for about nine years, and fell dead while on duty in the street shortly after midnight on Saturday morn- ing. He was thirty years of age, and was well thought of as an able and conscientious officer. Grundy was assisting to convey to Arthur-street Bridewell a man who had been arrested for com- mitting a breach of the peace. The officer had been obliged to bring the man out of his house owing to his violence, and when they had pro- ceeded along the street to the corner of him, Phythian-street, Grundy fell down dead at the feet of his prisoner. Sergeant Curran was along with been astheresa n l ties dn. o suggestion that the officer

div.head: WIDNES OFFICIAL'S SUDDEN DEATH,
div.p: WIDNES OFFICIAL'S SUDDEN DEATH,

Mr. John Shepherd, for forty years Market Superintendent of Whines, died suddenly on Saturday morning. Ile was in his 83rd year, and had not been in the best of health for some time, but, despite his age, he continued to dis- charge his duties until only a few days before his death. Mr. Shepherd was a native of Run- corn, and for three years was in charge of the river ferry system on the Cheshire side. Later he proceeded to Southport, where he became chief clerk in the Post Office, being retained Specially for his ability as a linguist, lie was almoner to the Widnes Lodge (2819) of Free- masons. During 1118 long connection with Wid- nes, Mr, Shepherd had made many friends, and his genial a.nd kindly disposition had won him the respect and .esteem of all.

TO TAKE
HONOUR FOR COUNCILLOR PEACOCK.

A warm glow of "Forestry" enthusiasm per- vaded the Blue Lion Hotel lodge-room on Sat- urday night, when a large number of members of Court Warrington 430 assembled to corrobor- ate the expressions and wishes contained in an illuminated address which was presented to the Mayor, who for many years has been an active worker for the lodge.

The presentation was to commemorate Coun- cillor Peacock's elevation to the Mayoralty. A number of ladies were present, and amongst these was the Mayoress, who also was the re-, cipient of a present from the lodge. The principal officers present, in addition to the two guests were :—Hon. members: Alderman Tinnion and Mr. J. Fulton-Smith; P.D.C.R.'s : Bros. W. Smith, G. W. Baines, H. James, treas- urer; J. Chrimes, secretary; and L. Davies; P.C.R.'s : Bros. W. James, H. James, jun., J. McDermid and E. Clayton; C.R. T. E. Cox; trustee, J. Gregory; district trustee, J. Walsh; Sister Baines, C.R., Sister Corradine, secretary, and Sister Turner, treasurer. Bro. J. CHBIBIEB presided, and in proposing the Royal toast, referred to the interest the Royal family were taking in their working class sub- jects, as was evidenced by the Royal visits to industrial England.

toast had been received, said that he honestly believed that Forestry ran in his blood, because both his father and grandfather were Foresters. When he was three years old his father was taken ill, the illness lasting until the speaker was about 16 years of age, and he remembered that during that time the Warrington Foresters used to make visits to their home, although his father 'belonged to a Bedfordshire branch, and bring assistance. There was no excuse for him (the speaker) being in the Foresters now. When he could he would help anybody who deserved it, although the first claim upon him would bel the Foresters, of whom he was so proud. His family had been poor, but they gave him the best education they could and allowed him to stay at school until he was 13, when he was in the ex-seventh standard at Wycliffe School. He remembered going to the old public-house—the Ram's Head—and being made a Forester. At that time he held different ideas to those he held to-day, because he would not go to the Court on account of it being held in a public-house. He had had his mind broadened, and he had never found that Forestry had led him wrong.

A Change of " flosses." After three years of keeping dway from the club he began to take an active interest in the society and became an auditor, and after a few years in various offices he relinquished the auditorship. He had just recently agreed to act as an auditor again, he now being the junior to Bro. Henry James, jun., who was an old office boy of his at Messrs. Crosfield's. (Laughter.) He had been Bro. James' "boss" and now Bro. James was his "boss." (Laughter.) He had had many kindnesses shown to him by the Foresters. When lie was a youth, employed on the Chesbire Lines, he worked from 5.30 at night until eight o'clock in the morning, and, as could only be expected, lie became sleepy about three o'clock in the morning, so an old Forester used to do. his work while he had a rest. These were kind- nesses he could never fully repay. He would never forget November 16th last, when he was accompanied to church by such a large number of Friendly Society workers.

Done Nothing Wrong. Alderman Tinnion had mentioned that he (the Mayor) had been to gaol. He would like tO allay the fears of some of his friends by saying he had dons nothing wrong. (Laughter.) It was the Forestry vein in him that made him go. A very refined-looking lady was brought up at the Borough Court on a charge of drunkenness, and the magistrates in their wisdom remanded her until the following Wednesday. In the meantime it was arranged with the Police Court Missioner that he should try to find a home for her if she agreed to go to one. She agreed and was sent to a Liverpool Home. He got inter- ested in the work and he wanted to see for him- self what there really was in it. Arrangements were made for a visit; and the 3fayoress and himself, together with the Police Court 3lissioner, got up at 5.30 in the morning, and on arrival at Liverpool they saw men and women leave the gaol. They visited other homes, and lie was very much impressed with the work. He did not want to go there for the sake of "putting his nose in "—it was to see if there was any good in it, and this was an idea of Forestry. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) He hoped he would always enjoy their confidence. "Remember," he said, "I am one of yourselves, and no better." (Loud applause.)

div.head: HAPPY INSPIRATION.
div.p: A HAPPY INSPIRATION.

Bro. J. FULTON-SMITH proposed " The Ancient Order of Foresters, and in particular Court Warrington No. 430." The institution of friendly societies, such as theirs, was a happy inspiration on the part of their grandfathers some eighty years ago, so that they could draw help in times of distress and sickness and when out of employment. They schemed not only to benefit themselves, but others, especially their own families. There was a tendency nowadays on the part of younger people to ignore the benefits to be derived from such schemes of put- ting money away for a rainy day. When they did not join associations such as that they were unprepared for rainy days. One of the most noble branches was the encouragement and ad- mission of ladies to their association, because, he thought that the ladies could get their brothers or other people's brothers, to join. (Laughter.) So by encouraging the ladies they had formed a recruiting branch. Juvenile Members Decreasing. During the last year or so a great change had come over the Friendly Societies which might lead to the crippling of the splendid benefits, and that Wal3 the decrease in the juvenile mem- bers, because unless they were bringing in young blood they were bound to decline. God forbid that such a calamity shonld befall the Fores- ters! Their financial position was strong, for they had 1:10,000,000. That was a big sum, but if it had to be distributed amongst the mem- bers, it would only work out at ..tlO for each man. They must keep up their income, for it was the most vital part of their existence. When a man joined a Friendly Society he was inde- pendent, and when a man was independent he could look the whole world in the face. (Ap- plause.)

' GROWTH OF THE COURT. Bro. J. CURIMES, in reply, said that in 1865, 49. years ago, the court consisted of 70 members, with total funds amounting to £B6, and at the present time the total membership was 440, with lands amounting to £1,650. During the eigh- teen years he had the honour to be their secre- tary the funds had increased from £1,071 to £1,650, and the membership from 239 to 440. They had also 204 members' wives entered for funeral benefits. During the past 18 years they had paid out of their subsidiary fund to mem- bers in distress £223. Their relative degree of solvency was 19s. 2d. in the X. He thought they could congratulate themselves upon the steady progress they had made. Thanks were due to the members who had taken an interest in their organisation. At every meeting of the court they had not less than 40 or 50 members present,. They could not expect to bring the young blood in their society to-day as they did four or five years ago, for they had the National Insurance Act, and they must work with it. They could not expect them to contribute to the State and to a voluntary insurance at the same time, but an endeavour should be made to get young people/to obtain their State benefits through their society, and perhaps as the younger ones grew older they would also contribute • to the voluntary scheme. They already had in the State section over 500 members. (Applause.)

MAYOR'S MANY EXCELLENT SERVICES. Bro. Alderman TINNION said they were met together to make an acknowledgment to Bro. Peter Peacock for the many excellent services he had rendered to the Friendly Society move- ment, in which he was a Hercules. He was not only a Forester, but belonged to the "Buffs," FI earts of Oak, Shepherds, and lie had been recently made an Oddfellow, and he had also been to gaol. (Laughter, and a Voice: "I am sorry to hear it!") _

I am proud th know it, retorted the Alder- man, with a merry twinkle in his eyes, because the fact of Bro. Peacock being for 25 years associated with this court showed that be has breathed the atmosphere of Forestry. (Hear, hear.)

The provisions for a rainy day were not the , chief things in Friendly Society work. It was that portion which enlarged a man's heart, quickened his sympathies, and laid the founda- tion of true brotherhood and true comradeship, that were valuable. The work Bro. Peacock had done had been great; he was a born worker, and whatever he placed his hand on he seemed to say, "Whatever you do, do it well." (Hear, hear.)
Alderman Tinn ion then handed the address to the Mayor, expressing the hopes and wishes of the lodge for his future.

div.head: ADDRESS. The address was as follows : Ancient Order of Foresters, Court " Warrington," No. 430,
div.p: THE ADDRESS. The address was as follows : Ancient Order of Foresters, Court " Warring- ton," No. 430,

, To Bro. Peter Peacock, P.G.C.R. We, the undersigned, on behalf of the officers and members of the above court, wish to express to you our hearty congratulations upon your elevation to the position of Mayor of the County Borough of Warrington, and we sincerely hope that your term of office as Chief Citizen may be abundantly successful.

At the same time we take this opportunity of testifying our appreciation of the faithful and successful services you have rendered in the various offices of our Order for a period of 22 years, and of the admirable way in which you have discharged your duties. As a token of our esteem we ask your acceptance of this address, with best wishes for your future happiness. January 31st, 1914. Henry James, jun., CR. Thomas Heacock, S.C.R. _

Trustees: John Gregory, P.C.R., Walter R. Smith, P.D.C.FI., and David Jones, P.C.R. Henry James, P.D.C.R., treasurer. John Chrimes, P.D.C.R., secretary. The address, which was mounted in a heavy gilt frame, was a fine example of the illumina- tor's art, its decorative scheme including a photograph of the Mayor.

PRESENTATION TO MAYORESS. Sister Mrs. CORRADINE, in presenting the Mayoress with a beautiful chain-work purse, said she was glad that the Mayoress had that afternoon been made an honorary member of their branch. On behalf of Court 430 she had pleasure in asking the Mayoress to accept that token of esteem and respect, upon which had been inscribed: "Presented to the Mayoress of Warrington, Sister Mrs. Peter Peacock, by the members of A.O.F. Court, Warrington, 430. January 31, 1914." (Applause) BEO. JOHN GREGORY, GiO senior trustee of the Court, in proposing the health of the Maior and Mayoress, spoke in a reminiscent vein upon his early association with Councillor and Mrs. Peacock; whilst BM. THOMAS RODEN, Bro. It. DAVIES, and Councillor Aacaza supported. . The toast was enthusiastically drunk.
RAN IN HIS BLOOD. The Mayor's Reminiscences.

div.head: RIBBON OF HONOUR.
div.p: RIBBON OF HONOUR.

- - - • - - - --- The Mayor then presented a ribbon and P.C.R. certificate to P.C.B. Pro. Henry James, jun. He said it was with pleasure he invested him with the ribbon of office, which showed to the mem- bers that he had passed through all the chairs in that Court. He also presented the framed emblem. This was the same kind of ribbon he (the Mayor) had received at the hands of the Court. He hoped Bro. James would meet with the same distinction as did his father. Bro. HENRY JAMES, sen., presented Bro. P. .D.C.R. Smith with a handsome clock for bring- l9l3. in the largest number of members during

div.head: MAYORESS REPLIES TO A TOAST.
div.p: MAYORESS REPLIES TO A TOAST.

---••-• ---- - - .^ ---•• P.C.B. &O. E. CLAYTON proposed the health of "The Ladies," and coupled with it the name of the Mayoress. In praise of the ladies he gave examples of the work of the women folk, including the district nurses, who went from house to house attending to the sick. The MAYORESS replied, saying that she thanked them from the bottom of her heart and would ,always treasure their kindness. Bro. 11. JAMES, jun., proposed the toast of ."The Visitors."

Bro. J. McDErmo and Bro. BAINES replied, the latter saying they had beard that the Mayor was a member of several Friendly Societies. It was only characteristic of his principle right through. He felt that he had done so much good in the Foresters and that he could extend that good feeling to members of other societies. They were not at all jealous, but proud he had learnt the Friendly Society lesson with the Foresters. (Applause.) Thanks were expressed to the artistes, the Press, and the Chairman for their services. The programme was punctuated with songs by Mr. J. H. Knowles and Mr. T. Stout, and a violin solo by Mr. A. E. Davies, who also made an able accompanist.

div.p: NOT COMING BACK. Runcorn's Interesting Account.

div.head: RUNCORN WORKS FATALITY.
div.p: A RUNCORN WORKS FATALITY.

(22), An inquest was held at PIIIRCOrR on Tuesday on Henry Jones single, 19 Byron-street, Runcorn, who died on SaturdaY fr6m the result of injuries received at Messrs. Castner-Kellner's Works, Weston Point, on January 19th. Deceased was engaged in hooking a chain OR to a bogey waggon laden with bleach. He gave the signal to start, when lie was heard to call out. He had got his foot in the check-rail, and had sustained severe injuries through the wag- gon wheel passing over it. A witness named Sutton said that only a few minutes previously he had warned the deceased that lie would be getting trapped. Dr. Boswell attributed death to exhaustion and shock, which was directly caused by the accident.
A. verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

div.head: 'EB
div.p: 'EB
RUARY 7, 1914
Thurdi Otius.
£I7I IN FREE-WILL OFFERINGS.
The scheme of free-will offerings in connection with St. Paul's Church has evidently been a success. The total raised by this means during the past year amounts to £l7l 18s. 10d.

div.head: TIIE PARISH CHURCH ORGAN.
div.p: TIIE PARISH CHURCH ORGAN.

It is proposed to have the organ in the War- rington Parish Church cleaned and repaired during the coming year. The cost of this neces- sary work is estimated at about £lO5, and donations are being invited for the purpose.

div.head: PARISH CHURCH OLD VESTRY.
div.p: PARISH CHURCH OLD VESTRY.

The work of restoration of the old vestry at the Parish Church is now well in hadd. The scheme includes the raising of the walls so as to hide the ugly roof, and the altering of the windows so as to bring them into uniformity with the windows of the new vestry. When the scheme is completed a defect in the church's existing architecture will have been removed.

div.head: FROM CHAPEL ROYAL TO MISSION.
div.p: FROM CHAPEL ROYAL TO MISSION.

The Rev. Richard Wood-Samuels, who was at one time connected with St. Paul's Church, Warrington, is coming from the Chapel Royal, Savoy, to St. Paul's to conduct a great mission organised by the Vicar, the Rev. W. Bracecamp. The services start on 14th February. Thirty years ago the Missioner was ordained at St. Paul's.

div.head: LANCASHIRE CONGREGATIONAL UNION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE CONGREGATIONAL UNION.

The Rev. F. A. Russell, Southport, has been nominated for the chair of the Lancashire Con- gregational Union in 1915. The yearly meetings of the union will be held at St. Helens on March 3, 4 am! 5. Mr. Russell ran up for the position at the last yearly meeting at Darwen, when Mr. Ephraim Hindle, Wilpshire, was elected.

div.head: CANON AND INDUSTRIAL UNREST.
div.p: CANON AND INDUSTRIAL UNREST.

The Rev. Canon Stevenson dealt with the present spirit of unrest in his sermon at the Warrington Parish Church on Sunday evening. This is a great time of social unrest, and I do not think, he said, anyone can remember so many disputes as have occurred in the last year or two, and I am sure that whatever our views may be we deprecate and are very sorry that such disputes should occur. We know that they mean suffering to many, that they do not breed good feeling, but that they are too apt to stir up strife and hatred.

div.head: GIFT TO WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: GIFT TO WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH.

Canon Willis, in the " Parish Church Maga- zine," announces that The Hon. Misses Ellinor and Elisabeth Wilson-Patten have given a very handsomely bound copy of the Bible in memory of their grandmother, Lord Winmarleigh's mother, whose name will be found in her own handwriting on the first page. The Rector has placed it on the lectern in the Lady Chapel, as it is not quite large enough for use in church, and has put the Bible now used in the chapel in the church in place of the present one, which is sadly in need of repair.

div.head: IVYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL TEA.
div.p: IVYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL TEA.

The large attendance at the Wycliffe annual congregational tea party in the Memorial Hall on Monday night was but a true reflex of the present state of the Church. After an enjoyable tea a concert of unusual merit was given, when the artistes were the Misses Corney, L. Fleming, E. Haviour, and E. llewitt; Mesdames Epworth, Haviour and Smallshaw; and Messrs. H. M. AsMoll, Bailey, Booth, A. Davies, 11. Hawthorn, J. Poole, and W. IL Wallington. The Rev. T. T. James, who presided, said they could congratulate themselves upon the large gathering at the completion of one year's work. That day coincided with his coming to Warring- ton twelve months ago—it was a happy anniver- sary.-
Mr. J. W. Slack and Mr. W. T. Witts proposed and seconded a comprehensive vote of thanks, and alluded to the Pastor's anniversary. Mr. W. 11. Payton was a capable accompanist.

div.head: AVYCLIFFE P.S.A.
div.p: AVYCLIFFE P.S.A.

The speaker at the meeting of the Wycliffe P.S.A. on Sunday afternoon was the Rev. T. T. James, and his subject was " The shadow of a great rock in a weary land." lie graphically described that as a desert, exposed to wind and storm, but a great rock was there to give shelter to those requiring it. They as men could make themselves rocks of shelter for their storm- tossed brothers by giving a helping hand, a look of sympathy, a word of counsel; in fact, they could always stand by the weak, ready to shelter them.

Mr. W. Beswick presided and led in prayer. The secretary, Mr. B. Farrar, read the lesson, announced an open meeting for tomorrow, Sunday, and made reference to the forthcoming 21st anniversary on the let of March. The Rev. T. T. James said it was pleasant to learn that there were several still in the P.S.A. who had been members all the 21 years of its existence. On behalf of the class the Secretary congratulated the Rev. T. T. James upon cele- brating his first anniversary of his ministry in their midst.

div.head: PITY THE PARSON!
div.p: PITY THE PARSON!

" The Christian Age" says of the modern minister: The preacher has a hard .time. If his wife sings in the choir, she is presuming. If she doesn't, she isn't interested in her husband's work. If a preacher reads from notes he is a bore. If he speaks extemporaneously he isn't deep enough. If he stays at home in his study, he doesn't mix enough with the people. If he is seen in the streets, he ought to be at home getting up a good sermon. If he calls on some very poor family, he is playing to the gallery. If he calls at the home of the rich, he is an aristocrat. Whatever lie does, someone could have told him how to do better. And yet, after all, the life of a true minister of the Gospel is the happiest life that can be lived.

div.head: Weak Lungs and Gastritis:
div.p: Weak Lungs and Gastritis:

8 Prince's Road, Richmond, Surrey. Dear Sirs,—lt is 15 years ago since I began taking Angier's Emulsion, on the advice of my doctor. I suffer from weak lungs, coupled with chronic gastritis, and, owing to the delicate state of my stomach, Angier's is the only Emulsion I can retain, although I have tried all other makes. I cannot digest proper meals, frequently taking nothing but milk for weeks, and I don't know what I should do without the Emulsion. I find it especially useful for relieving the racking cough from which I frequently suffer. (Sd.) (Miss) A. RANDALL. ANGlEgks;tiu •

div.head: MATTER SHELVED FOR A TIME.
div.p: MATTER SHELVED FOR A TIME.

The agenda of the Trades and Labour Council on Tuesday evening was of an ordinary char- acter, the only subject calling for a long discus- sion being the resolution of the Gasworkers' and General Labourers' Union. The President, Mr. E. Itandells, presided over a moderate attend- ance.

A letter was read from the Norman Angel League asking permission for one of their speakers to address the Council on the peace question. This was agreed to. and February 26th was fixed as the date. It was also decided that Mr. C. Dukes represent the Council at the Peace Society meeting in the Co-operative Hall on February 19th.

div.head: ANNUAL HOLIDAY QUESTION.
div.p: ANNUAL HOLIDAY QUESTION.

Arising ....t .. a letter received from the Blackpool Town Council, inviting the Trades Council to a conference on the holiday question, a discussion took place as to whether an annual holiday week could not be instituted similar to other towns. Various views-were expressed, and it was ultimately decided that, favourable as the Council were to the subject, it would be wiser to refer the matter to the various unions to con- sider.

div.head: WORKING CLASS REPRESENTATION.
div.p: WORKING CLASS REPRESENTATION.

Whether or not political bodies should be allowed to affiliate with the Council was a ques- tion round which a long discussion ranged. The resolution, which was brought forward by the Gasworkers' and General Labourers' Union, was as follows: "That this Council invite the affilia-. tion of the Independent Labour party and the British Socialist party, with a view of pressing forward working class representation." Several members discussed the question from the trade union standpoint, arguing that as the Council were a body composed only of trade unionists, it was not within their scope to press such an invitation as that conveyed in the reso- lution.

On the other hand, it was stated that as there might be a general clash of arms by the three Parties concerned, and whose objects were much of a similar nature when local representation was considered, it was very imperative that such affiliation be invited.
Ultimately it was decided to indefinitely post- pone the question in order to give the members a further opportunity of studying the subject before coming to a definite decision.

After shelving the Parliamentary representa- tion question for a few months, it was. decided to accept the following notice of motion from Mr. Howard for discussion at the next meeting of the Council: " That a conference of all trade union branches be called to consider the advis- ability of putting forward a candidate at the next general election."

SOUTH AFRICAN STRIKE. Mr. Dukes made a general reference to the South African Labour trouble, and to the tac- tics adopted to suppress- trade unionism in the country. He illustrated the methods which were being used at present in England by opponents of labour, and finally moved the following reso- lution : " That this Council protests 'against the sup- pression of trade unionism in South Africa by public armed force, as violating the elementary rights of citizenship. div.head: LIVELY RUNCORN MEETING.
div.p: A LIVELY RUNCORN MEETING.

" Englishmen " With Foreign Names. There were lively scenes at a Runcorn Tory meeting on Tuesday evening. Viscount Deer- hurst came in for a number of pointed inter- ruptions. Along with-the noble lord was Mr. Jersey de Knoop, the prospective Conservative candidate.

Speaking about Home Rule, the Viscount said the men in the North of Ireland had said that they would not have Home Rule. They had been told by Mr. Tom Wing—(loud applause) that it was all bluff that Ulster would fight. He could assure them that Ulster would fight, and Ulster would be right. lie (the speaker) had been challenged to say a word about their mem- ber, Mr. J. F. L. Brunner. (Cheers.) He was a member of the sect that went to make up the great coalition, and what he (the speaker) chose to call " one of the Little Englanders." It would be disastrous for this great country not to keep up its naval strength. The Radical party might have saved a few pounds. A Voice: "A hundred million pounds." "Yes," said Viscount Deerhurst, "hut they spent now £lO for every one saved then." (Laughter.) A great number of Little Englanders, although they might be nationalised Englishmen, were, perhaps, not Englishmen themselves. Voices: " Oh," and uproar. Continuing, Lord Deerhurst said it was very peculiar when they got a man like Baron de Fores't— Voices : "And Mr. Jersey de Knoop." Who were not born British subjects, they in- variably got them going outside of the Little Englanders, whose only idea was retrenchment. (Loud laughter.)

div.head: ALTERATIONS IN ROCK GARDENS.
div.p: ALTERATIONS IN ROCK GARDENS.

Any alterations intended to be made in this department should be accomplished as soon 'as possible, so that planting may take place before the season is too far advanced. When sharp frost is over, it, may be found necessary to reL duce some of the stronger-growing plants to make room for choicer subjects, such as hardy primulas, which are not grown so much as one might expect, considering their hardy constitu- tion. They will live through a severe winter, provided they have good drainage. Their habit of raising themselves above the surface of the soil renders it necessary to apply a top-dressing of good soil in the autumn.---" The Garden2t

From this enlarged electorate the proportion due to the Tory candidate was 936, whereas lie increased his poll by 737 only. For Home Rule the votes cast increased by 3,269 as compared with the last election. 12,267 votes were cast for Home Rule and 5,564 against, _ _
Hardicker was the only candidate who had the advantage of having previously contested the constituency.
No effort was spared by the Conservatives to whip up the absent and out-voters. One elector was brought from Switzerland to vote for Mr.• Hardicker.

Despite the announcement made by the League Emergency Committee last week that the match with Hull Kingston Rovers, post- poned owing to the recent strike, will be played on the Monday following Easter Monday, we are officially informed that this match at Hull will be played on Easter Monday. Warrington, on the other hand, were rather poorly represented, the absence of the two Browns, Waywell, Naylor and Harmer considerably weakening their ranks. A trial was also being given to a new player, Steel, in the threequarter line—a rather risky experiment against a team of the calibre of Wigan A.

, It- was a poor game, at least as far as the Warringtonians were concerned; in fact, it was the worst exhibition of football I have seen the Combination men give on their own. heath this season. The forwards were completely off their game, and their tackling was poor in the extreme, and at times the speedy threequartere of the opposition were allowed to elude the clutches of man after man. The two most prominent players in this department were Arnold and Critchley, the latter being respon- sible for Warrington's goals.

BROOKES THE LEADING MAN. Brookes and Douglas were up against a smart pair in' Hesketh and Jeavons, but they came out fairly successful. Brookes was one of the most prominent players on the Warrington side, and scored their only try, and had the other players followed his example in the matter of tackling perhaps the •Wiganers would not have been allowed to cress their, lines on four occasions. Douglas at times was apt to hold the ball too long, otherwise he• gave a fairly good display. Among the threequarters Daintith was easily the hardest worker and most useful, player on his side. Lack of support, however, nullified a lot of his work. Steel, who was chosen to play centre, was not a success in that position, and at limes he allowed the "Colliers" to gain a lot of ground and come perilously near scoring. However, when he transferred on to the wing, le shaped much better, and gave flashes of really " brainy" play, and he was the prime mover in the splendid piece of work which led up to Brookes' try. With a little more practice I think he will develop into a useful man. Baker shaped well on the other wing, and in the first half made a great effort to get over on two occasions and had exceedingly hard lines, but Seddon, the Wigan full-back, was the stumbling-block. Brown was only moderate. Jordan did many smart things at full-back, but he is rather slow, and could not be com- pared with Seddon, the visiting custodian. For Wigan, Hesketh scored two tries, and Harry Price one, which he was successful in converting. He also had hard lines when he hit the post from another attempt, after Haigh had scored Wigan's fourth try.

div.head: RYLANDS' STILL ADVANCE.
div.p: RYLANDS' STILL ADVANCE.
N.U. CUP.—Fourth Qualifying Round.

Rylands' Recs. met Firs-lane, at Leigh, last Saturday in the fourth qualifying round of the Cup, before a record crowd for the ground. The home team won the toss and Stretford kicked off against the wind. The home, team returned, and, with the aid of the ' wind, attacked. After 13 minutes' plat, the ball struck Warren in the face and re-bounded in Crank's hands, enabling that player to score under the post. Dooley kicked the goal. Rylands' pressed after this, but could not break through. Half-time arrived with the score : Firs-lane, 1 goal 1 try (5 points); Rylands', nil. Atkinson commenced the second half for the home team, but Rylands' at once proceeded to bombard the home line. Slater grounded under the posts, but was brought back for some in- fringement. A score was not long in coming, however, as the ball travelled to Carter, then to Morris, and back to Carter, who got over. The goal-kick failed. From a pack close in Gallop dropped a goal. From a pass from Carter to Laws, Warren scored, the goal-kick failing. Broadhurst scored the next try, Warren adding the extra points. Firs-lane were now a beaten team and the game ended: Rylands' Recreation. 2 goals 3 tries (13 points); Firs-lane, 1 goal 1 try (5 noints).
The feature of the game was the fine full-back play of P. liorrocks. After the match Firs-lane laid a protest against Laws, Carter and Warren, which failed.

div.head: 1 Warrington Workingmen's Associa:
div.p: 1 Warrington Workingmen's Associa:
N.A. CENTRE.
MEETING OF REPRESENTATIVES.

The Ereshwater Fish Preservatioia League held a meeting at the Nag's Head Hotel, Man- chester, on Saturday, to discuss the question of furthering the cause of the close season for coarse fish. The N.A.A. Emergency Committee were invited to attend, and representatives were present from Bolton, Wigan, Crewe, St. Helens and Preston.

The N.A.A., at the general meeting at Barn- furlong, unanimously decided to observe the close season laid down by the F.F.P.L., and by doing so it will most certainly make matters work more amicably for all concerned. • We understand that by this amalgamation the F.F.P.L. has handed over the deeds of the Leeds and Liverpool Canal to the N.A.A. This alone shows what can be done for the benefit of the angler by associations holding meetings of this kind and making terms with each other, or better still, amalgamating to take over fresh fisheries, and each bearing a share of the cost for stocking. It would be far better for all concerned, and the moneys received from the subscriptions of members could be spent in pro- viding better sport, instead of the high rents at present paid by associations, and these rents must be paid for waters if any society wishes to increase its membership. I can vouch for the Warrington section of the N.A.A. being quite willing to join in any such scheme.

div.head: GOWY.
div.p: THE GOWY.

The unexpected again happened at the Gowy. It was thought that the stream, under the con- ditions, would fish well. It did not. Several members killed fish, but none large enough to go to the board. Several members, it is said, on hearing that a few fish have been taken from certain haunts, race to the spot and fix their rods, so that no other member has a chance of fishing the same haunt, although there is room for both, one at the beginning of the swim, and one at the tail end. There is no rule to stop any person from doing this, but at the same time it is not sport; and at present matters will have to be left to the anglers' sportsmanship who are interested in this matter.

Wilderspool Brewery V. St. Barnabas'. On the Brewery enclosure. The home team put the visitors' goal in danger, and were awarded a free kick for hands against Long, from which the ball was sent over the bar. The visitors' defence were now kept busy and Barnes scored for the Brewers. From the centre kick the game was very fast, and bora teams missed chances by poor shoothig. WIDNES AND DISTRICT ALLIANCE. Ditton St. Mary's v. Stockton Heath. At Ditton. From a long shot towards goal the visitors rushed down, but the home goalie par- tially cleared. Welsby received the ball and sent between the posts and scored for the Heathens. The home team now exerted more pressure on the visitors' goal, and gained a corner, and from the flag kick the scores were made equal. The Saints scored four more goals, and the game ended in a win for the home side by five goals to one.

div.p: ALTPINCHAM AMATEUR CUP. ' First Round.

Oughtrington United v. Latchford. At Beatley. The following players turned out :—Oughtrington United :Burrows; F. Thom- asson and Moss; 11. Thornasson, Kay and Wigan; W. Thomasson, Shaw, Holt, " Curley " Thomasson and Rouse. Latchford: Kite; Has- pell and Carter; Downs, E. Webb and Siddall ; Smith, P. Webb, Lees, Fogg and Tinder. From a goal kick Latchford attacked, and Fogg, gain- ing possession, passed out to Tinder. The latter made tracks towards the home goal, and opened the score after fifteen minutes' play. The home- sters now made a spirited attack at the visitors' end, but could not break down the defence of own lines, where Lees made a passwell out to Tinder, who again converted, jtinuoinaddtsghPie:ed ulitir' Carter and Kite, and were driven back the visitors two goals in front, by which total they led at the interval. Smith made a grand run along the touch line, and finished with a good centre in front of the United's goal, where Tinder eluded the home backs and beaded the ball into the net, Burrows being quite helpless to save. Even play fol- lowed until a good effort by Holt, who trans- ferred to Rouse, caused the visitors' citadel to be besieged, but the 'final shot was wide of the mark. A spell of midfield play followed, and later the United successfully appealed for a penalty for hands against Carter. Thoznanson was entrusted with the kick, and placed the ball in the net out of the reach of Kite. Result : Latchford, three goals; Oughtrington -Mao& one goal.

div.head: FRIENDLY MATCHES.
div.p: FRIENDLY MATCHES.

Grappenhall it-. Wilfrid's v. Higher Walton. At Grappenhall. St. Wilfrid's started and became aggressive, the visiting left hack clear- ing grandly. Watson was prominent with a smart run on the right, his final attempt skim- ming the bar. Davies and Parr got going on the left, and from the first-named player's centre, Richards opened Grappenhall's account. The visiting left wing started a movement and Grappenhall were kept on the defensive until half-time. Interval: Grappenhall, one goal; Higher Walton, nil. The "Saints "-kept the visitors on the defence and from a centre from Watson, Richards in- creased the lead. Grappenhall still kept up the pressure, and Richards, added a ,third. Walton tried hard to reduce -the lead, but the Grappen- hall defence was not to be beaten. Final: Grappenhall, three goals; Higher Walton, nil.

div.head: SHOTS AT GOAL.
div.p: SHOTS AT GOAL.

Spencer, the Excelsior centre-half, is getting goals every week of late. Pritchard, the Excelsior centre-forward, found his lost form with a vengeance last Saturday. Oughtrington United had not lost a matuh on their own ground for three seasons until Satur- day. Then Latchford defeated them by three goals , to none in the Altrincham Amateur Cup tie. Tinder, who is an old Latchford player, is this season the club's emergency man.
He turned out on Saturday as outside left, and scored all the three goals..
Kay. at centre-half, war.3' the best man on the United team. Robinson was not able to turn out owing to illness. .
This caused a wholesale re-arrangement of the Latchford team.
----- Carter proved a worthy deputy for Robinson, and S. Smith and P. Webb were a dangerous pair on the right. Haspell gave a good exhibition of defensive tactics. - • • '
Great Sankey administered the first defeat to the Adult School. Glover, Stephens, and Ilond were fine in defence. -

W. Hunter played an untiring game. "Never say die," was the Adults' motto, but they were up against a better team. Stockton Heath defeated Weston by four goals to none. • Jones, Denny and Smith were the pick of the Heathens. Nancollis saved a penalty kick, taken by IT. Sankey. Molyneux and Aspey played well in their re- spective positions. The final stages of the Stockton Heath and Weston match were chiefly fighting, not foot- ball. • The referee should have been more strict with his ruling. The Excelsiors made their position a strong one at the head of the Second Division. Knight made some clever saves in the home goal. Hatton gave a good exhibition at centre-half. 31illington scored both goals for the Emmanuel Old Boys. Morris, Pritchard and Warburton were the pia of the visitors. Wilderspool Brewery lads have scored their first point. St. Barnabas' were fortunate to get a point. --Vernon, the home full-back, scored for them.
„ Shuttleworth appears to be out of shooting form. _
Stockton Heath Reserve are not making much rTo.e 4 in the Widnes Alliance. m. They have lost on successive Saturdays by 4-1 and 5-I._
_ _ The Fairfield United are to be complimented on their splendid victory over the Divex.

div.head: HOCKEY.
div.p: HOCKEY.

STOCKTON HEATH DEFEAT WESTERN. Stockton Heath were the visitors at the West- ern ground on Saturday, and after a keen game won by six goals against three. Last season Stockton Heath won by seven goals to three.

From the bully Stockton Heath got into the home circle, Bainbridge putting behind. The visitors continued to press, but could not score. From a free hit Western got away, Newton being tested with a hot shot from Fletcher, which he just cleared by putting behind. From the corner Gregson opened the scoring for Western, after 15 minutes. The home team were now playing up strongly. Fletcher adding another after 20 minutes. Play was now very even, until with five minutes to go Ayer got away on the right, and, after a fine run, centred close in, Richardson scoring. From the bully Bainbridge worked through the defence and scored. half-time: Stockton Heath, two goals; Western, two goals.

The second half opened with another fine run, Bainbridge again getting through and scoring. Stockton Heath continued to press strongly, Bainbridge hitting the upright with a hard shot, from which Baxter scored on the re- bound. Western now got going, Watkin scor- ing. The home team continued to play up strongly, but could not add to their score, the centre-half and left wing putting in some fine work. From a corner hit Richardson obtained possession, and passing out to Ayer, the ball was taken into the home circle, Richardson scoring. The visitors now .pressed hard, the home defence conceding several corners in rapid succession, from one of which Richardson even- tually scored. Result: Stockton Heath, six goals; Western, three goals. Stockton Heath are away to-day to Alderley Edge.

div.head: LATCHFORD'S EASY WIN.
div.p: LATCHFORD'S EASY WIN.

Latchford Ist met Southport on the Birkdalel Cricket Ground last Saturday, and the game ended in an easy win for Latchford by 5-1. After the first ten minutes Latchford were com- pletely the better team. Had it not been that they fielded a rather experimental side, which did not combine as well as one would like, the score would undoubtedly have been much bigger. The ground was in fine condition and a fast game seemed in prospect. At first Latchford could not get going, but the initial attacks of Southport were repelled by Pletcher and Wil- kinson. After about ten minutes Latchfor& settled down and the forwards began to show a little more combination. This soon material- ised, for Knight hooked the ball into the net from an awkward position. Several good, passes from his inside forwards sent Pearson between the backs, but twice he hit the goalkeeper and once he was given offside.

The second- half was mostly composed of attacks on the Southport goal, Knight scoring two more goals and Pearson two. The last goal came from a fine burst by Pearson and Isher- wood. Southport scored one goal from a break- away.. _
The home team were best represented by their left full-back, whose lusty work saved his side time after time.

In the first half the Latchford play was rather disjointed, but the second half saw some really good play amongst the forwards. Fletcher, at right-back, was in his best form, and was the outstanding man on the side of the visitors. The second team match was cancelled, owing to Bowdon's inability to raise a full eleven.

div.head: CULT OF CARPET BOWLING.
div.p: CULT OF CARPET BOWLING.

The annual tournament for the Carpet Bowl- ing Championship of England and Wales (held under the auspices of the McGaw Carpet Bowling Association) will take place at Birmingham on Thursday, February 26th. Apart from the cup and gold medals for the winners other handsome prizes are given. Entries close on the 20th inst., and the Honorary Secretary, Mr. A. C. Hills, 13, Cottingham-road, Pen ge, London, S.E., will be pleased to forward full particulars ' to any club upon hearing from them.

div.head: CROSS COUNTRY.
div.p: CROSS COUNTRY.

Warrington A.C. on Saturday had two packs running over a 71; miles course, which provided fast moving, in addition to a nice stretch of Ploughed land. The-junior section started first., and returned with A. Inman leading from G. W. Hunt, G. Bennett, J. Hayes, A. Potts, E. Gib- son, P. W. Price and T. Howliston.

The seniors were led, at a very fast pace, by A. Burgess, who finished nearly 50 yards ahead of W. Bolton, who was clesely followed by C. \Tose, J. Hanson and A. Gregson, then came 11. Jepson, T. Turton, and the others, in close order. Burgess finished strongly, and reprodue- tion of the form shown would make him a force to be reckoned with in the coming champion- ships. Notwithstanding the fast nature of the course Burgess's form was distinctly the best of his fairly long experience.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 7, 1914.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 7, 1914.
GOOD SITOP Wanted, central position.--Rent and particulars to Frank Hickman, Lyme- street, Warrington.
M o n ey .

There were some striking features about medi- cated wines brought to light yesterday at the annual Licensing Sessions for Warrington. ,A representative of the local Temperance party contended that these wines were much worse than ordinary alcohol. He surprised the Court by remarking that even as a temperance man he would prefer to see persons go to the public-house and get honest drink than make use of medicated wines. There were three applications for new licences, and one for alterations of existing premises. All the applications for new licences were refused, and that for alterations granted. The Chief Constable suggested that in future applicants for new licences should be prepared to grant something in return for the privilege.
The Mayor presided at yesterday's annual Licensing Sessions over a full Bench of magis- trates. /

It is very satisfactory, said the Mayor in open- ing the proceedings, to find there were fewei cases of drunkenness. Whilst Warrington is still rather high, compared with other towns, the figures do not give a fair comparison, because circumstances have arisen to show a higher per- centage than was actually the case. As to the conduct of the licensees generally, with one exception, that has been very satis- factory, and the Bench are very well satisfied with the way they have conducted their busi- nesses.

THE CHIEF CONSTABLE'S REPORT. The Chief Constable reported that the licensed houses numbered 187. These figures showed a reduction of two, as compared with those of last year. The population of the borough in 1911 was 72,166, consequently there was one licensed house to every 385.9 inhabitants. During the year four Special Sessions for the transfer of licences were held, at which 26 transfers were granted, alehouses 12, beerhouses `2, beer "off" 12, 14 more than in 1912. With reference to the drunkenness, there is a decrease of 18 in the number of persons pro- ceeded against as compared with the previous year. The figures for the past four years are as follows: 1913, 461 males and 93 females—&s4; 1912, 471 males and 101 females-572; 1911, 477 males and 104 females-581; 1910, 470 males and 114 females-584. Of the 554 persons proceeded against 345 were residents of the borough and 209 strangers to the town.

Drunken Saturday. The days of the week on which drunkenness occurred are as follows: Sunday 77, Monday 58, Tuesday 44, Wednesday 51, Thursday 31, Friday 50, Saturday 231-554. One hundred and two cases occurred in Bridge-street, 37 in Butter- market<street, 32 in Iforsemarket-street, 26 in Winwick-street, 2..1 in Mersey-street, 19 in Bar- bauld-street, 18 in Sankey-street, 14 in Knuts- ford-road, 6 at Market Gate, and 279 in othei thoroughfares and public places in the borough. The actual number of different persons proceeded against was 491, as during the year 30 persons were charged twice each, 7 three times each, 2 four times, 2 five times, and 1 six times. There are 16 clubs registered in the borough. No complaint has been made to the police against them during the year. During the year one licensee was proceeded against as follows: George Eastwood, Crown and Sceptre Inn, Buttermarket-street, for permitting riotou:, conduct upon his licensed premises. Fined £lO and costs on December 9th, 1913. A new tenant has since taken over the licence, and, under the circumstances, I have not deemed it advisable to oppOse the renewal of the licence of the house in question. Nearly 2,000 surprise visits of in- spection were made by the police to licensed pre- mises during the 12 months, and on a few occasions the attention of the licensees had to be drawn to minor irregularities, but generally the houses have been well conducted. ALDERMAN'S APPLICATION GRANTED. Alderman Bolton applied for permission to alter the Royal Exchange, Golden-square, Mr. Longton, on his behalf, said it was proposed to remove the present living accommodation and provide that in a building adjoining. There would be no increase in the area of the licensing accommodation, and the living premises would be cut off from the licensed portion. Although he rather hesitated, said Counsel, at creating such a precedent, Alderman Bolton is prepared to pay over .11.00 to the compensation fund. - - --
--The Chief Constable said that he had no objection. The plans showed an improvement in the house. r .
The magistrates granted permission to alter.

A BREWERY FIRM'S CLAIM. Temperance Party's Successful Objection. Messrs. Cunningham, brewers, asked for an "off beer" licence for their brewery in Owen. street. Mr. Madden, for the firm, said the brewery was not licensed for selling "off," and there was no other brewery in Warrington which had not such a licence. There was no reasonable ground why Messrs. Cunningham should not have similar facilities.

They did a large trade in this part of Lanca- shire amongst people who did not require more than half-a-dozen bottles of beer or stout pm week, and it was for the convenience of the,so half-a-dozen bottlers (laughter) that the licence was sought. The other breweries had licences to sell not less than a dozen, but Messrs. Cunningham did not want such a licence. They were more moderate in asking for one for half-a- dozen. They•had an " off " licence in Frogliall- lane, but that was 11 miles from the brewery, and it inconvenienced people to go there.

shop, the nearest being the Cheshire Cheese at Latchford. The shop would close on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday at nine o'clock, Thurs- day at 1 p.m., and Friday and Saturday at 16 p.m., except on the day before Christmas and Walking Day, when he would ask for an exten- sion to 11 o'clock. No harm could be done in granting the licence. Mr. Batty asked that it be not granted, as there were ample facilities. Applicant, in answer to Mr. Batty, said that most of his customers came from the Cheshire side. He would keep the drink trade apart from his grocery trade, but would not have separate premises.

div.head: LARGE BOTTLED TRADE:_ .
div.p: LARGE BOTTLED TRADE:_ .

Tames 6-1;;;;L-gh;r-a-said his firm did a large bottled trade. When people came to the brewery they could not take the order, and they had to send them to Froghall-lane to leave it. This was a great inconvenience to their custom- ers and hampered their trade. The majority of our customers, he added, are six-bottle people. (Laughter.) Mr. B. B. Batty, who represented the local Temperance bodies, asked if the firm did a good jug trade at Froghall-lane, and the anst‘er was that they did. How many barrels a week do you do?—We don't open on Sundays, and we do two to three barrels.
You would not do a jug trade at the breweryl —No.
Am! never sell less than balf-a-dozen bottles? —No.

NO LICENCE TO tit GlvtN UP./ • Mr. Batty said he understood that if this licence was granted to the brewery the firm would give up the other licence. Mr. White (Magistrates' Clerk): There is no offer to give up a licence. Mr. Batty said that altered the position, and he would have to go on with his case. Why, Mr. Cunningham, should you have dif- ferent treatment from the rest of the brewers?— We want the same as the others have got. The Chief Constable: You made a similar application last year and were refused ?—Yes. Can you tell us any change in circumstances why you should have such a licenceF—ln making inquiries we found similar breweries had been granted licences two years ago. If the magistrates decide to give this licence, are you prepared to give up the licence at 29, Froghall-lane?—lt is my brother's, and I arn not in a position to say. Mr. Batty said that the firm had an "off" licence at Froghall-lane, 300 yards from the brewery.
Mr. Madden: It is a mile away. The Chief Constable: They are both exagger- ating. (Laughter.) I can give the correct dis- tance.
Finally, the Bench refused the application.
NEW APPLICATION REFUSED.
Alfred Wright, grocer, wanted an "off" wine and spirit licence for 727, Xnutsford-road. Mr. A. Browne, for applicant, said that there were no licensed premises near Air. Wright's

div.head: WHY NOT IN CHESHIRE?
div.p: WHY NOT IN CHESHIRE?

The Chief Constable (to applicant): Your Counsel and yourself stated that your customers come across the Swing Bridge?;--Yes. Do you know that the magistrates have noth- ing to do with people in Cheshire?—They arc the most of my customers. Why don't you take a shop in Cheshire and provide for your customers?—No answer wat.- given. The application was refused.

div.head: MEDICATED WINES CILALLENGED.
div.p: MEDICATED WINES CILALLENGED.
Remarkable Statements by the Temperance Counsel.

The most interesting application was the last. In this Oscar Harris, chemist, 747, Knittsford- road, Latchford, applied for a wine licence. Mr. Forshaw appeared in support and Mr. R. B. Batty again opposed the application on behalf of the local Temperance bodies. Mr. Porshaw said it was not an ordinary appli- cation, for they only sought to sell medicated preparations. The law was so absurd on this point that a fully qualified chemist could not sell articles such as medicated wines without being fortified with a licence. The application was a matter of public necessity. Mr. Harris was the only chemist in the district and the nearest chemist was about two miles away—in Bridge-street. It would be grossly unfair to Mr. Harris to refuse the licence. Ho asked the Bench to take a broad view of a case like that.

div.head: ALCOHOL IN MEDICATED WINES.
div.p: ALCOHOL IN MEDICATED WINES.

Mr. Harris, in answer to Mr. Forshaw, said he only wanted to sell medicated preparations. On account of his being unable to sell these pre- parations he believed that he lost custom, be- cause people going into town for the articles would probably buy things there, which other- wise would have been bought at his shop. Mr. Batty: Your advocate says the law is absurd. Is it? Witness; Ask him, he said so.
Mr. Batty: Do you know anything about the alcoholic strength of medicated wines? May I take the average as four times that of ordinary beer? Witness: I have no doubt. _

Mr. Batty: Is it that the law is absurd because it compels people to come before their Worships to ask whether they can sell liquors at four times the strength of beer? Witness : It is a matter of public necessity. Mr. Batty pointed out that Messrs. Boots, Ltd., were the largest body for medical preparations in the world, and they did not sell the articles Mr. Harris was endeavouring to get permission to sell.

Witness: I would like to Boots have not a shop in t. Mr. Batty: That does not ma\ Mr. Batty read several statements said to have been given by prominent medical men, and asked witness if ho agreed with them. He replied that there was some good to be derived from certain medicated wines.

div.head: "HONEST DRINK."
div.p: "HONEST DRINK."
Is it not far better for people who want a drink to walk two or three minutes and get an honest drink?—l do not know.

When they are in a public-house don't they get honest drink?—l do not agree. Do those who publish the insidious notices about the wines know they are much more alcoholised than reported?—Are they? Are you suggesting that the sale of these medical preparations should be encouraged? Is it not safer, wiser and better for people to get what they want in the public-houses?—No. Mr. Batty: I will tell you there is 22 per cent. of alcohol in a certain wine. Dr. Joseph: You are wrong in saying 22 per cent. It is not so much as that. Mr. Batty: I can quote proof of the amount of alcoholic strength. The British Medicti; Association Journal, from analyses, showed it tq be considerably above that. That journal'6 statement is accepted by the medical profession and also in Court, and there are other tuedicated wines even worse.

A DOCTOR'S VIEWS. Dr. Robinson, who said lie practised in Latch- ' ford said be thought the licence should bo granted. He did not see any harm in giving a licence of this kind. If people in the Latchford district wanted these wines they had to go to town for. them. He supposed that was some inconvenience.

- Mr. Batty again quoted opinions, which, he said, had been expressed by prominent medical men. Mr. Batty: Do you agree with what these men say?---I think it is a matter of opinion. Do you?—l think they have their uses. You have seen the advertisements of these wines?—Yes. Is there any truth in them?—They are exag- gerated. Mr. Batty: They are a tissue of lies.

APPLICATION REFUSED. Mr. Batty, addressing the Bench, asked the justices to seriously consider the question of these medicated wines. Dozens of people were continually being led astray by the use of them. He asked the Bench to refuse this application. The Mayor announced that the application would not be granted. The Chief Constable hoped the magistrates would not grant new licences unless some other licences were given in return.
The Mayor announced that the adjourned Sessions would be held on 6th March. The music licence for the Star Kinern Picture House was granted.

div.head: Independent Oddiellows.
div.p: Independent Oddiellows.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Dis• trict of the National Independent Order of Odd- fellows was held on Saturday at the Cattle Market Inn, Warrington. The Grand Master, Bro. Blackshaw, presided, and was supported by D.G.M. Bro. Pennington. There was also a good number of delegates present. The balance sheet showed an increase of _CH over the pre- vious year. There was .290 paid out in 1913 for funeral claims, leaving the district funeral funds worth £475. The auditors, P.P.G.M. Pester and P.G. Crozier, gave their report, which was adopted. The question of being repre- sented at the annual Moveable Committee called for some discussion. This conference is to be held at Norwich in Whit-week. Ultimately the matter was referred back to the lodges for fur- ther consideration. P.P.G.M. Longsliaw pre- sented the retiring* Grand Master, Bro. Black- shaw, with a splendid jewel for services rendered to the district. It was resolved that the D.G.M. Bro. R. Pennington, be the G.M. for the present year. It was also adopted that P.O. Bro. G. Crozier be the D.G.M. for 1914. It was also decided that the present secretary, P.G. Jos. W. , Perry, and treasurer, P.P.G.M. William Pen- nington, retain their positions. P.P.G.M. William Hill undertook the position of placing the regalia upon the newly-installed officers. It was also resolved that the annual bowling main take place as early as possible.

div.head: Pneumonia, Not The Poison.
div.p: Pneumonia, Not The Poison.

At an inquest on Thursday, conducted by Deputy Coroner F. A. Jones, it was stated that the deceased, William Allen Harrop, of 4, Dal- ton-bank, had drunk a quantity of liniment from a blue bottle labelled "poison," whilst he was strange in his manner, but the evidence of the doctor shattered the idea that the deceased had committed suicide, for death was due to double pneumotiia.—Annie Harrop, wife of de- ceased, said her husband was 37 years of age, and was a carter employed by Messrs. Buckley and Co. On January 21 he went home, saying that some bricks had fallen on him. The ser- vices of a doctor were engaged, and he pre- scribed the use of liniment. Deceased became very strange in his manner, and she went for a doctor. On her return she found the house in darkness, and her husband refused her admit- tance, saying he was going to set fire to the house. A man made an entrance and found de- ceased lying across the bed. Harrop was re- moved to the Hospital. Mrs. Harrop saw that the bottle of liniment had been taken from shelf and was almost empty. He kept sayirif "I have done it."—Dr. Smith, the police Bar exarniDa"

"THE FOURTH DEGREE.'' Warrington Buffs Hold a Roll of Honour Exaltation. UNIQUE R.A.0.8. EVENT. For the first time in the annals of modern Buffaloism in Warrington the 4th Degree, or the Roll of Honour Exaltation, took place at the head- quarters of the "Tom Sangster" Lodge (No. 1,418), Bridge-street. Over 200 members of the Order assembled to witness the unusual cere- mony, and these came from Manchester, Liver- pool, Runcorn, St. Helens, Widnes, Frodsham, Earlestown. Lymm and Southport. The first part of the programme was the regalia visits, and a splendid array of the differ- ent artistical chains made a vivid picture. The name's of the lodges were: "Duke of Con- naught," Manchester; the combined lodges of Warrington; "Sir Gilbert Greenall " Lodge, Daresbury ; the Lymni Lodge; the Widnes lodges; Runcorn " Knights of the Golden Horn" (übique encampment), and the Knights Chapter of the Lancashire, Cheshire and Isle of Man Province, and Manchester Knights Chapter. The Exalting Officer (the "Right Honourable Sir" W. B. Rawson) was next admitted to the exalting chamber, followed by his numerous officers, who were as follow: Sponsors, Bro. S. Gray. KISSING ON THE STAGE. "I ought," says Maurice Farkoa, in the February Number of "The Patrician," "to know something about 'Kissing on the Stage,' because I have been kissing since 1895, when I made my music-hall debut in 'An Artist's Model,' produced at Daly's Theatre. It was my lot then to make love as a Frenchman to Miss Louie Pounds. On that occasion my laughing song made such a hit that I have never looked back since. A full list of the different types of lover I have played in my time, and the pretty actresses' to whom I have had to make love would probably allow an ingenious mind with a taste for figures to build up an interesting computation as to the number of kisses that I have contributed for the public amusement. What a list it is! Where could I find prettier actresses to whom to make love or cleverer actresses in the art of making love on the stage seem real? A vainer man than myself might feel conceited Over the experience. Take the list again: Ethel llaydon, Marie Tempest, Florence Collingbourne, Edna May, Evie Greene, Hilda Moody, Zena Dare, Delia Mayne, Lily Elsie, Denise Orme, Isabel Jay, Constance Dreyer, Mabel Sealby."

MANIKIN TO MARQUISE. The wildest dreams inspired by the perusal of threepenny novelettes appear to have come true in the case of Minna, erstwhile manikin, maid of all work, barefoot dancer, and now the Mar- quise de Villevert, who was acquitted'at Berlin on a charge of stealing from a tailor who had emPloyed her in her days of poverty as a mani- kin. After a life full of adventure, in which alternately she had skilly and caviar, Minna appeared on the Paris and London variety stages as a barefoot dancer, finally winning the heart and hand of the Marquis de Villevert, who mar- ried her in London. On his death be left her and her two children handsomely provided for. The Marquise was arrested while visiting her mother at Zerbst, but the Court acquitted her as stated above.
